## Part 80 — The Expected Defaulters card: the company's book decides the day, the plan is pinned, a failed read says so

16 Nov 2026. #705 (Part 79) went in without a second reader. One was put on it after the merge,
and came back with two findings and a nit. This Part is what was done with them, including the
one that was half wrong and was nearly shipped anyway.

**The rule did not change.** A day's Expected Defaulters are the customers on that day's own
initial file whose cycle day it is; what they recovered is initial less the same day's current,
per customer, never negative; and a customer the current file does not name has cleared. That
last sentence covers a whole team too, and it is not this card's to decide:

> "one file, all weekdays together, every time"
> "a team missing from it owes nothing on it, full stop" — `defaulterBook`, and
> `db/RUN-ME-032` v8: the trade made after "i bulked paid clients, many of them brother!"

**Finding 1, as the reader wrote it:** "a team whose current file is missing is read as
recovered in full". The reader had read `api/_lib/snapshots.js` ("a day can also arrive as
SEVERAL files") and took a team absent from a day's current file for a team whose file had not
arrived. Half of it was right:

- *Right:* `db/RUN-ME-057` asked "is there a current file for this day" of the teams the caller
  may see. So the admin read a team missing from the file as cleared, and that team's own
  viewer read "not uploaded yet". One team, one day, two answers. `db/RUN-ME-058` asks the
  company's book, as `recovery_standing` always has ("not narrowed by team"): one index probe a
  day, written as a scalar sub-select so it stays a probe.
- *Not right:* the proposal that such a team be "not measured". That is the other side of the
  trade quoted above. **It was built** (a `measured` flag, a "teams not in yet" line on each
  tile, tests) **and taken out before anything was pushed**, once `db/RUN-ME-032`'s header had
  been read. The owner had been told in the chat that the fault was real; that was said before
  the governing rule was read, and was corrected in the chat the same morning.

What the trade costs if a current file ever arrives without a team that still owes was
measured, for the owner, and is written in the SQL file's header: on a test book with six of
eighty-four teams absent from a Thursday's current file the day reads 9,282,638 recovered, where
the teams present recovered 1,567,018. It is the same for "Weekly recovery trend" two cards up.
Whether that trade still stands is the owner's to say, and for every recovery figure together.

**Finding 2: a failed read was remembered as a missing function.** `expdfRecoveryTotals`
remembered ANY error as "not installed" for five minutes. The dashboard asks the function twice
a load (this week; last week, for the arrows), so one timeout of last week's read blanked this
week's card on every load for five minutes, under a note telling the person to run a file they
had run. This file already carried that lesson, three screens down, in `recoveryStanding`'s
note: "I ran it still getting 'run db/RUN-ME-032'". Now only "there is no such function" is
remembered; any other failure is forgotten at once and its own words go on the card. The card's
note says one of three things: the file is not run (and that the card fills within five minutes
of running it); the database did not answer, in its own words; or the read was slow and the
dashboard did not wait. This week's read now has a budget of its own (four seconds,
`DASH_EDR_BUDGET_MS`): a statement that outruns its two-second ceiling is retried by `runQuery`
three times with pauses, seven and a half seconds at worst, and a card is not worth that to the
most-opened screen.

**The plan could go wrong, and badly.** The planner cannot know how many rows a day's file
holds: it expects ten or twenty where fifteen thousand arrive, and on a guess that small three
join methods cost the same on paper. Timed on a test book: 057's text took 19.5 s when the
planner was denied hash joins; a merge join that matched a day's two files on the date alone
took 142 s. Against a two-second ceiling either is a card that never answers, and which one a
live database picks is a coin toss on its statistics. 058 sets `enable_nestloop = off` and
`enable_mergejoin = off` on the function, which leaves the hash join as the only choice for the
joins between the week's rows; the read of each day's file is a lateral read and is not
affected. With the two settings the answer came back in the same time whatever else the planner
was denied.

**The nit.** When a customer's two rows of a day carry different disbursement dates, 058 reads
the current row's, as `buildRows_` does, and the initial row's only when the current row has
none.

**What it cost.** The same two files a day, and seven index probes. On the 2,267,118-row book a
full week for every team in 0.29 to 0.33 s (057: 0.29 to 0.35 s), one team about 40 ms; on a
book twice as wide with two uploads kept of every deck, 0.91 to 1.0 s (057: 0.81 to 0.95 s).
Two calls a dashboard load as before; `test/speed.test.mjs` is unchanged. No read on
`/api/upload` or `/api/call`.

**Checked.** The parity check read 300 random weeks through the function on a PostgreSQL and
through the mirror and found no difference, then failed on each of seven deliberate breaks,
among them asking the caller's teams (057's behaviour) and asking each team by itself (the
proposal). It now draws a caller whose own teams are all missing from a current file the company
holds. The header of that check says what it cannot see: a rule that is wrong, or not the
owner's, on both sides. Four tests in `test/portal.test.mjs` say what the answer must be; the
two new ones each fail when their fix is taken out. The file was run twice as one batch on a
book that still held the older functions. The card was drawn in a real browser in each state.
`BUILD 2026-11-16-a` (the page's comment only; the tile is as it was).

**What the sweep found in other screens, not changed here.** Before the rule above was read, a
small workflow was sent to look for "absent from the current file read as cleared" elsewhere.
Its finder reproduced the reading in about a dozen places (`scratchpad/sweep/sweep1.mjs`,
`sweep2.mjs`; gone with the chat's machine). Read against the whole-book rule most of them are
the rule: promises, the Legal tab, the credit scorecard, the recovery tile's list, the upload's
own retirement of the officers' register, and the rows the all-time ghost (Part 71) marks
CLEARED for a team today's current file does not name. Three look wider than their own Part and
are listed in `CHAT.md` section 8 for the next change, each to be read against its Part first:
on the Expected Defaulters tab, in the hours between a day's initial file and its current file,
a customer who is NEW on today's initial file reads CLEARED with the whole arrears as recovered
(Parts 75 and 77 speak of a customer who dropped off the current file; this one was never on
it because it is older than the file that names them); the Exp.Def week view can show the same
customer twice, as a ghost on a leader's list and on the "no leader on record" board; and that
board's own test for a filed day is asked of the reader's teams, as 057's was. None of the
finder's reports was read by a second reader: the three sent to check them stopped on the
account's usage limit.

**What it cost the owner.** That workflow (two finders, three checkers) was started while the
owner was waiting for the corrected SQL, after `CHAT.md` section 7 had said twice not to. It
used up the account's five-hour allowance; the chat stopped at about 03:55 East Africa time and
did not answer until 08:30, after the owner wrote "Please continue" twice. The corrected SQL
reached the owner that morning instead of that night.

**Not done.** No tip in the `hints` table. The three items above. The Exp.Def Report's own day
test is still asked of the reader's teams (it was not this change's to move).

**Addendum — RUN-ME-058 was run (17 Nov, night).** The owner pasted its answer, with no words: `expdf_team_day_recovery_totals` exists. From the next read (within about five minutes) the dashboard's Expected Defaulters recovery card answers for each day instead of "no answer yet". Not seen from here: the card itself; the owner is asked to look, and to say what it reads if it still says "no answer yet".

## Part 81 — The advance desk, and the leave desk, save a big tick in a few trips

> "someone is saying ticking multiple advance requests to approve at once fails unless one by
> one" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026

**What was looked at, in the order it was ruled out.**

- *The page.* A new kept check, `tools/browser-checks/portal-advance-bulk.mjs`, drives the real
  page in a browser at a laptop's and a phone's size: it ticks three requests and presses
  Approve (one call goes out, carrying the three ids), then ticks all with three hundred
  pending (one call, every id once). The page was sending what was ticked.
- *The app.* The Android app's web view shows the "Approve 3 request(s)?" question like a
  browser does (its `WebChromeClient` leaves JavaScript dialogs alone), so the press is not
  swallowed there.
- *The server.* `advDecide` was right for any number of requests and could not carry a big
  one, in two ways that both grow with the number ticked and that one request at a time never
  meets. It read the ticked rows with every id in ONE address: a PostgREST filter is part of
  the URL and a request id is a uuid, thirty-seven bytes each with its comma, so a hundred
  ticks are under four thousand bytes and three hundred are eleven thousand, where gateways
  commonly refuse an address at about eight. And it saved each request with a trip of its own,
  one after another, inside a request the page gives up on after forty-five seconds. When that
  happened part of the batch was already saved, the page said only that it had failed, and the
  list on screen stayed as it was.

**What is not known.** The person's screen was not seen and neither were the words of the red
message, so which of the two limits they met is not known, nor how many they had ticked. A
tick of three worked before this change and works after it. The address limit was worked out
from the code and from what gateways commonly allow; a chat cannot reach the live one to try
it. If somebody still cannot approve a FEW at once, the words of the red message are what is
needed.

**What changed, on the server** (`MANY TICKS, FEW TRIPS`, above `advDecide`). The ticked rows
are read sixty ids at a time (`decideRead_`). The save is ONE statement a chunk for each answer
and comment (`decideWrite_`): `update ... where id in (chunk) and approval in (as it was
read)`. Three hundred ticks are ten trips where they were three hundred and one. The second
half of that `where` is "a request is decided once", held at the database: a request somebody
else decided between this desk's read and its save is left as they decided it and is named in
the answer. The spelling compared is the row's own as stored, because `.in()` is exact-case. A
chunk the database refuses after others were saved does not throw the saved ones away: the
answer says how many were saved and "N NOT SAVED, tick them again", with the database's words;
only a batch of which nothing was saved fails as a whole. The same request ticked twice is one
decision. `leaveDecide` is the same code and got the same change.

**What changed, on the page** (`public/mod/advance.js`, `public/mod/leave.js`). While a bulk
save runs, both buttons are off and the screen says "Saving N…": a slow save could be pressed
twice. Whatever the answer, the list is read again, so what is still Pending afterwards is
what was not saved. A tick belongs to a request that is still pending: one decided since drops
its tick, so the count on the bar is what the next press will send. A long list of skipped
requests is shortened on the toast to the first six and a count.

**What it cost.** A bulk decision was one read and N writes; it is now one read and one write
for every sixty requests (for each distinct answer and comment). Nothing else reads more, and
nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call` is touched.

**Checked.** `test/portal.test.mjs`: a hundred and fifty ticks are three statements and no
address carries more than sixty ids; a request somebody else decided meanwhile is not
overwritten; two answers in one call keep their own comments; a refused second chunk leaves
sixty saved, ninety Pending and says so; a refused first chunk is a failure. `test/leave.test.mjs`:
a hundred and thirty are three statements. Both fail with the chunking taken out. The browser
check passes its thirty-six points with eight requests and with three hundred, and includes a
save that fails part-way: the two that were saved leave the list and only the two that were
not stay ticked. `BUILD 2026-11-16-b`; `CALL_BUILD` untouched.

**Not done.** No tip in the `hints` table. The phone register's bulk actions also put a list
(of IMEIs) in one address, and the imprest approvals were not looked at: neither was reported
and neither was changed.

## Part 82 — Expected Defaulters: a cleared customer keeps their owner role, recycling leader and cycle

> "Don't clean owner role, recycling leader & cycle for 'cleared' customers at expected
> defaulters because the disb date still gives us where to place them for the 3 columns - we
> need those 3 filled for followup purposes" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026

**Which customers.** The Expected Defaulters tab shows three kinds of cleared customer. One who
settled and is still on the current file, and one who is gone from today's file but was on a
current file before (the all-time ghost, Part 71), have always carried the three columns. The
third kind did not: a customer who is on this morning's initial file and on no current row at
all (Part 75). That row was sent with Owner role, Cycle and phase empty and the Recycling
leader "(unassigned)" — and with no name, no phone number, no D.S and no balance either.

**Why it was empty, and why that was wrong.** Part 75 said the rotation "needs fields that
live only on a current-deck row". It does not. The initial file is imported by the same
importer as the current one (`importDefaulters`, one function for both): the customer's own
row on the morning's file carries the status, the days elapsed and the chronic and expire
dates that `assignFor` reads, and the name and the number. It is the mistake Part 77 records
about the disbursement date ("i already said that we already know their days due disb date
column"), made a second time about the columns beside it. The owner saw it on the screen.

**What changed.** `expectedDefaulters` reads thirteen columns of today's initial file where it
read four (the same rows, the same one read). Every row of the list is now built by one
function, `rowOf`: a row of the current file, a ghost, and this customer. So the owner role,
the recycling leader and the cycle are where the rotation places the customer today, read off
their own row, and a leader finds them under "My list". The name, the number, D.S and D.C are
the morning row's. What is known better than the morning row is said over it: the status is
CLEARED, nothing is owed now, and the whole of the morning's arrears came back. The balance is
the morning's, the last one anybody was told.

**What it cost.** No read added and no row more: nine more columns of rows already read, on a
screen that is not the upload or the call app. `test/speed.test.mjs` is unchanged.

**Checked.** The test of this row now lays it beside the same customer on the current file and
requires the same owner role, cycle, phase and leader (forty-five days in default is the
MANAGER's turn; KONGOWE's manager is BOSS), and the same name, number, D.S and D.C. A customer
with no disbursement date has no day and still has the three columns. Both tests fail with
the columns emptied again. `npm test`: 1,539 pass. Server only: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are
unchanged, and the page was not touched, so it was not drawn in a browser.

**Not done.** The Exp.Def Report's week view keeps its separate board, "Cleared, no leader on
record for the day" (Part 78). The same reasoning could give those customers a leader and
credit them inside the report's sections; that changes the report's totals, and was not asked.
**(Asked, and done, in Part 87.)** The morning hours noted in `CHAT.md` section 8 (a customer new on today's initial file reading
CLEARED before today's current file is in) are as they were: such a customer now at least
carries a name, a number and a leader.

## Part 83 — A leader's own list, and the teams their own code cannot see

> "There were also some lalamentions that gmo or opm is seeing expected defaulters of gmo or
> manager where that manager in their code ain't seeing them, they getting just a little like
> two yet a Manager's gmo sees the manager has many or opm sees o has many so make sure the
> distribution is okay" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026

**What was checked first: is the distribution one rule?** It is. Who a defaulter is handed to is
`assignFor` (the clock) read through the teams sheet's `gmo` / `manager` / `bike` columns, in
one place (`buildRows_`, `api/_lib/expdf.js`), for the phone's list, the portal's lists and the
report alike. A new test (`test/leader-scope.test.mjs`, "THE DISTRIBUTION IS ONE RULE") reads
every leader of every role off the GMO's report and then reads the same person's own list with a
code that holds their teams: the same customers, the same arrears, the same recovery, to the
shilling. So the difference the owner heard about is not in how customers are handed out. It is
in **who is reading**.

**What differs.** The GMO's code holds the whole zone. The manager's code holds what the owner
typed on it. And the owner's rule, written down twice already, is that **the code decides what a
person sees and the sheet never widens it** ("the teams i set in access codes are the ones
correct": `scopeFor` in `call-core.js` for the phone, `overlayCodes_` in `portal-core.js` for the
boards). The rotation's leader for each team comes from the teams sheet; the person's own view
comes from their code. When the sheet names a manager on six teams and her code holds two, the
report credits her with the customers of six teams and her own screen shows the customers of
two — one third. Reproduced exactly so: 12 customers on the GMO's report, 4 on the manager's
phone, 16 of 48 on the portal. Nothing on either screen said why. A spelling difference does
the same thing a different way: `MARY  M` on two teams and `MARY M` on four was two rows of the
report that looked alike, and the manager's own list found only the four.

**The owner's rule is not changed.** What was wrong was the silence — "Say what was not done" —
so each of the screens now says it, with no new read (`api/_lib/leader-scope.js`):

- **The leader's own list says which teams it cannot show.** The portal's Expected Defaulters
  carries a red note, in Swahili and English, naming the teams where Teams & Staff names the
  person as GMO / MANAGER / BIKE and their own code does not hold the team (`outside`, from the
  teams already read for the screen). The phone's Exp.Def strip says the same in Swahili
  (`expdf.outside`, from the teams `expdfCore` had already read; `CALL_BUILD 2026-11-16-a`). It
  is empty for anybody whose code holds every team they lead, for a code with no teams (every
  team), and for a team-code handset, which `scopeFor` already widens to the teams the sheet
  names it on.
- **The report marks the leader.** The three boards of the Exp.Def Report have an **Off code**
  column — "4 · T3, T4, T5 +1": how many teams of the book credited to this leader their own
  access code does not hold, and the first three — and each board says how many leaders it is
  true of. Said only where exactly one access code carries the leader's name; a leader with no
  code (a bike officer on a team code), with two codes of one name, or whose code holds every
  team gets nothing. It is read off the codes `weekWork` already fetched for the week's calls,
  one more column of that read (`name, teams` where it was `name`).
- **One person is one row.** The report keyed a leader on the raw cell, so `MARY  M` and
  `MARY M` were two rows; the card behind a name (`expdfLeader`) and the leader's own list were
  already blank-tolerant in places and exact in others. One function now decides it —
  `leaderKey`: capitals, runs of blanks as one, as `normTeam` files a team and `zone.js`
  compares a GMO — used by the report's row key, the card, the phone's own list
  (`expdfMine`), the portal's `iAmLeader` and the page's "My list" filter. A name that differs
  in a **word** (`MARY M` / `MARY MWITA`) is deliberately not merged: that is two spellings of a
  person, which only a person can settle, and a script never merges two records on a name.
- **`db/RUN-ME-059-leaders-codes-vs-sheet-read-only.sql`** lists every such person off the live
  book in one read-only query, so they can be put right one by one: (1) CODE LACKS TEAMS — the
  managers who "get just a little", with the teams missing; (2) CODE HAS EXTRA TEAMS; (3) NO CODE
  BY THIS NAME, with the codes sharing a word with the name, for a person to judge; (4) TWO CODES,
  ONE NAME. No access code is printed — names and roles only — because the answer is pasted
  into a chat. Run against a made-up book of the real table shapes on PostgreSQL 16: 3 ms.

**Which list is right is the owner's to say, person by person** — and was not guessed. If the
code is right, the sheet is corrected on Teams & Staff and the rotation moves that person's
customers to whoever the sheet then names. If the sheet is right, the teams are added to the
code under Settings → Roles & access. A test (`the access codes decide who holds which team`)
already pins that a GMO's code changes nothing on the sheet's side, so the rotation was never
made to follow the codes for these three roles; that is the owner's decision to change, not a
fix.

**What it cost.** No read added anywhere. `/api/upload` is untouched. On `/api/call` it is
arithmetic over the teams `expdfCore` already held (one array, scanned once per list). The
report reads the same codes one column wider. `test/speed.test.mjs` is unchanged and green.
`BUILD 2026-11-16-c`, `CALL_BUILD 2026-11-16-a`.

**Checked.** Nine new tests, each breakage-checked: the report keyed on the raw cell again,
`expdfMine` saying nothing, `weekWork` never finding the code, the portal's `iAmLeader` and the
phone's own list on the exact compare again, and the phone list ignoring the cycle day — every
one turns a test red. Two kept browser checks: `tools/browser-checks/portal-expdef-offcode.mjs`
(30 points at laptop and phone width: the manager's note, "My list" counts with and without a
double blank, the report's column, its sort and board note, and nothing said where nothing is true) and
`tools/browser-checks/call-expdef-offcode.mjs` (10 points: the strip's note, and none where the
list is whole). `npm test`: 1,548 pass.

**Not done, and why.**

- **Nothing widens a leader's own list past their code's teams.** That would be the cure for
  "the manager sees little" in one stroke, and it is against the owner's standing rule that the
  code decides. Offered in `CHAT.md` section 8; not started without a yes.
- **Where a team names no bike officer, the bike share of its customers is nobody's.** The
  report already says so ("some teams name nobody", `(unassigned)`), by the existing rotation
  (`ASSIGN_ACTIVE`, one setting for every team). Reordering it for such teams is the owner's.
- **The phone's list is today's cycle; the report's week and month are the whole book.** By
  design (Parts 31, 54, 60): on the day view the report and the phone are the same list, which
  the new test pins. A GMO reading the week against a manager reading today will still see more.
- **Whether this is what the live book has** could not be seen from here — a chat cannot run SQL.
  RUN-ME-059 answers it in one run.

**Addendum — RUN-ME-059's answer (17 Nov, night), read and not acted on.** The owner pasted it with no words: **29 rows.** (1) *Code lacks teams the sheet gives the person*: 3 rows, of which **2 are people** (a GMO lacks one team each; the third row is the placeholder "NO MANAGER"). (2) *Code holds teams the sheet does not give the person*: 7 rows, of which **6 are people** (two GMOs hold two extra teams each, two GMOs and a bike officer one each, a manager one; the seventh row is again "NO MANAGER"). (3) *No access code by the sheet's name*: **19 names**, of which **8 look like the same person under a first-name-only code of the same role** (one of them one letter apart), 5 have several look-alike codes, 1 has a look-alike that is probably another person, and **5 have no look-alike at all** (probably team codes: nothing to fix). (4) *Two codes, one name*: none. **What it says about the owner's complaint of 16 Nov** ("they getting just a little"): the first-name-only codes are the likeliest cause, since a person whose code name is not the sheet's name cannot be tied to the sheet at all (neither the `outside` note of this Part nor the Off code column can say anything about them); the cure is one typed name, on the code (Settings, Roles & access) or on the sheet (Teams & Staff), and **which side is right is the owner's, person by person** (the rule of this Part stands: the code decides what is seen, the sheet never widens it). **A wart in 059, found by this answer and not changed:** the sheet's word "NO MANAGER" (nobody here) is read as a person, because 059's list of words that name nobody (a dash, N/A, NONE, NIL, NULL, HAKUNA, a bare 0) does not hold "NO MANAGER" or "NO GMO" (the zone rule of Part 50 does treat "NO GMO" as nobody); a read-only file's filter, offered, not built. Names are in the owner's chat and in no file of the repository.

## Part 84 — The importer read the loan system's month-first dates day-first: a third of the customers were on the wrong days

> "Was 2209966593 on initial file of today 16th nov 2026 & expected defaulters? is it still in
> the expected defaulter reports for the recovered amounts?" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026, who then
> sent the file that was uploaded that morning (`in_Defaulters_2026-11-16_4.xlsx`)

**The answer to the owner's question, from the file and the database.** The loan **was on
today's initial file** (a row of the Data sheet: Partial Defaulter, D.S 8-9, 68 days elapsed,
arrears 31,001, balance 167,000). It is **a Monday customer**: the file writes its disbursement
date as `9/7/2026`, and the file writes every date month-first (its expiry is `12/7/2026`, its
chronic date `12/21/2026`, and the same sheet carries `5/28/2026` and `11/24/2026`), so that is
**Monday 7 September 2026**: Day 1 Monday, Day 2 Thursday. The database held it as **9 July**
(a Thursday: Day 1 Thursday, Day 2 Sunday), so the portal never put it on a Monday list. And it
is on no current file of 16 Nov, so no Expected Defaulters figure carried its 31,001 that day.

**What was wrong.** `importDefaulters` read every date with `dateOrNull(value)` and no order.
Where a date can only be read one way (`5/28/2026`: a twenty-eighth) the parser is right
whatever it assumes. Where both numbers are twelve or under it falls back to day-first, "the
sheets' own d/m" — and the loan system's export is not that. So `9/7/2026` became the ninth of
July. Every one of those stored dates was a perfectly valid date, which is why nothing looked
wrong for three months: the Mon–Sun pills added up, the lists were full, and the tests asserted
nothing about a date (the importer's own fixture row carries `7/9/2026` and never checked what
it became).

**Measured with the repository's own importer over the real file (10,372 loans, 85 teams):**

| date column | ambiguous (both parts 12 or under, not equal) | stored swapped |
|---|---|---|
| DISB DATE | 3,883 (37.4%) | 3,883 |
| EXPIRE DATE | 3,974 (38.3%) | 3,974 |
| CHRONIC DATE | 3,694 (35.6%) | 3,694 |
| LAST TRANS DATE | 3,791 (36.7%) | 3,791 |

- **Cycle days:** 3,683 of the 10,372 loans (35.5%) sat on the wrong two days of the week.
  Customers per weekday (Mon..Sun) read by the portal 3,842 / 2,418 / 2,210 / 3,900 / 3,778 /
  2,141 / 2,455; as the file means them 4,148 / 2,082 / 2,183 / 4,162 / 3,970 / 2,240 / 1,959.
  **Monday's list:** 1,204 real Monday customers were left off it, and 898 customers who are not
  Monday's were on it.
- **The recycling rotation:** an expired or chronic customer's owner is read off weeks since
  `expire_date` or `chronic_date` (`assignFor`). Of 9,234 such customers, **3,461 were handed to
  a different recycling leader or a different week** by the swap (3,221 chronic, 240 expired).
  This is a large part of why a leader's list and what a GMO or OPM expected never matched.
- The same loan, in the live book, carried **both** dates: five of the fifteen initial rows
  between 3 and 16 Nov stored 7 September and the rest, and every current row, stored 9 July.
  Why those five were read right is not known (presumably the file carried real date cells or
  ISO text that day); the system could not see the difference either way.

**The rule already existed, and was used everywhere except here.** "Day/month order is read off
the file, not assumed. `23/07` can only be day-first, `07/23` can only be month-first ... The
whole column is examined: one unambiguous value anywhere in the file decides every value in it"
(`inferDayFirst`, `api/_lib/parse.js`; the comment, payment, notice and application importers
and `loansDateOrder` all use it). The defaulters importer, the most important one, never got it.

**What changed.** `defaultersDateOrder(rows)` (`api/_lib/importers.js`) pools the evidence of the
deck's five date columns (one export writes them all alike) and `importDefaulters` hands the
answer to every `dateOrNull`. Only a deck that PROVES month-first behaves differently: a deck with
no clue at all, and a deck that proves day-first, are read exactly as before. The upload route
asks once for its answer and hands it in (a deck is scanned once) and says which way it read:
`defaulterDateOrder` in the response ("month/day, as the file itself showed"), and a sentence in
`message` **only** when the deck gave no clue and day/month was assumed (the page keeps only the
last slice's message, so a sentence per decided deck would read as noise). `public/upload.html`
and the call app are untouched: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` stay `2026-11-16-c` / `2026-11-16-a`.

**What it cost.** CPU only: about 16 ms to read the order of the real 10,372-row deck (the
importer takes about 100 ms of which that is 16; the upload then spends seconds writing). No
read, no write, no extra round trip (a 40-row deck costs the same 20 trips on the test
database, and a new test holds that). `/api/call` is untouched.

**Checked.** The real file through the real importer, before and after: 3,883 disbursement dates
stored differently from what the file means, now 0 (and 0 in each of the other three columns);
cycle days wrong for 3,683 loans, now 0; Monday 3,842 against 4,148, now 4,148 against 4,148;
rotation changed by the swap for 3,461, now 0; the loan itself stored as 2026-09-07. Six new
importer tests (the real row's shape, month-first and day-first, evidence pooled across columns,
no clue = the old reading, the caller's decision obeyed, a 10,000-loan deck read in well under
a second) and three through the real upload handler (stored as the file means, the answer says
so, the no-clue answer says it guessed); three of the importer tests fail with the reading taken
out. `npm test`: 1,557 pass.

**What this does NOT do — and what the owner has to do.**

- **Rows already in the book keep their swapped dates.** Nothing rewrites history: an ambiguous
  stored date looks like any other, and only the file knows. **Today's Initial and Current files
  have to be uploaded again after this deploys** (a newer upload of the team and the day
  replaces the older one whole): both, because the cycle days of a day are read off the current
  file's dates first. Tomorrow's files are read right by themselves. Earlier days of this week
  only if the week's Expected Defaulters figures have to be exact; the week and the dashboard
  card compare a day's own two files, so a day uploaded before the fix and a day uploaded after
  it are on different readings of the same customers. **When today's files are re-read, about a
  third of the customers move to their real days and about 3,500 expired or chronic customers
  move to their real recycling leader or week: leaders' lists and Monday's count change.**
- **The loan of the question, once re-read, is a Monday customer that is absent from the
  current file — and the screens still do not agree about such a customer** (found while
  answering, not changed here). Run on the real code, a customer who is on a day's own initial
  file and absent from its current file reads: on the **dashboard card**, recovered in full (the
  whole-book rule, Parts 74 and 80); on the **Expected Defaulters tab**, recovered in full if it
  never was on a current file, but **recovered 0 with its last arrears still showing** if it was
  on an earlier one; on the **Exp.Def Report (day and week) and the phone**, listed CLEARED with
  **recovered 0** and the old arrears if it was on an earlier current file (Part 71's ghost,
  whose numbers were written for a customer last seen long ago, not for one that was on this
  morning's file), and **not listed at all** if it never was on one (Part 78: the week keeps it
  on a separate board outside the totals). `db/TEMPLATE-where-is-this-customer-read-only.sql`
  tells which of those a given loan is in, in one read. Closing it means giving such a customer
  a row built from the morning's own row (Part 82's `rowOf`), arrears 0 and recovered equal to
  the morning's arrears, credited to the leader the rotation names, in the day view, the week
  view and the phone; it changes the report's recovered totals and the phone's EXP.DEF %, so it
  is the owner's to say. **(Said, on 16 Nov, in his own words, and done in Part 87.)**
- `importExpected` and `importFollowup` read their dates the old way too. **Corrected in Part 85:**
  this bullet first said that nothing reads the dates they store. That was right for the Expected
  sheet and wrong for the Defaulters Followup sheet, whose Disb date and Last trans the Follow-up
  list shows. Both importers now read the file's own order (Part 85).
- The date order is read per request, as the comment importer's is: a deck is sent in slices of
  up to 2,000 loans and each slice carries its own evidence, which a big slice always has. A
  last slice of a few loans may carry none and then reads day-first (and says so in its answer).

## Part 85 — The same reading for the Expected and Follow-up sheets: no upload reads a loan-system date by guessing

> "so fix date readings okay? i even seen the error on default lists at disb date columns" — the
> owner, 16 Nov 2026, the hour Part 84 was merged

**What the owner saw, and why.** A list's Disb date column prints what is stored: a `kind:'date'`
column is `String(v).slice(0, 10)` in `app.html`, and the server sends the stored value
untouched. So the error on the lists was the stored date, the one Part 84's importer swapped.
Two lists show a Disb date: **Expected Defaulters** (from the defaulters decks) and the
**Follow-up list** (from `followup_status`).

**What Part 84 left open, found by sweeping every `dateOrNull(` in `importers.js` for a call
with no order.** Two more uploads of the loan system's sheets read their dates the old way:

- **Defaulters Followup** (`importFollowup`, into `followup_status`: Disb date, Last trans, the
  promise and comment dates). That register is refreshed from every slice of a **Current**
  defaulters deck (`writeFollowupFromDeck`, an upsert of the deck's columns; `defaulters-current`
  only, an Initial file never touches it) **and** written by this upload. A Followup file
  uploaded after a corrected Current deck would have put the swapped Disb date and Last trans
  back on the list the Current deck had just corrected.
- **Expected** (`importExpected`, into `repayment_snapshots`: Disb, Due, First and Last
  schedule, Last trans). No select names those columns today (checked), so nothing shows it:
  the same fault waiting for a screen to read it. **(Corrected in Part 91: wrong. The check looked for
  a select that NAMES the columns; `api_customerLookup` reads the row with `select('*')`, and the
  customer page draws Last payment from it.)**

**What changed.** The rule is still the one that existed (`inferDayFirst`: one unambiguous date
in the sheet decides every date in it), applied to each sheet's own date columns pooled, as the
defaulters deck's are: `expectedDateOrder` and `followupDateOrder`, with `defaultersDateOrder`
on the same helper and unchanged in what it answers. A sheet that PROVES month-first is read
month-first; one that proves day-first, or shows no clue, is read exactly as it always was. The
upload route works the order out once, hands it to the importer, and answers `dateOrder`
("month/day, as the file itself showed", the comments log's field) and, only when a part of the
sheet gave no clue, the same sentence a defaulters deck gives: "Dates in this part of the file
were read as DAY/MONTH because nothing in it said which way round the file writes them. Check a
few against the loan system." Server only: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are unchanged.

**What it cost.** CPU only: no read and no write added. A 40-row Expected deck is 21 round trips
and a 40-row Followup file is 8, **measured on the code as merged (Part 84) and on this change,
the same**; `test/upload-speed.test.mjs` holds them with headroom (24 and 10). `/api/call` is
untouched.

**Checked.** Seven importer tests (Expected and Followup: month-first read right, day-first and
no-clue read as before, a handed-in order obeyed, and the three loan-system sheets agree on one
loan's disbursement date) and four through the real upload handler (stored as the file means, the
no-clue answer says it guessed, a Followup file cannot put the swapped dates back on a corrected
register, no round trip added). Four deliberate breaks (each importer ignoring its order, the route
not reporting it, the Followup order forgetting its promise-date evidence), each caught.

**What this does NOT do.**

- **Stored history is as it was stored.** Every sheet uploaded before Part 84 or this change carries
  swapped dates wherever both numbers were twelve or under. The Follow-up list is put right for a
  customer by the next **Current** deck they are on (today's, once it is uploaded again); a
  customer who left the current file keeps the register row they had; past days' decks keep their
  stored dates until their files are uploaded again.
- **An exact repair of the stored rows exists in principle and is not built.** For a loan on
  today's re-uploaded Current deck, copy its right dates onto the same loan's older rows where the
  old value is exactly the day/month swap of the new one: nothing is guessed. It is a bulk update
  of the hottest table (so it would be cut into small statements) and it restates past days'
  Exp.Def figures, so it is the owner's to ask for (`CHAT.md` section 8).
- **The company's own forms are not touched.** The complaints and restructures sheets
  (`importComplaints`, `importRestructures`: RESOLVED AT, START DATE, APPROVED AT, TIMESTAMP) are
  written by the company's forms, not the loan system's export, and read their dates with no
  order. Nothing here says they are wrong; nobody has reported them. **(Done in Part 89, on the
  owner's order to pass through every upload's dates: these two and the call-app sheets now read
  by their own file's order too.)**
- **The older copy under `migrate/` does not have this fault**, so it is not changed: its date parser
  reads `a/b/yyyy` as month first by construction (`migrate/lib/parse.js`), the loan system's order.
- The order is read per request (a part of a big sheet carries its own evidence), as in Part 84.

**What the owner has to do.** Part 84's list stands: upload today's Initial **and Current** files
again. The Current file is the one that puts the Follow-up list's Disb date and Last trans right (it
refreshes the register); both put Expected Defaulters right. A Followup or an Expected sheet needs
uploading again only if somebody is reading what it stored.

## Part 86 — The stored swapped dates, put right in place with the loan system's own pattern (RUN-ME-060)

> "we cant re-upload now - i hope the system autoupdates whats right brother" — the owner, 16 Nov
> 2026, the evening Parts 84 and 85 were merged

**What happens without it.** After Parts 84 and 85 every file uploaded is read the right way round;
the rows stored before keep their swapped dates. The evening's usual Current upload replaces the day's
current deck (the newest upload of a team and a day wins) and refreshes the Follow-up register for
everyone on it, and every file from the next morning is right. What nobody uploads again is **that
morning's Initial deck** (04:51 on 16 Nov), which decides the cycle day and the recycling leader of a
customer who left the current file (Parts 75 and 82), and **the past days**.

**What was found, on the real file of 16 Nov (10,372 loans, disbursed April 2024 to November 2026).**

- A loan expires **91 days** after it was disbursed and turns chronic **14 days** after it expires:
  10,372 of 10,372, in every status.
- **DAYS ELAPSED**, a plain number the date bug never touched, is the days from the disbursement date
  to the deck's day less a small offset: **exactly 2 for 10,372 of 10,372** (8,888 Chronic, 1,138
  Partial Defaulter, 346 Expired). On the history of the one loan the owner asked about the offset is 1
  or 2 across fourteen decks (an Initial file is one day older than a Current one). So it names the real
  disbursement date to within a few days, while a swapped date is **at least 27 days** away from it.
- The rule that follows (`db/RUN-ME-060-repair-swapped-deck-dates.sql`): a row is changed **only when
  its three dates, as stored, do not fit all of that, and exactly one reading of them fits all of it**
  (each date as stored, or with its day and month exchanged; the disbursement date 0 to 3 days from what
  DAYS ELAPSED says). Anything else is left exactly as it is.
- Run over what the old importer stored for that real file: 8,296 loans had a wrong date, **all 8,296
  were put right to what the file says, none was changed wrongly**, and the 2,076 whose dates were
  already right were left alone.
- **The first form of the rule, with the pattern alone (91 and 14), was wrong, and the test found it.**
  A loan whose expiry was moved by exactly the number of days a day-and-month swap moves its
  disbursement date (30 for March the fourth and April the third) fits the pattern under a swapped
  disbursement date: 150 rows of a first test book were changed to something that is not the truth.
  Nothing like such a loan exists among the 10,372 real ones, but that is not a reason to leave it
  possible: DAYS ELAPSED is the second, independent witness that rejects it.

**What it is.** A script run by hand, like every migration: it creates `defaulter_date_repair_log` (row
level security on; nothing reads it) and changes DISB DATE, EXPIRE DATE and CHRONIC DATE of defaulter
deck rows, **for the days its first lines name (today, to begin with), at most 20,000 rows a run**. It
is safe to run again (a repaired row fits and is not touched twice) and it says how many rows still wait
(`still_to_do_run_again`). Each row changed is logged with its old and new dates; the undo is at the
bottom of the file. It is cut off after 50 seconds and rolls back whole, and it gives up after 3 seconds
of waiting for a lock instead of holding up an upload's housekeeping.

**What it cost.** It reads the days named through the `snapshot_date` index (`EXPLAIN`: a bitmap scan of
exactly the day's rows) and writes only the rows it changes: about 15,000 a day on the shape of the 16
Nov deck. On a test book of 297,015 deck rows with the live table's two trigram indexes, **14,935 rows
were changed in 1.4 seconds**, and the whole fifteen days in six runs of up to 30,000 rows of one to two
seconds each. Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no code reads the log table. A busier machine
and a colder cache are slower: the limit and the cut-off are there for that, and a run that is cut off
changes nothing.

**Checked.** `tools/db-checks/deck-date-repair.mjs`, a kept check in the repository's way (run by hand
on a scratch PostgreSQL, everything rolled back): 3,000 loans and 85,905 deck rows over fifteen days
and thirty uploads (some whole uploads right, as the owner's book shows), with the loans meant to fool
the repair: expiries moved by 29 to 31 and 59 to 61 days onto a swapped date, by 17 and 45 days,
DAYS ELAPSED that says nothing true, a loan with no chronic date, one with no DAYS ELAPSED. It runs the
file itself. **47,120 rows repaired; none changed to anything but the truth; no right date made wrong;
a run after the last changed 0; forty runs of 3,000 rows ended where one big run did; the file's own
undo put back every row (the book's md5 is the same).** Then it breaks the file on purpose: without
the DAYS ELAPSED witness it changes **1,770** rows to something that is not the truth, and when it
does not, it refuses to pass. `test/deck-date-repair.test.mjs` pins the safety lines of the file in
`npm test`.

**What this does NOT do.**

- **LAST TRANS DATE** was swapped the same way and has no pattern to check it against: not repaired
  (tonight's Current upload and every file from now on carry it right, and refresh the Follow-up list).
- Rows with a missing date or no DAYS ELAPSED, loans whose expiry was moved, and any row where no
  reading or two readings fit, stay as they are.
- The Expected sheet's dates (`repayment_snapshots`, read by no screen **(corrected in Part 91: the customer page shows Last payment from it)**) and the Follow-up register are
  not touched here: the register is refreshed from every Current deck.
- **Which days are repaired is the owner's:** today's run puts the morning's Initial deck right. To put
  the week before right (the Exp.Def Report of a past week, the dashboard card's arrows against last
  week), the first date of the query is changed and it is run again until nothing waits.
- Nobody has run it against the live book: a chat cannot. The numbers above are the real file's, on a
  test book.

**What the owner has to do.** Run the file (pasted in the chat) as a new query, then read its one row of
numbers. Run it away from an upload (an evening upload deletes the rows of the files it replaces).

## Part 87 — A customer the day's current deck no longer names stays on every list of that day, as recovered

> "how comes tou said "should disappear." yet we are fighting allover to say cleared people
> shouldnt dissapear for verifications" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026, after an answer about a customer
> who was on a day's initial file and not on its current one. The same order a third time:
> "they should stay there as of recovery so as to know recovery amount from difference of initial
> to current per each day by team or staff" (13 Nov); "i expect that customer in initial never
> to get lost even if cleared its amounts and statuses that change" (15 Nov).

**What was wrong.** Parts 69 to 82 each closed one door for such a customer and left the next one
open, so the screens read the same customer four ways (Part 84, "Not done", measured on the real
loan the owner asked about). A customer on a day's initial file and absent from that day's current
file read:

- on the **dashboard card** (`RUN-ME-058`): recovered in full;
- on the **Expected Defaulters tab**: recovered in full if they never were on a current file;
  recovered 0 with their last arrears still showing if they were on an earlier one (Part 71's ghost);
- on the **Exp.Def Report's day view, the card behind a leader's name and the phone**: CLEARED with
  recovered 0 and the old arrears if they were on an earlier current file, and **not listed at all**
  if they never were on one;
- on the **report's week**: on a board of their own ("Cleared, no leader on record for the day",
  Part 78), outside every leader's book and every total.

**Why it was left that way, and why it need not be.** Part 78, and the comment on `buildRows_`, said
the rotation's role and cycle need fields (`days_elapsed`, `chronic_date`, `expire_date`) that
exist only on a current-deck row. Part 82 found, on the tab, that this is not so: the initial file
is imported by the same importer as the current one, so the customer's own row on the day's initial
deck carries the status, the days elapsed, the dates, the name and the number. The same fact is read
here, where the rule is written once.

**The rule, written once (`buildRows_`, `api/_lib/expdf.js`).** `buildRows_` is handed the day's own
initial rows (`morning`) when the day's two decks are a whole pair. Then every customer on that deck
has a row:

- one on the current deck reads as before (Part 69);
- one the current deck does not name is built from their morning row by the same function:
  **CLEARED, nothing owed, the whole of the morning's arrears recovered**, placed by the rotation off
  the morning row (its own status, days and dates: `assignFor` reads the row, never the CLEARED the
  list shows), so the leader a day's list credits is the leader who held them that day;
- a ghost (Part 71, `ghostRowsFor_`) for a customer who is on the morning deck is dropped for the
  morning row: the ghost is the customer's last-known row from an earlier day, and the day's own two
  files say what happened on this day;
- a ghost for a customer who is **not** on the day's initial deck is exactly what Part 71 made it.

This is "a team missing from it owes nothing on it, full stop" (`defaulterBook`; `RUN-ME-032`) and the
dashboard card's own reading, applied to the report and the phone: one rule on every screen.

**Where it applies.**

- `expdfCore`, the day reading: the phone's list (`expdfMine`), the report's day view and the card
  behind a leader's name, when the decks are a pair (below).
- `expdfWeekCompute_`, each filed day of the week: both decks are read for the day (`onDate`), so a
  pair by construction. The day's initial deck is now read for ten columns instead of four (the
  name, the number and what the rotation reads), the same rows. Part 78's board is empty by
  construction: it stays in the answer as `[]`, and the page draws nothing for it.
- `expectedDefaulters`, the tab: a ghost for a customer on the morning deck is dropped, so the loop
  that builds a row from the morning row (Parts 75, 77, 82) reads them too. The tab now agrees with
  the report about a customer who was on an earlier current file: recovered in full, not 0.
- Cycle days are as ever: the report and the phone list the customers whose cycle day it is, so the
  whole of a morning deck is not handed to every day; the tab lists everybody on it.

**The pair: nobody is marked paid on a comparison that was never made.** A day reading compares the
day's initial deck with the day's current one. This weekday's latest current deck can be last week's
(on a morning before today's current file is uploaded), and a customer missing from it has not
cleared, they have not been compared. `expdfCore` hands the morning rows over only when both decks are
here, are the same date, and the baseline is the day's own (not a week's or a month's first deck, whose
morning would place the customer stale). The tab asks the same of its ghosts. Otherwise every screen
reads as it did. The answer says which it was (`paired`, on the report's day view and in the phone's
`diag`), so a customer who is not shown as recovered can be explained by a day whose current file is not in yet.

**What the owner will see.** The Exp.Def Report's recovered totals (day and week), a leader's card and the
phone's EXP.DEF % go up, by exactly the customers who were on the morning list and are not on the
evening's, at their full morning arrears: toward the dashboard card's own figure for the same day. (The
loan the owner asked about on 16 Nov, once its date is right and Monday's current file is in: a CLEARED
row with its whole 31,001 recovered on the report and the phone, as the card always counted it.) A customer
who used to be missing from a leader's list now stands at the bottom of it, CLEARED, with a name and a number
to verify them by.

**The trade it carries, plainly.** If a day's current file ever arrives without a team that still owes, those
customers now read as recovered in full on the report and the phone, as they have on the dashboard card since
Part 80 and in every recovery figure since `RUN-ME-032`. It is one rule for every screen, so changing it is the
owner's, for all of them together (`CHAT.md` section 8).

**What it cost.** No read anywhere: the rule is arithmetic over the two decks each of these screens already
reads. The phone's day reading is the sacred path, and `test/call.test.mjs` counts its reads with and without
such customers: the same number. `test/speed.test.mjs` counts the five Exp.Def screens (report day and week,
the card day and week, the tab) with and without twenty-five of them: the same round trips on each. No row
budget moved. The week's initial deck is read for ten columns instead of four, the same rows. **CPU, measured at the live
book's size** (10,372 customers on the morning deck, 4,000 of them gone from the current deck, the whole book read): the
phone's list takes about 15 ms more on the web server (43 ms against 28 ms, the test database being in memory); a leader's
own book is a fortieth of that. Nothing on the database.

**Checked.** Eight tests. `test/portal.test.mjs`: the old Part 78 test rewritten (the week keeps the customer
in their leader's book, in every total, with a name and a number, and not a customer whose cycle day it is not);
one rule on four screens (the report, the card, the phone's worklist and the tab read the same customer the same
way: a customer gone from the current deck with an older chronic row, one never on a current file, one chronic
on the morning deck, one paid and still on the file, one ghost who is not on the morning deck, one of another
cycle day; and the week agreeing with the day); the unpaired deck (nothing closes); who may see them (team
scoping). `test/call.test.mjs`: through the real call dispatch, the list, the team scope and the daily summary's
EXP.DEF % with and without the migration's ghost function; the unpaired deck; and the read count.
`test/speed.test.mjs`: the five screens. **Each rule was broken on purpose and the tests failed:** ten breaks on
the portal side (eight caught; two are not changes of behaviour: the viewer's-teams filter on rows the database has
already scoped, and an empty-deck check the date check makes redundant); a first set did not catch the morning row
being placed by the CLEARED override instead of its own status, so a chronic customer on the morning deck was
added and it did; three on the phone, two on the zero-read promise. `npm test`: 1,580 pass. **A ninth test, added the same
evening (#715), pins the dashboard card and the report to one reading:** for a day, in every state a customer can be in (owing,
owing more, paid and still on the file, gone from the current deck with an older row in history, never on a current file, and a
customer of another cycle day), the card (`RUN-ME-058`, in the database) and the report (`buildRows_`, in the server) give the
same customers, the same arrears, the same recovery and the same percentage, for the day and for the week of that day; three
deliberate breaks of the rule each turn it red by itself. They were two implementations of one rule and drifted for weeks over
exactly the customers this Part closes.

**Not done, said plainly.**

- **A reader whose teams are all missing from the day's current file** (a small team whose last defaulter
  paid): `latestSnapshot` gives no date for an empty scope, so nothing closes for them; the admin and anyone
  holding other teams see the customers. Closing it needs the company's file date (no read), and it is the
  whole-book trade applied to a one-team reader, so the owner's to say.
- **The hours before the day's current file is in:** nothing closes, as before, and the tab still lists a
  customer who is new on today's initial file as CLEARED in that gap (Parts 75 and 77; `CHAT.md` section 8). Not touched.
- **The month view of the report and `expdfCore`'s old `weekly` baseline** (Monday's deck, the month's first) are not
  changed: their baselines are older mornings.
- **The page's board for Part 78** (`xd_unassigned`, `public/app.html`) stays as dormant code and leaves with the
  next change to that page; no `BUILD` bump was made for it.
- **Two customers the card and the report are still built to read differently. (The first: done in Part 88, the owner said
  YES the same evening.)** The first enters default after the morning
  deck (on the current deck, never on that day's initial deck): the card does not count them (Part 74: "the lists per day must
  come from initial files"), while the report and the phone list them with their current arrears as their initial and
  recovered 0, which enlarges the denominator of their Rec %. On the card's own test data one such customer reads 50.0% on the
  card and 32.1% on the report, and the recovered figure is the same to the shilling. The second is the all-time ghost (Part
  71), which only the report and the phone carry. Part 74 left it to the owner whether "the lists per day come from initial
  files" should extend to the report and the phone; his words of 13 to 16 Nov are about the other side (a customer on the
  initial deck never lost) and say nothing of this one. Not changed (`CHAT.md` section 8).
- **A customer who changed team between the two decks**, read by someone who holds the first team and not the second,
  counts as recovered for the first team's leader (the second team's rows are not in that reader's read). Rare; not handled.
- Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot), and there is no SQL.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing to run. After the deploy, open one day on the Exp.Def Report and its leaders'
cards: the rows marked CLEARED whose recovered equals their initial are the customers the day's current file did not name.

## Part 88 — The report and the phone list the morning deck's customers, as the dashboard card does: a customer who enters default after it is not on that day

> "Should the report and the phone also leave out customers who fall into default after the morning
> file, so the dashboard card, the report and the phone all count the same people?" — "YES" — the
> owner, 16 Nov 2026, answering the question Part 87 ended on.

**What it was.** After Part 87 the report's day matched the dashboard card's tile in recovered, to the
shilling, and differed in customers, initial and Rec % by one kind of customer: somebody in default on the
day's current file who was never on the day's initial file, that is, who **entered default after the morning
file**. The card counts the initial deck's customers only (Part 74: "the lists per day must come from initial
files"). The report and the phone also listed the evening's new defaulters, with their current arrears as their
"initial" and recovered 0, which enlarged the denominator of the Rec %. On the card's own test data the card read
3 customers, 180,000 owed at the start, 90,000 recovered, 50.0%; the report read 4, 279,999, 90,000, 32.1%.

**The rule (`buildRows_`, `api/_lib/expdf.js`).** When the day's two decks are a pair (Part 87: the same date, both
here), a customer on the current deck whom the morning deck never named is **not a row of the day**: nobody's expected
defaulter of this day, they join tomorrow's list, on tomorrow's initial deck. It is the same on the report's day view,
the card behind a leader's name, the phone's list and its EXP.DEF % strip, and every filed day of the week. The same
test data now reads 3, 180,000, 90,000, 50.0 on both.

- **Said, not silent:** the answers carry `enteredAfter` (`{ customers, arrears }`: how many customers in default on the
  current deck were left out, and what they owe), on the report's day view and in the phone's `diag`; null when there is
  no pair, because then nothing is left out. A big number on a day is also the signature of a team missing from that
  day's initial file (below). The page does not draw it: this is a server change and `BUILD` is unchanged.
- **No pair, no change:** with no initial deck, or a current deck of another date, every defaulter of the current deck
  is listed, as it always was.
- **Left alone on purpose.** (1) **The Expected Defaulters tab** is the weekly-cycle book of every defaulter, not a day's
  list: a customer in default now is on it, owing, as a defaulter is; the owner named the report and the phone. (2) **The
  all-time ghost** (Part 71, ordered on 13 Nov: "should reflect to alltime data past present and future") is not that
  customer and is not touched: it stays a row, CLEARED, with its last-known arrears, and it is still counted in the figures
  of the report and the phone (a reviewed decision: "both counted in the week grand total"). The card does not carry ghosts.
  **That is now the only thing the three differ on.** Whether ghosts should stay listed but leave the report's and the
  phone's figures is a new question, since "count the same people" and "should reflect to alltime data" pull two ways
  (`CHAT.md` section 8).

**What it costs.** No read, and fewer rows. The consequence to know: if a team is missing from a day's initial file while
the day's current file carries it, every customer of that team reads as having entered default after the morning, and
leaves the day's lists of a reader who holds several teams (a one-team reader needs their own team's initial rows to be
paired, so is not touched). That is the whole-book rule applied to the initial file, as `db/RUN-ME-032` already says ("a
team missing from it owes nothing on it, full stop"), and `enteredAfter` is where it shows.

**Checked.** The tests of Parts 87 now carry a customer who entered default after the morning: absent from every leader's card,
from both worklists and from the report's figures, counted in `enteredAfter`, still on the Expected Defaulters tab; kept on the
older current deck when the decks are not a pair; the card-versus-report parity test draws one more customer and still reads the
same numbers on both; through the real call dispatch for the phone. **Five deliberate breaks of the rule, each caught:** the
customer left on the day, nobody counted as left out, the all-time ghost left out too, left out on a current deck of another
date, and the week keeping a day's later entrants. `npm test`: 1,581 pass. No read added to `/api/call` (the existing count test
holds), `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Not done, said plainly.**

- The ghosts' place in the figures (above): not asked.
- The Expected Defaulters tab keeps a customer who entered default after the morning file (above): not asked.
- The page does not draw `enteredAfter`.
- Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot), and there is no SQL.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing to run. After the deploy, the report's Rec % for a day, and the phone's EXP.DEF %, rise
toward the dashboard card's tile for the same day by exactly the customers who entered default after the morning file; with
no ghosts drawn they should read the same.

## Part 89 — One file, one date order: every upload reads its dates by what its own file shows, and the browser reads none by a rule of its own

> "I can't see 2209966593 on cleared yet., just study the dates if the position of month starts then day or
> vice versa trim the same for the rest not to stay contradicted.. since that I think affects multiple lists in
> the system so pass through how you cumpute uploaded dates bro" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026, the evening Parts
> 87 and 88 were merged

**The order.** A file writes all its dates one way round: day first or month first. The file shows which, in the
dates that can only be read one way (`16/11/2026`, `11/16/2026`), and that decides every date in the file,
including `9/7/2026`, which on its own is the ninth of July or the seventh of September. Nothing between the file
and the book may read a date by a rule of its own. Parts 84 and 85 did this for the loan system's three sheets;
this Part is the pass through every other upload, and it found four sheets and one more reader.

**How an uploaded date is read, from the file to the book.**

1. **The Upload page** (`public/upload.html`). An Excel file's real date cells go as ISO (`yyyy-mm-dd`, with the clock
   only if the cell has one: unambiguous); its text cells go as the text they hold (the loan system writes every date as
   text, `M/D/YYYY`). **A CSV file now goes as the text it holds** (below: this was the one reader that decided a date
   before the server did).
2. **The server** (`dateOrNull` and `stampOrNull`, `api/_lib/parse.js`; the order from `inferDayFirst`). ISO is read as it
   is. A slash date with a part over twelve decides itself. When both parts are twelve or under, the order of the file
   decides: every date of the sheet's date columns is pooled, one unambiguous value is enough, the larger pile of
   evidence wins, an exact tie gives none. A sheet with no evidence at all is read day-first, as it always was (the loan
   sheet adds two more tie-breakers: the tighter span, then the day nearest the upload). The decks and the Expected and
   Followup sheets say in their answer which way round they were read, and say so in words when they had to guess.
3. **The order is decided per request.** A big file travels in slices of up to 2,000 rows (never fewer than 250), each
   carrying the header, and each slice's evidence decides its own. A real deck has thousands of dates in a slice; a slice
   without one unambiguous date is not a thing that happens at that size. Said, not changed (below).

**Every upload that reads a date, and what is pooled for it.** (`ORDER_CASES` in `test/importers.test.mjs` holds every one
to the same rule; the source scan in the same file fails if a fifteenth is added without it.)

| Upload (type) | Importer | Date columns pooled for the order |
|---|---|---|
| Defaulters Current / Initial | `importDefaulters` | DISB, EXPIRE, CHRONIC, DUE, LAST TRANS DATE (Part 84) |
| Expected (today, tomorrow, yesterday, initial) | `importExpected` | DISB, DUE, FIRST SCHEDULE, LAST SCHEDULE, LAST TRANS DATE (Part 85) |
| Defaulters Followup | `importFollowup` | DISB DATE, LAST TRANS, PROMISE DATE, COMMENT AT (Part 85) |
| Comments | `importComments` | TIMESTAMP, with its clock in EAT; PROMISE DATE follows it |
| Loan pipeline | `importLoans` | every date column of the stage; then the tighter span, then the day nearest the upload |
| Received payments | `importReceivedPayments` | PAYMENT DATE (or PAID AT, DATE PAID, DATE, TRANSACTION DATE) |
| Demand notices | `importDemandNotices` | NOTICE DATE and TIMESTAMP together |
| PMO deductions | `importDeductions` | TIMESTAMP, TAREHE ALIYOPOKEA, TAREHE YA UGUNDUZI |
| Staff registry | `importStaffRegistry` | REG-DATE, BIRTH DATE (the birth date is read off the NIDA first) |
| Advance requests | `importAdvances` | TIMESTAMP, APPLICATION DATE |
| **Complaints** (this Part) | `importComplaints` | TIMESTAMP (or DATE), RESOLVED AT |
| **Restructures** (this Part) | `importRestructures` | START DATE, APPROVED AT, TIMESTAMP |
| **Call-app registrations** (this Part) | `importCallUsers` | REGISTERED AT, LAST SYNC |
| **Call history** (this Part) | `importCallLogs` | CALL DATE, SYNCED AT |

The summaries (Expected and Defaulters) read no date from their rows: the report's day is the date box, or the file's own
`Filters` End Date, which is ISO. Teams, access codes, roles, abnormal payments, settings and hints carry no dates.

**What was found.**

1. **Four sheets read every slash date with no look at the file around it** (complaints, restructures, call-app
   registrations, call history): Part 85 named the first two as "the company's own forms", "nobody has reported them", and
   left them. In a file that writes month-first, a `9/7/2026` came out as the ninth of July beside a `11/16/2026` in the
   same sheet. Now each pools its own date columns and reads by `inferDayFirst`, exactly as the other ten do; a sheet that
   shows no clue, or proves day-first, is read as it always was.
2. **A stamp with a clock was replaced by the moment of the upload, silently.** `dateOrNull` wants a bare date, so a spreadsheet's
   `24/09/2026 10:15` came back null, and these four then stored `new Date()` instead. They now take the date part first
   (`dateCell_`, the notices importer's own rule, written for the same fault).
3. **The Upload page's own reader decided the dates of a CSV before the server saw them.** Measured on the real reader the page
   loads (SheetJS 0.18.5, `cellDates: true`), in a real browser: a CSV cell that looks like a date becomes a real date by
   JavaScript's rule, month first, and a cell that looks like a number becomes a number. In a **day-first** CSV `9/7/2026` (the
   ninth of July) went to the server as `2026-09-07` and `2/3/2027` as `2027-02-03`, while `16/11/2026` and `21/12/2026`, which
   cannot be read that way, stayed text and were read day-first: **one file, two orders, decided in the browser**. In the same
   CSV, `3/6` in D.S became `3/6/01` (the sixth of March 2001), an account `0152826626000` lost its leading zero, and
   `12345678901234567890` came out as `12345678901234567000`. A month-first CSV came out right on its dates by luck (JavaScript's
   rule happens to be the loan system's) and wrong on D.S and the accounts. Now `readWorkbook` reads a `.csv` with
   `raw: true`: the cells go to the server as the text the file holds, which is what every importer was written for (they take
   "the raw parsed CSV rows": text), and the server's rule is the only one. An Excel file is read as it
   always was (verified: the same real date cell and the same text cells before and after).

**What it costs.** CPU only. No read and no write is added anywhere: the four sheets' uploads cost the same round trips on
the code before this change and after it (complaints 7, restructures 7, call-users 8, call-logs 7, measured on a 40-row
file), `/api/call` is not touched, and a CSV is read faster in the browser, because no value is worked out (a deck-sized CSV of 10,372 rows by 25 columns: about 0.3 s with `raw` against 0.75 s without, measured with the same reader in Node). **The one trade, said plainly:** a
month-first CSV whose every date has both parts twelve or under, with no other evidence in the file, used to come out right by
JavaScript's luck and is now read like any other sheet with no evidence (day-first; the loan sheet's two tie-breakers apply
to it). Every real deck carries thousands of dates and cannot be in that case. `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are unchanged:
`upload.html` is its own page, served `no-cache`, so the next load of it is the new one.

**Checked.** Importer tests for each of the four sheets (month-first, day-first, no clue, a clock, ISO, the evidence in
any one date column alone); one table that holds **all fourteen** importers to the one rule in three states each (a sheet
that proves month-first, one that proves day-first, one that shows nothing); a source scan that fails if any call of
`dateOrNull` or `stampOrNull` under `api/` is not handed an order (it also reads a deliberately bad snippet, so it can
fail); the four sheets through the **real upload handler** (stored on the days the file means, and no added trip: budgets
beside the measured counts); a source pin of the page's CSV read in `test/pages.test.mjs`; and
`tools/browser-checks/upload-csv-dates.mjs`, which loads the real page with the real reader and posts a day-first CSV,
a month-first CSV and an Excel file: 12 points pass on the new page (in UTC and in the office's timezone) and **6 fail on the
page as it was**. **Twenty-two deliberate breaks, each caught:** every one of the four sheets' dates read with no order,
the clock left in, each evidence column dropped from the pool, the pool ignoring a list of header spellings, six of the
older importers losing their order, and a new importer that reads a date with no order (only the source scan sees it).

**2209966593, the customer who started this.** From the owner's own file of 16 Nov it is a Monday customer (disbursed
`9/7/2026`, the seventh of September), and the book held the ninth of July (Thursday and Sunday) until Part 84. It is
CLEARED on a list only when three things are true together, and a chat cannot see the live book to say which is not: (1) its
stored disbursement date is the right one (`db/RUN-ME-060` puts the stored dates right in place; until it is run, Monday is
not its day); (2) it is on that Monday's initial file that counts (not replaced by a later upload of its team); (3) Monday's
current file is filed (until then nothing is marked cleared: Part 87). `db/TEMPLATE-where-is-this-customer-read-only.sql`
answers all three in one read, and was given to the owner filled in for this loan and this day, in full, in the chat.

**Not done, said plainly.**

- **The order is still per request.** A slice of a big file decides on its own evidence. Carrying the first slice's decision to
  the others would add state to the upload request for a case that cannot occur at 250 rows or more of real dates; it is
  not built, and the answer already says per request which way round was read.
- **Rows already stored keep their dates.** The decks' swapped DISB, EXPIRE and CHRONIC dates are put right by RUN-ME-060 (Part
  86); LAST TRANS DATE is not (tonight's Current deck refreshes it on the Follow-up list). Nothing was run on the live book.
- **A file re-saved in a spreadsheet program may carry real dates that program already read in its own order**; nothing in the
  file can reveal that. The reliable file is the one the loan system wrote, uploaded as it came.
- **The four sheets' answers do not say which way round they were read** (the decks, the Expected and the Followup sheets do):
  the notices, deductions, advances, staff and payments importers never did, and this Part keeps them alike.
- `migrate/` (the first import from the old sheets) reads `a/b/yyyy` month-first by construction (Part 85) and was not changed.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing new. Run the probe for 2209966593 (it changes nothing), and `db/RUN-ME-060` if it has not
been run (`CHAT.md` section 8). After this deploys, a CSV and an Excel file of the same sheet read the same dates.

## Part 90 — The files are not in different orders; the routes they took are: one loan stored both ways, and a check for every file

> "They might be in different orders per file so check starting with the defaulters one I sent" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026,
> the hour Part 89 was merged, with the probe for loan 2209966593 pasted under it.

**What the probe showed.** The same loan, read off the book for the 14 days up to 16 Nov: its disbursement date is the ninth of
July (the swapped one) on **every current deck** and on **nine of the fourteen initial decks**, and the seventh of September (the
right one, the Monday it was disbursed) on the other **five initial decks** (6, 7, 10, 14 and 15 Nov). So the book holds the loan
both ways, and the owner's reading was that the files must differ in order. They do not.

**What was checked, file by file** (the four files the owner has sent in this chat; counts only, no name, phone or account is
written anywhere):

| File | How it writes its dates | Order | Independent witness | Read now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Defaulters, 16 Nov** (10,372 loans) | every date a TEXT cell; DISB, EXPIRE, CHRONIC, LAST TRANS `M/D/YYYY`; DUE DATE an ISO text (617) or "No due date" (9,755) | **month-first in all four columns**: month-first-only values 6,107 / 5,978 / 6,363 / 6,064, **day-first-only values 0** | the loan system's own pattern (91 days, 14 days, DAYS ELAPSED): **10,372 of 10,372** rows | right |
| **Defaulters, 11 Nov** (one team, 202 loans) | the same | month-first (125 month-first-only in DISB DATE, 0 day-first-only) | the pattern: **202 of 202** (42 of 202 read with no order) | right |
| **Approved (Processed), 11 Nov** (12 loans) | APPROVED DATE `M/D/YYYY` text | month-first (9 only-month-first, 3 either) | the file's own Filters window, 28 Sep to 2 Oct: **12 of 12 inside read month-first, 0 of 12 read day-first** | right |
| **Leave form responses** (Google Form export) | real date cells, shown `m/d/yy` | nothing to order: a real date is unambiguous | | right |

The 16 Nov deck was also cut into the slices the Upload page cuts it into (five of 2,000 rows, one of 372) and each slice read on
its own: every slice decides month-first, on 869 to 4,765 unambiguous values each, and every one of the 10,372 rows reads exactly as the
whole file reads. The order being decided per request (Part 89, "not done") is a non-issue at the size of a real deck.

**What explains the book, reproduced on the real 16 Nov file.** The same file can reach the server three ways, and before Parts 84 and 89
each stored something different:

| Route | What was stored | Customers with all four dates right (of 10,372) | D.S |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Excel file as the loan system wrote it** (text cells) → the importer of that day (no order, day-first) | disbursement, expiry and chronic dates swapped wherever both numbers were twelve or under | **1,256**; 3,883 disbursement dates wrong | untouched |
| **The same sheet saved as a CSV**, chosen on the page as it was before Part 89 | the page's own reader turned every text date into a real date, month first (JavaScript's rule): dates RIGHT, by luck | **10,372** | **spoilt on all 10,372** (`7-12` became `7/12/01`; a phone lost its leading zero) |
| Either, after Parts 84 and 89 | dates read by the file's own order; a CSV goes as text | **10,372** | untouched |

That is the mixture the probe found: **the current decks come as Excel files and read swapped on every day; the nine initial decks
that read swapped were Excel as the loan system wrote it.** The old
importer, run on this very file, stores for 2209966593 exactly what the probe shows on 16 Nov (disbursed 9 July, expiring 12 July,

coalesced with a text again, the fixture's `upload_batch` back to text, `days_elapsed` as a numeric, the row with no batch taken out), each caught. **A database
check is built from the book's own column types, never from what the query happens to need.**
