## Part 91 — The Follow-up list is a copy, and RUN-ME-060 does not reach it: is any Disb date later than today? (RUN-ME-062)

> "In the defaulter followup nav, try check if there exists any future date than today in the disb date column to confirm all dates
> are okay" — the owner, 16 Nov 2026, the evening they ran the corrected `db/RUN-ME-061`, with its answer pasted above the message.

**What the owner's audit showed** (the corrected RUN-ME-061, twenty uploads of 10 to 16 Nov). The 16 Nov uploads read **all fit as stored**: `db/RUN-ME-060`
put them right. The **current decks of 10 to 15 Nov and the initial decks of 11, 12 and 13 Nov still read about 20% fit as stored and about 80% fit only if
swapped** (the 15 Nov current of 22:47 reads exactly 2,076 and 8,296, as the real 16 Nov file does when read the old way; the 12 Nov current of 23:18 is a
partial of 3,171 rows); the initial decks of 10, 14 and 15 Nov came right; `neither` and `missing` are 0, so RUN-ME-060 can put every one of those rows right.
And **no upload has a date-like D.S**, which corrects Part 90's guess about the five initial decks that read right (not CSVs: see there).

**What the Follow-up list is.** `followup_status`, the register behind the Follow-up tab and the phone's Defaulters list. It is written by two routes only:
a **Current** defaulters deck (`writeFollowupFromDeck`: one upsert of each customer's Disb date, Last trans, DAYS ELAPSED and status **as the deck was read at upload**,
stamped `deck_date` with the deck's day; an Initial deck never touches it) and the "Defaulters Followup" sheet. **A copy, not a view of the deck rows.** RUN-ME-060
repairs `defaulter_snapshots` and nothing else (the file does not name the register), so until a Current deck is uploaded after the fix the Follow-up list shows
what the importer of the day stored. Parts 85 and 86 said "the register is refreshed from every Current deck": true, and it is the cure, not a repair already made.

**The check: `db/RUN-ME-062-followup-list-dates-read-only.sql`.** Read-only, one table, one statement, about two seconds for 60,000 rows (a 30-second ceiling),
nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`. It prints no name and no number of a customer: a loan number and a team.

- **Test 1, what was asked.** A loan is not disbursed tomorrow, so a Disb date later than today (the East Africa date) is wrong. It counts them, gives the earliest
  and latest, says how many a swap of day and month would put in the past (the old importer's mark) and how many no swap explains (a day over 12, or day = month), and
  lists up to eight, farthest first. It counts only what the tab lists (a customer with a status or arrears), and says how many hidden rows have one too. **Last trans
  gets the same test** (not asked: the same mistake sits in that column and nothing repairs it by pattern).
- **Why test 1 cannot confirm anything on its own.** A swapped date lands in the future only when the real date's day is the **12th** (12 Jan 2026 stored as 1 Dec
  2026), and no 2024 or 2025 date ever does. The other swapped dates stay in the past and look fine. "None later than today" is therefore weak evidence; it is the
  second test that confirms.
- **Test 2, the witness.** A row carries three facts that must agree: the day of the deck that wrote it (`deck_date`), the Disb date, and the loan system's own
  DAYS ELAPSED. `deck day - Disb date - DAYS ELAPSED` is 0 to 3 for a right date (RUN-ME-060's window, written once there and repeated here, pinned) and at least 27 days
  off for a swapped one, so each row is sorted into **fit as stored**, **fit only with day and month exchanged** (a swapped date) or **neither** (a restructured loan, a row the
  Followup sheet wrote last), by the day of the deck that wrote it. The answer line says "all right" only when nothing is later than today AND test 2 found no swapped date.
- **`deck_date` came from an optional migration** (`db/migrations/2026-08-04-followup-deck-date.sql`) that nothing says was run. The file reads it through `to_jsonb(r) ->>
  'deck_date'`, so it runs with the column and without it; without it test 2 says it could not be made, and the answer never says "all right" on test 1 alone.

**What it will show, and the cure.** Unless a Current deck was uploaded after the fix (#711, 16 Nov), the list holds what the old importer stored: dates
later than today for the loans whose real day was the 12th, and about four fifths of the dates of the others swapped. **The next Current upload rewrites every customer on
it with dates read right** (nothing to run: the owner's "i hope the system autoupdates whats right"). Customers who left the book are retired by that upload (no status,
no arrears: the tab does not list them). **No repair of the register was built:** it would restate the hottest table by hand, in the working day, for hours of difference.
If somebody needs the list right before the upload, the exact repair exists in principle (copy the repaired deck row's Disb date onto the register row where the register's
date is its swap and the row fits only so), and is the owner's to ask for.

**Checked.** `tools/db-checks/followup-dates-audit.mjs`, on a PostgreSQL, with the table made from the **real** `create table` blocks of `db/schema.sql` and the real migration
(Part 90's lesson: a fixture built from what the query needs, not the book's types, passed a query that failed on the owner's keyboard). Four registers (swapped with future
dates; swapped with none; clean; without the `deck_date` column): every line the file prints equals a count made in JavaScript from the same rows, the examples in order, the
deck days; no name is printed; the book is byte-identical afterwards; the verdict reads right in each; the file as pasted (its own East Africa expression) prints the East Africa
date; and **seventeen deliberate breaks** (a date today counted as later, a placeholder counted as shown, the window widened or started at 1, a row fitting as stored counted as
swapped, the test made without a stamp or on placeholders, Last trans today counted as later, the hidden rows counting the shown ones, the examples nearest-first, three deck days,
the swap not made, a swap in the future "explaining" it, the verdict forgetting test 2, "all right" with no test made, a clean register called not all right, `deck_date` read as a
column) each change the answer or make the file fail. 60,017 rows: 1.5 s; 60,000 rows of the table's real width: 1.8 to 1.9 s. `test/followup-dates-audit.test.mjs`

## Part 92 — Dates, everything that is wrong, one matter at a time: the order, and matter 1 (RUN-ME-064, every date in the book)

> "Repair everything that's wrong brother I can't be perfect to detect every where dates are wrong. When we finish disb dates, we have transactions dates at received, we have last trans
> date column and other dates checkup and different excels might come with different fomarts am not sure. - repair one per time so that users see progress on the rised matters" — the owner, 17 Nov 2026

**The order the owner's words give, each matter its own change, merged when it is green and reported on its own:**

1. **Find where dates are wrong, anywhere** (this Part): one read-only scan of every date column of the book, so nobody has to know where to look. `db/RUN-ME-064`.
2. **Received payments' transaction dates** (`received_payments.paid_at`): the reader and the stored rows (Part 93 when it ships).
3. **Last trans dates**: the decks' `last_trans_date` (db/RUN-ME-060 repairs Disb, Expire and Chronic and never touched it: `db/RUN-ME-066`, Part 94), the Expected sheet's, the register's.
4. **Every other date, and "different excels might come with different formats":** which readers still fall back to day-first when a file gives them nothing to decide by, and which formats no reader understands (the formats: Part 95; saying when a date cannot be read, and the company forms' fallback, are the rest); the notices' and deductions' dates asked of themselves and put right where they prove it: Parts 97, 98 and 100).
5. **Disb dates, finished:** the owner's runs of `db/RUN-ME-060` for 10 to 15 Nov and 1 to 9 Nov (Part 91), and the repair of each customer's last-known deck row, offered.

**What was found in the code while planning (read, not yet run on the live book; each is a matter above).**

- **`importReceivedPayments` decides day or month from that file's own payment dates alone** (`inferDayFirst`), with none of the two fallbacks the approved-loans importer has (`tightestSpanIsDayFirst`, `nearestToDayIsDayFirst`, `loansDateOrder`).
  A payments file whose dates all have both parts twelve or under, which is every file of a day from the 1st to the 12th of a month, gives it no evidence, and it **reads day-first: `11/10/2026`
  (10 November, as the loan system writes it) is stored as 11 October.** Not seen on the live book (nobody has sent a payments file, section 8 of `CHAT.md`); it is what the code does.
  `paid_at` is a date and `created_at` is the moment of the upload: a payment is uploaded within days of being made, so the upload's own time is a witness that does not depend on the order rule.
- **The company's own forms** (complaints, restructures, advance requests, call-app sheets) read their dates by the file's own evidence only (Part 89), and a small file of early-in-the-month dates has none:
  the same fallback to day-first, on files a Google Form writes month-first (`6/22/2026 11:29`).
- **`dateOrNull` understands ISO (`2026-07-09`) and `a/b/yyyy` or `a-b-yyyy` only.** A month written as a word (`09-Jul-2026`), a dotted date (`09.07.2026`), `2026/07/09`, `20260709` and an Excel serial number
  (`46210`, a date cell that arrived as a number) read as **nothing**: the date is lost without a word. The upload does not say how many it could not read.

**Matter 1: `db/RUN-ME-064-every-date-in-the-book-read-only.sql` (pasted in full in the chat).** It finds every column of date, timestamp or timestamp-without-zone type of every base table of the `public` schema from
`information_schema` (so a table made by a migration is in it, and it names no table itself: a test fails if it does), reads each table **once** through one dynamically built query per table (`query_to_xml`, all of the
table's date columns in one pass) and prints, per column: rows, filled, earliest, latest, **later than today** (the East Africa date; for a timestamp, a day ahead of now) and **before 2020**.

- **A flag, not a proof.** `FUTURE?`: a later date in a column where that is not normal (a payment, a transaction, a disbursement, a comment, a creation time: the old importer's swap puts a date there, so do a typo and a wrong
  year). `OLD?`: a date before 2020 in a column that is not a birth date. **Not flagged**, and the line says "a later date is normal in this column": an expiry, a chronic date, a due date, a promise, a schedule, a start or end,
  a next, a deadline, a validity, a retirement, and `snapshot_date` (tomorrow's sheet). The words are in one place in the file and a test pins them.
- **Cost.** One pass over each table: **5.4 s on a book of the live book's size** (2.3 million deck rows, 900,000 Expected rows, ten date columns between them), one process, a 45-second ceiling, nothing written, no lock beyond a
  read. Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no code that runs for a user changed.
- **Checked.** `tools/db-checks/every-date-audit.mjs` runs the **whole of `db/schema.sql`** (30 tables, **82** date and timestamp columns, the enum, the indexes) on an empty PostgreSQL inside one transaction, fills nine tables and a
  view with every kind of value the file must tell apart (a date later than today and one on today, one before 2020 and one on 2020, a later expiry and promise and tomorrow's sheet, a birth date from 1975, a moment a minute ahead and
  one two days ahead, rows of nothing), and compares **every one of the 82 lines with a direct query on its own column** (rows, filled, earliest, latest, later than today, before 2020), the flags with the rule written out again,
  the order (flagged first), the ANSWER line, the East Africa clock, and that the tables are byte-identical afterwards; and **seventeen deliberate breaks** (a boundary moved, a threshold moved, an exemption dropped or widened, a view counted,
  the earliest taken from the latest, the filled count taken from the row count, the columns numbered in no order, only some tables read, the flags in the wrong order, the ANSWER counting the wrong flag) each change the answer.
  `test/every-date-audit.test.mjs` (6 tests; eleven deliberate breaks of the pins, each caught) pins read-only, one process, the ceiling, that no table is named, the catalogue, the clock, the words.
- **Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot). A date can be wrong and still in the past, and later than today is only the visible tip: the pattern tests are `db/RUN-ME-061`, `062`, `063`; for a table
  with no pattern the witness is the upload's own time (matter 2 for payments). What the scan finds is read by a chat and answered: the owner pastes the ANSWER line and the flagged lines.

**What the owner has to do.** Run `db/RUN-ME-064` (pasted in the chat) and paste the ANSWER line and every line marked `FUTURE?` or `OLD?`.

## Part 93 — Dates, matter 2: received payments' transaction dates (the reader, and RUN-ME-065)

> "Repair everything that's wrong brother I can't be perfect to detect every where dates are wrong. When we finish disb dates, we have transactions dates at received ..." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026 (Part 92 has the whole order).

**What was wrong (read in the code; nobody has sent a payments file, so it is what the code does, not what the live book holds, until `db/RUN-ME-065` is run and answers).** `importReceivedPayments` decided the
day/month order from the file's own payment dates alone (`inferDayFirst`): one value with a part over twelve decides every value. **A payments file of one day from the 1st to the 12th of a month has no such value:
every row is `11/10/2026`, both parts twelve or under, and it fell through to day-first. The loan system writes the month first, so the 10th of November was stored as the 11th of October** (every payment of the
file, a month early, each a valid date and nothing looking wrong); a file of the 12th of November was stored as the 11th of December: in the future. The approved-loans importer had the two rules that decide such a
file (`tightestSpanIsDayFirst`, `nearestToDayIsDayFirst`, Part 89's `loansDateOrder`); the payments importer never got them.

**The reader (stops it at the source; `paymentsDateOrder`, `importers.js`).** Evidence first, exactly as before; where there is none, the tightest stretch of days (a report covers a short period: `11/9, 11/10, 11/11` is three
days, not September, October and November); where that cannot tell either (one day, every value alike), the day the file is uploaded (`nearestToDayIsDayFirst`: the reading that puts the dates nearest it). The day is the one the
page names (`meta.uploadDate`) or, without it, the server's clock in East Africa: one definition, `uploadDayKey_` in `upload.js`, used by the approved loans and the payments. With nothing to decide by it falls back to day-first, as it
always did, and the answer says so. The upload's answer says which rule decided (`dateOrder`: "month/day, because that puts the file's dates nearest the day it was uploaded"). **Cost:** arithmetic over the rows in hand: no read and
no write added (the trip budget of a small payments file is unchanged: 8 trips). Checked: three importer tests, one through the real upload handler (a day's file of `11/10/2026` sent on the 10th is the 10th; the same file sent
on 12 October is the 11th of October; a file with its own evidence says so in the old words), eight deliberate breaks of the reader and its wiring (one a mutant that changes nothing: the span asked before the evidence, which can
never differ because a span needs every value ambiguous).

**The repair: `db/RUN-ME-065-repair-swapped-payment-dates.sql` (pasted in full in the chat).** The witness is the upload's own time (`created_at`, East Africa). A payment is uploaded the day it is made or within days, and received
payments are pruned at two weeks; the two readings of an ambiguous date are at least 27 days apart, so at most one lies in the stretch. The rows written in the same minute are one upload, judged together because the old reader
decided for a whole file:

- a row is a candidate when its stored date is **not** in `[upload day - 14, upload day + 1]` and the other reading **is** in `[upload day - 7, upload day]`;
- its upload is a **swapped upload** only when it has **no row with a day over twelve** (that is evidence: the file was read by its order, so it was read right), **no ambiguous row that fits as stored**, and at least one candidate;
- only the candidates of a swapped upload change. A late payment in a file that was read right, a row no reading fits, a date whose day and month are the same: left alone.

**The one case it cannot tell apart:** a payments file uploaded a month late whose dates read the other way round land on the upload day to the day: repaired as if swapped. It is written in the file.
It also puts right the **copies in `notice_payment_ledger`** (a payment made after a notice, kept for good, with its date) of every payment repaired, by the payment's id and only where the copy still carries the old date; a book
without that table (a migration run by hand) is repaired all the same; a copy whose payment was pruned before this run cannot be put right here. **Every row changed is in `payment_date_repair_log`** (old and new date, the upload's
day), the undo is at the foot of the file, and a second run changes nothing. It changes `paid_at` and nothing else (a test pins that), prints no name (the first eight characters of an id, and dates), and has a 3-second lock and a
50-second statement limit.

**Checked.** `tools/db-checks/payment-date-repair.mjs`: the WHOLE of `db/schema.sql` on a PostgreSQL, 475 payments in 55 uploads (a day's file read day-first in two slices written in different minutes; a right file with the edges
of the fortnight; a right file with a late payment and a row that would fit the other way, which carries evidence; a one-row swapped file stored in the future; a swapped file with three same-day-and-month rows; a file with rows that fit
as stored and rows that fit only the other way, left alone; an upload written at 01:00 East Africa time, the day before in UTC; a stored day of exactly twelve; the edges of both windows; rows with no date; forty random uploads, right
and swapped; a ledger with copies of repaired payments, one corrected by hand, one of a pruned payment, one of a right payment): every payment's date after the run equals a **model of the rule written again in JavaScript**, only
`paid_at` changed, the ledger equals the model's, the answer's numbers equal the model's, a second run changes nothing, **the file's own undo puts every row back byte for byte**, a book without the ledger table is repaired all the same,
and **eighteen deliberate breaks** (a window moved at each of its five edges, the evidence rule dropped, the ambiguous-fits rule dropped, two rows required, the uploads told apart by the day, the UTC day, a stored day of twelve left alone,
the date not exchanged, same-day-and-month rows counted as ambiguous, the log not kept, the ledger not put right, the hand-corrected copy overwritten, the ledger step on a book without it, the answer counting the wrong source) each change the
outcome or make the file fail. `test/payment-date-repair.test.mjs` (9 tests; seventeen deliberate breaks of the pins, each caught) pins the one column written, the limits, the log, the undo, the ledger guard, the witness and its windows, the
columns against `db/schema.sql`, no customer data, the reader's wiring and the kept check.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot): the counts are the test book's. **The same last resort is still in the company's own forms** (complaints, restructures, advance requests, the call-app sheets: a
small file of early-in-the-month dates has no evidence and reads day-first) and **`dateOrNull` still reads ISO and `a/b/yyyy` only** (matter 4). Payments uploaded and pruned before this run are gone: only what the book holds is put right.
A payment uploaded a month late is the one coincidence above. The deck's `last_trans_date`, the Expected sheet's dates and every other table are the next matters.

**What the owner has to do.** Run `db/RUN-ME-065` (pasted in the chat) when no upload is running and paste its answer: how many were put right, how many are still dated outside their upload's fortnight, and the example lines.

## Part 94 — Dates, matter 3: the decks' Last trans dates (RUN-ME-066)

> "... we have last trans date column ..." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026 (Part 92 has the whole order: "repair one per time so that users see progress on the rised matters").

**What was wrong.** The old defaulters reader read every date of a deck day-first and the loan system writes them month-first (Part 84), so wherever both numbers of a date were twelve or under the day and the month were stored swapped.
`db/RUN-ME-060` puts DISB DATE, EXPIRE DATE and CHRONIC DATE right because the loan system's own pattern checks them (91 days, 14 days, DAYS ELAPSED). **LAST TRANS DATE came in the same file by the same reader, swapped the same way, and has no
pattern of its own**, so RUN-ME-060 never touched it (its header said so). It is the date behind the "Last payment" of a loan on the Follow-up list, and a swapped one often shows itself: a stored date later than the deck's own day, or before
the loan was disbursed, is one the loan system never wrote.

**How it is repaired: `db/RUN-ME-066-repair-swapped-last-trans-dates.sql` (pasted in full in the chat), run AFTER RUN-ME-060, for the same days.** A guess is not enough to rewrite a column with no pattern, so it changes an upload only when **the
upload itself proves it was read the wrong way round, twice**, and a row only when the date it would become is a date that row could have. An upload is every row written under one upload number for one day and one kind of deck (the old reader decided
for a whole file, so an upload is swapped all through or right all through):

1. **RUN-ME-060 put right at least three of its rows, and they are at least half of the rows of the upload that fit the loan system's pattern.** Read from `defaulter_date_repair_log`, which is why 060 is run first. The half is not decoration: the reader
   that has been live since 16 Nov decides per request (per slice of a file), so a small slice that gave it no clue could leave a few swapped rows inside an upload that was otherwise read right, and three of them must not make the whole upload a swapped one.
   A real swapped file is about 80% (8,296 of 10,372 on the real 16 Nov deck).
2. **At least three of its rows carry a LAST TRANS DATE that is impossible as stored and possible with day and month exchanged** (before the loan's disbursement or after the deck's own day; exchanged, between the two) on a loan whose dates fit the pattern.
   RUN-ME-060 proves the date columns of the pattern were read day-first; this proves that the Last trans column was, which the first proof cannot: a file whose Last trans column arrived as real date cells while the others were text would pass the first proof and fail this one.

**A row is changed only when** its upload has both proofs, its loan's three dates fit the pattern (so its Disb date is right), its LAST TRANS DATE has another reading (day twelve or under, and not equal to the month), that other reading lies between the
Disb date and the deck's day, and it was not changed before. Left exactly as they are: a row with no Last trans date, a date with a day over twelve (it was read right), a day and month the same, a loan RUN-ME-060 could not put right (restructured, no DAYS ELAPSED,
no chronic date), and every row of an upload with no upload number (the old rows from before batches cannot be told apart).

**The proof is read from the date as it was uploaded** (`coalesce(log.last_trans_old, last_trans_date)`), because a run that stops at the row limit changes some of an upload's witnesses and a proof read from the current date would be gone on the next run
and strand the rest of the upload: found while designing the "run again until 0" flow and pinned by a scenario (three rows changed two, then one) and by a deliberate break.

**It says what it left alone.** The answer has nine lines (rows in the days, uploads found swapped / left alone, rows with another reading in swapped uploads, how many are safe, changed now, **still to do: run it again until 0**, left alone because the
loan's dates do not fit (or RUN-ME-060 is not finished), left alone because the other reading is not possible, rows with another reading in uploads not found swapped) and then **one line per upload**: `2026-11-10 initial 3f2a9c1e: 10,372 rows; RUN-ME-060 put right
8,296; 311 show the exchange: SWAPPED`, or why it was left alone (no upload number; RUN-ME-060 put right none of it, so it was read right or 060 has not been run for that day; too few of its rows; no Last trans date of it shows the exchange). No name and no
loan number are printed.

**It changes `last_trans_date` of the deck rows and nothing else.** Every row changed is in `defaulter_last_trans_repair_log` (the date as uploaded and the new one), a row in that log is never changed twice (a second run changes nothing; after the undo the rows stay in the log
and are not changed again), the undo is at the foot, and the file has a 3-second lock and a 50-second statement limit and says in plain words, before it makes or changes anything, if RUN-ME-060 was never run ("Run db/RUN-ME-060 first...").

**Cost, measured on a book of the live book's size.** `SCALE=1 node tools/db-checks/last-trans-repair.mjs`: **2,332,800 deck rows, about 855 MB with the live table's indexes** (the date, date-and-type, team-and-ref and the two trigram indexes besides the schema's three), the
six days 10 to 15 Nov (**129,600 rows**, every one the old reader's, in 12 uploads): **RUN-ME-066 changed 50,000 rows in 4.2 to 4.6 s (two runs), the remaining 5,920 in 1.0 to 1.1 s, and a run with nothing left to do takes 0.7 s**, against the 50-second limit
(RUN-ME-060 on the same book: 4.9 and 5.0 s, 4.4 and 4.6 s, and 0.1 and 0.2 s for its 101,430 rows). Afterwards **all 129,600 rows of the six days hold the real Last trans date, and the other 2,203,200 deck rows have the same checksum before and after**
(the run fails if they do not). It reads the days named through the `snapshot_date` index and the two logs, and writes only what it changes. Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no code that runs for a user changed (`BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged).

**Checked.** `tools/db-checks/last-trans-repair.mjs` runs the WHOLE of `db/schema.sql` in a scratch database and **the real RUN-ME-060** first (it makes the log the proof is read from; the model of 060 is compared with its log and with the dates it leaves,
row for row), then this file: 14,924 deck rows in 37 uploads, 25 of them swapped, 3,375 Last trans dates exchanged. The fixture knows the truth and has an upload made to stand on each line of the rule and fall just short of it: exactly three repaired rows, two (with
the exchange shown on three), a swapped slice of five in an upload of thirty-five that was read right, an upload swapped but whose own dates show no exchange, swapped rows with **no upload number**, and an upload changed across several runs; a right upload on the SAME
day and kind as a swapped one; restructured loans, loans with no DAYS ELAPSED and no chronic date, DAYS ELAPSED eleven days off in each direction on loans whose dates otherwise fit, a last transaction before the disbursement (165 rows) and one after the deck's day (123),
rows with no last transaction, and dates whose day and month are the same. It passes only when: after every run (four runs of at most 1,500 rows) every row equals **a model of the rule written again in JavaScript**, and every row changed equals the real last transaction it
was stored from; no row stored right and no other column was touched; the answer of every run and **the verdict of every upload** equal the model's; the run that hit the limit says how many remain and the last one says 0; a narrow window (10 to 12 Nov) changes only
those days; small runs (a hundred rows, thirty-five of them) end where one big run ends; a window with no upload answers zero; a book where RUN-ME-060 never ran is told so; and **the file's own undo puts every row back, byte for byte**. **Twenty-eight deliberate breaks** (a proof moved
or dropped, the half dropped or made a twentieth, the second proof's two halves dropped one at a time, rows with no upload number judged as one upload, the uploads told apart by day and kind, a bound dropped on either side, a row that does not fit changed, a date with no other
reading made a candidate, a changed row changed again, the proof read from the current date, the exchange not made or not made on a twelfth, DAYS ELAPSED widened either way, every row counted as repaired, no row limit, the window ignored, the log empty or with the dates
the wrong way round, the wrong column, the wrong still-to-do, the wrong verdict) each change the outcome: **28 of 28**. `test/last-trans-repair.test.mjs` (12 tests) pins the one column written, the limits, the log, the undo, the guard, both proofs and their numbers, the pattern and the exchange against RUN-ME-060's,
the columns against `db/schema.sql`, no customer data, the answer's lines and the kept check.

**Two mistakes of mine the check found, said plainly.** (1) The first fixture's "loans whose three dates can all be misread" **cannot exist**: the chronic date is 14 days after the expiry, so their days of the month differ by 14 and cannot all be twelve or under. Its special
uploads were empty or tiny, and half its checks passed on nothing. The fixture now builds its special loans from the days that exist (and throws when it cannot), and **counts the kinds of row a break needs before any break is believed** (two breaks were "not caught" because the fixture lacked the row each needs: a last transaction before the disbursement, and DAYS ELAPSED off on loans whose
dates otherwise fit; a broken file that fails to run is counted by the check as a failure of the check, not as a caught break). (2) The first rule proved an upload by three
repaired rows alone; written down as a risk before it shipped, the share and the second proof were added.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot): the counts above are the test book's. **`due_date`** of the decks (the importer's fifth date column, `DUE DATE`) was swapped the same way and is NOT repaired here: the scan of RUN-ME-064 shows
whether any row holds one, and the same two proofs would carry it once its bounds are known (matter 4). **The Expected sheet's `last_trans_date`** (`repayment_snapshots`: the customer page's "Last payment" reads it first, Part 91 addendum) has no witness of its own and no log
of a repair to read; **the Follow-up list's** was rewritten whole by the 17 Nov Current deck (RUN-ME-062 found 0 of 10,401 later than today). An upload with too few rows to show the exchange (a deck of a few dozen loans) is left alone and listed, not guessed. **A date that is swapped
and still inside the loan's days (both readings possible) is changed on the upload's proof alone**: that is the rule's whole premise, the all-or-nothing reading of the old importer, measured on the real file (Part 90: month-first in all four date columns, nothing day-first).

**What the owner has to do.** After RUN-ME-060 for a window has said `still_to_do_run_again` 0, run RUN-ME-066 (pasted in the chat) with the **same two dates**, away from an upload (an evening upload deletes the rows of the files it replaces), **again until its "still to do" line says 0**,
and paste the nine lines and the list of uploads. For 10 to 15 Nov it is about 130,000 rows: two or three runs.

## Part 95 — Dates, matter 4a: the formats a spreadsheet writes a date in (one reader, `parse.js`)

> "... different excels might come with different fomarts am not sure." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026 (Part 92 has the whole order).

**What was wrong.** Two forms were read, ISO (`2026-07-09`) and `a/b/yyyy` (or `a-b-yyyy`), and **every other way a spreadsheet writes a date came back as nothing, in silence**, and the row went in with an empty date:
`09-Jul-2026`, `9 July 2026`, `Jul 9, 2026`, `09.07.2026`, `2026/07/09`, `20260709`, an Excel serial number (`46210`: a date cell that arrived as a number), and a slash date with a clock (`7/9/2026 14:03`, which only the
stamp reader knew). Two hazards beside them: **a date that does not exist was returned as one** (`dateOrNull('31/02/2026')` gave `2026-02-31`, which the database refuses, so the whole slice of the upload fails; and
`stampOrNull('31/02/2026 10:00')` gave **3 March**: `new Date("2026-02-31T10:00:00+03:00")` rolls over instead of failing).

**What changed (`api/_lib/parse.js`; no front-end file, so `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are unchanged).**

- **One place reads the new forms: `moreDateParts_`**, asked AFTER the two old forms by both readers (`dateOrNull` through `dateParts_`, `stampOrNull` directly). Month names (English and Swahili, whole words: `Sept`, `Septemba`, `Mei`, `Julai`;
  never a guess at a prefix), with an optional weekday before (`Thu,`, `Alhamisi`) and ordinal (`9th`); year first with a slash or a dot; day.month.year with dots; compact `YYYYMMDD` (1900 to 2099); an Excel serial number; and an optional clock
  after any of them (`14:03`, `2:03:11 PM`). A name decides the month, so these need no order; a dotted pair is ordered by **the same rule as a slash pair** (a part over twelve decides, then the file's order, then day-first): ONE function,
  `dayMonthOf_`, now decides it for the old forms and the new alike (it replaced the copy written inline in each reader).
- **A date has to exist** (`validDate_`): 31 February, 31 April, 29 February of a year with none, month 0, day 0 and year 0 are no date for either reader, whatever the form: the cell reads as unreadable instead of failing the slice or
  becoming the next month.
- **The file's own evidence reads dotted dates too** (`inferDayFirst`, `tightestSpanIsDayFirst`, `nearestToDayIsDayFirst`), so one file keeps one order.
- **The company's own sheets** (complaints, restructures, notices, deductions, advances, staff, call users and call history) cut a cell at its first space before reading it (`dateCell_`, to drop a clock), which would have turned `9 July 2026` into
  `9` and kept the new forms away from them. A cell that reads whole is now read whole; any other cell is cut at its first space exactly as before.
- **The serial window and the fraction rule are choices, written down.** An Excel serial number is taken for a date only from 2010-01-01 to 2040-12-31 (40179 to 51501), and a fraction is a clock only when it has four digits or more (`46210.4375`):
  a five-digit number in a date column is nearly always a date, but an amount in a misplaced column (`45000.00`, `45000.5`) must not become one. `46210.5` (exactly noon) is therefore NOT read; say so if a file ever shows one.
  A phone, an account, a TIN, an amount with a comma, `12345`, `99999`, `30260709` and a word are not dates (tested).

**What did NOT change.** **Whatever the old readers read is read exactly as before:** the old code is kept in `test/date-formats.test.mjs` as a yardstick and compared with the new over **60,000 generated strings** in the old forms (both orders, with
and without a clock, with junk after): the same date, except where the old one returned a date that does not exist. The two old forms are tried first, untouched; a day over twelve still decides the order; two-digit years are read as before.

**Cost.** CPU only, and almost none: 675,000 calls of `dateOrNull` took 170 ms before and 204 ms after (the common M/D/YYYY value is read by the same two regular expressions as before, then checked to exist); a deck's 50,000 date cells cost about
2.5 ms more. No read and no write added; nothing on `/api/upload`'s round trips or on `/api/call`.

**Checked.** `test/date-formats.test.mjs` (16 tests): fifty-two new forms each read as the date they are by both readers; the clock comes with the stamp; the order of a dotted date; the evidence; the old readers' own examples; the 60,000-string
comparison; the dates that do not exist; the list of things that must not become dates; **20,000 generated dates written in every form read back as themselves** and every Excel serial of 2010 to 2040 read as the right day; the importers
(a deck in month names, serial numbers and dotted dates in every one of its five date columns; payments; a complaint, a restructure and a notice with a date written with spaces; a cell the company importers cut at its first space is still cut there);
and a pin that **one function reads the forms and both readers use it**. **Twenty deliberate breaks of `parse.js`** (each form dropped in turn, the Swahili names, a month taken by its first three letters, the compact form for any year, the serial window opened,
an amount-like fraction taken for a clock, the fraction not a clock, 31 allowed in every month, every year a leap year, the stamp reader not checking, the stamp reader not reading the new forms, the order read the other way, dotted dates not evidence,
the end anchor dropped, the clock tail taking anything, the weekday not read) are each caught. `npm test`: all of it passes.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **A date that still cannot be read is still stored empty without a word**: telling the person on the Upload screen how many cells could not be read, and an example, is matter 4b (next: a per-slice number the page adds up, as
`receivedAbnormal` is). (2) **The company's own forms still fall back to day-first when a small file gives no evidence** (matter 4c): changing it needs one real file of each, because a rule written without seeing the file is the guess this
order is against (section 8 of `CHAT.md` asks for them). (3) A month with no day (`July 2026`) and a weekday alone stay unreadable on purpose: a day is never invented. (4) The Upload page's own spreadsheet reader is unchanged (real date cells already
arrive as `yyyy-mm-dd`). (5) Nothing was run on the live book; nothing needs running there: no SQL.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing. Files in those forms are read from the next upload on; files already uploaded keep what was stored (an empty date stays empty: upload the file again if it matters).

## Part 96 — Dates, matter 4b: a date no reader could read is counted out loud (the Upload screen says how many, with examples)

> "... different excels might come with different fomarts am not sure." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026 (Part 92 has the whole order; Part 95 is the formats).

**What was wrong.** A cell that held something and did not read as a date came back as NULL: the row went in with an empty date (or, in the sheets that need one, with the moment of the upload), and **nothing on the screen said so**. Part 95 reads
many more forms; a form nobody has seen, a typo (`9/31/2026`), a word in a date column (`sometime`), a shifted column, would still go in silently.

**What changed.**

- **`unreadableDatesOf(type, rows, { stage })` (`api/_lib/importers.js`)** counts, for an upload of that type, the cells of its date columns that hold something and do not read, and keeps up to three distinct examples (each cut at thirty characters).
  It reads **the same column lists the importers read** (`DEFAULTER_DATE_COLUMNS`, `EXPECTED_DATE_COLUMNS`, `FOLLOWUP_DATE_COLUMNS`, `PAYMENT_DATE_COLUMNS`, the loans' `DISB DATE` and `APPROVED DATE`, and the company sheets' own lists: one definition of which columns are dates) and
  **the same reader**, the company's sheets through `dateCell_` exactly as their importers do, so a cell is counted only when the importer really lost it. **Parity is tested against the importers themselves** (below).
- **What is not counted:** an empty cell; the ways the loan system and the company's sheets say "no date" on purpose (a dash, `N/A`, `nil`, `none`, `null`, `TBD`, `hakuna`, a bare `0`, `No Due Date`); anything the reader reads. **Whether a cell reads never depends on the order of the file**
  (with both parts twelve or under both readings are real dates, with one over twelve that part decides), so no order is asked: a first draft passed the order along, and the mutation run showed it changed nothing (an equivalent mutant), so it went.
- **Which uploads:** the defaulters decks (current and initial), the four Expected sheets, the Defaulters Followup file, received payments, approved loans (**not** the application stages, which ignore the file's own date columns, so they lose nothing and say 0), complaints, restructures, call users,
  call history and demand notices. **Not counted yet:** the comments log (it counts its own unreadable stamps, as before), the staff registry, the deductions and the advances (stamp-or-day cells), the two summaries.
- **The server answers a plain number, not a sentence.** `/api/upload` returns `unreadableDates: { count, examples }` on every slice of those types (`{ count: 0, examples: [] }` when everything read, so the slices can be added up) and nothing on the others. There is no server sentence on purpose: `message` is per-slice text and
  the page keeps only the last slice's (the abnormal-payments note in `upload.js` says why). **Automatic feeders read the field.**
- **The page adds the slices up and says it once, in its two languages** (`public/upload.html`: `sendInSlices_` sums like `duplicates`; the Done message): "⚠ ANGALIA: tarehe 7 kwenye faili hii hazikusomeka (mfano: “sometime in July”, “soon”, “later”) ... hakuna tarehe iliyokisiwa" and "⚠ WARNING: 7 date(s) in this file could NOT be read (for example ...) They were
  NOT stored as written (left empty, or the day of this upload where the sheet needs a date) and no date was guessed. Check the file's date columns." A file that read in full says nothing, and a type with no such field gains no stray zero. The page is its own no-cache page: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are unchanged.

**Cost.** CPU only: one more pass over the date cells of each slice (a deck's 50,000 cells: a few milliseconds in all), no read and no write: **a defaulters upload costs the same round trips with and without unreadable dates** (a test counts them), `/api/call` untouched.

**Checked.** `test/unreadable-dates.test.mjs` (11 tests): the five columns of a deck each count; the placeholders, the empty cells and every readable form do not; examples (three, distinct, cut); **PARITY: over 3,000 generated deck rows, and over Expected, Followup, payments and approved loans, the count equals the number of

Also pinned: **no cell makes a date reader slow**: thirteen hostile cells of
100,000 characters (spaces, dots, slashes, chains of clocks, weekdays, month names, digits) take about 15 ms through the three readers in all, so the regular expressions of Part 95 cannot be made to backtrack.

**Read against the rule, and said plainly: "0 exchanged" and "7 of 7 fixable" are not "nothing to repair" and not "repair those".** 067 asked whether a stored date is the number's day *exactly exchanged*, and none is. The twelve dates later than today, all of them among the 280, show a different, exact relation:
**the stored date is the number's day with day and month exchanged, and a day early** (number 12 Oct → stored 9 Dec; 12 Sep → 8 Dec; 12 Aug → 7 Dec; 12 Jun → 5 Dec), and in ten of the twelve the stamp carries the same impossible day. All twelve are real 12ths of a month, as they must be:
a swap reaches the future only for a real day of 12 (Part 91). The 248 notices made in the app agree with their number to the day (the app writes the number from the date); the imported ones that agree (566) are what the register's script made.
For the deductions, 067's "put in order by exchanging the discovery date" is **true and not proof**: the five rows are one case (received 5 Jun 2026, discovered 6 May 2026, submitted 6 Jul 2026, as stored) and exchanging the *received* date instead (6 May), or both, puts the three dates in order just as well,
so the file cannot say which one was read the wrong way round. The two rows of the other case (discovered 6 Dec 2026, a day later than today, submitted 20 Jul 2026) are different: the submission day cannot be read two ways, and whichever way the received date is read, the discovery date's other reading (12 Jun 2026) is the only one that fits.
067's header said "not proof" and still named only the discovery date: that was incomplete.

**Where the extra day comes from: not found.** Looked for, in this order, and each step recorded because the next chat should not look again:
(1) **the importer.** `importDemandNotices` as of the last commit of 12 Oct (the day the 846 came back) is the same code as today: `dateOrNull(dateCell_(NOTICE DATE), dayFirst)`; nothing in it can make a date a day early, and no other code under `api/` writes `notice_date` but the app's own notice form.
(2) **the Upload page of that day.** It formats an Excel date cell with the browser's own `getFullYear / getMonth / getDate` (never the UTC form), and had since 22 Oct at least. (3) **replayed in a real Chromium set to `Africa/Dar_es_Salaam`**, through the page as it was before Part 89: a day-first CSV cell `12/9/2026` arrives as `2026-12-09` (an exact exchange, no day lost), a month-first one as `2026-09-12`, a text date with a part over twelve stays text,
and an Excel file whose date cells hold the true serials (written outside the browser) arrives exact, date-only cells and cells with a clock alike. Nothing that could be run produces "exchanged and a day early". What is left: the cells of the register sheet as they were on 12 Oct, or a reader on the machine that uploaded them (only Chromium is on the cloud machine; Safari and Firefox were not tried).
So the repair below is keyed to the **relation**, which is exact and which the live book shows, and not to a mechanism; and the answer it prints describes every notice it leaves, so the next step is built from numbers and not from this guess. **(Part 100 reads that answer: 251 of the 252 left are the same shape, the page replayed in nine time zones still does not make it, and the repair of them is RUN-ME-070.)**

**RUN-ME-068 (`db/RUN-ME-068-repair-impossible-notice-and-deduction-dates.sql`, pasted in full in the chat): it changes only what the row itself proves.**

- **A notice** (imported: its upload date is set) is changed **only when all three hold:** (1) its notice date is **later than the day it was uploaded** (a register sent on 12 Oct cannot hold a notice dated 9 Dec; the row's own upload day is read, not a day typed into the file); (2) its number (`HMCL/<initials>/<dd>/<mm>/<yyyy>`, TEXT, which no date reader ever touched) carries a real day not later than the upload day;
  (3) the stored date **is that day with day and month exchanged, or exchanged and a day early**. The notice date is written back as the number's day. Its **stamp** (`created_at`) moves with it **only if the stamp's own day is also after the upload day and is that same exchange**: it goes to the number's day at the same time of day in East Africa. Its **recoveries in `notice_payment_ledger`**
  (RUN-ME-041a, kept by notice date, joined to the notice by `(ref, since)`) move to the new date, so they stay on the notice; a ledger row that would meet the same payment already kept at the new date stays where it is. This reaches beyond "later than today": a real 11th of a month lands in November, after the 12 Oct upload and not later than today, and is just as impossible;
  067 could not see those, and nobody knows how many there are until this runs.
- **A deduction's discovery date** is changed **only when all hold:** it is **later than the day the case was submitted**; the submission day cannot be read two ways (its day is over twelve, or the same as its month); the discovery date has another reading (a day of twelve or under, not the month); that reading is **not after the submission day** and **not before the money was received under either reading of the received date**. One reading fits: it is written.
  A deduction discovered **before the money was received is not changed**: the answer prints each such case with which readings put it in order (the discovery only, the received date only, both), so that the right dates can be said once, from the register.
- **Left exactly as they are, and counted:** every notice dated after its upload day that fails one of the three tests (with the reason: no possible number day / the stored date is not that day exchanged); every app-made notice; every imported notice whose date merely differs from its number; every deduction not in the list. **The answer describes the imported notices that still differ from their number** (how many; one day early or late, within a week, further; against the exchange; the eight most common differences; the stamp; eight examples: dates and eight characters of an id only),
  because the 268 that are not later than today are not understood yet: those of them dated after their upload day with the same relation are repaired, **the rest are not touched** (a notice dated again after its number was made looks like one of them, and the owner's rule of 14 Nov is that a new rule is never invented for old ground). **No name, no loan number, no notice number, no amount is printed.**
- **Every row changed is in a log** (`demand_notice_date_repair_log`, `pmo_deduction_date_repair_log`, `notice_ledger_date_move_log`: old and new values, not readable through the public API), a row in a log is never changed again, so the file is **safe to run again** (the second run changes nothing and says so) and **an undone row stays undone**; the undo is at the foot, three statements, each restoring exactly what the logs name.
  A book without RUN-ME-041a is refused before anything is made ("Run db/RUN-ME-041a first"); the live book has the ledger.
- **Cost.** About 1,200 rows read, a few written: a fraction of a second on the live book; **1.9 s on a book a hundred times the live one** (100,000 notices of which 5,000 to repair, 10,000 deductions, a ledger of 40,000 rows). A 3-second lock limit and a 30-second ceiling that rolls it all back. Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no code that runs for a user changed (`BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged).

**Checked, on a PostgreSQL made from the real schema.** `tools/db-checks/notice-date-repair.mjs`: the whole of `db/schema.sql`, the two real migrations that add `notice_id` and `upload_date`, and the real RUN-ME-041a (the ledger and its primary key); the three log tables are made from the file's own DDL, never declared by hand (RUN-ME-061's lesson).
239 notices (made in the app; right; the shape of the twelve for every month, with a suffix on the number and six kinds of stamp; real 11ths that land in November; a plain exchange; the same shape before the upload day; other relations; a number later than the upload day; no usable number, lower case, a day that does not exist, a month 13; a day that cannot be exchanged; already in the log; a second upload day; stored dates within days of the number's day),
71 ledger rows (some meeting the same payment already at the real date; one customer with two notices), 103 deductions (late and fixable; the submission day readable two ways; the received date's other reading after the fix; late and not fixable; discovered before the money, in four shapes and eight cases; in order; nothing filled in):
**every row of the three tables, the three logs and every line the file prints equals a model written again in JavaScript** (70 dates changed, 51 stamps moved, 41 ledger rows moved, 9 deductions put right); a second run changes nothing; the undo puts every table back byte for byte and a run after it changes nothing; a book without the ledger is refused with nothing made; an empty and a clean book answer;
and **47 of 47 deliberate breaks of the file each change the outcome** (or, for the two guards, fail on the row they are for: a number typed `31/04`, a ledger row meeting another). `test/notice-date-repair.test.mjs` (12 tests; **46 of 46 deliberate breaks of the pins caught**) pins what a later edit must not loosen: the six tables written and no other, the limits, the guard, nothing printed that names anyone, the three-part proof, the stamp rule, the ledger and its move log, the deduction proof, that a number is read exactly as RUN-ME-067 reads it (one definition) and the exchange is RUN-ME-060's, `MATERIALIZED`, the columns against the schema, and the kept check.
**Three mistakes of mine the check found, said plainly.** (1) **The first undo would have failed on a real book:** it moved every ledger row at the new date back to the old one, including a row that already sat there with the same payment, and ran into the primary key. The moves are logged now and the undo restores exactly those. (2) The fixture's rows for an "earlier run" had old and new reversed and no stamps, so the undo tried to write an empty stamp: the fixture was wrong, not the file, and is built like a real log now. (3) The first read-back keyed ledger rows by (customer, payment), which folds two rows into one: found as a failure of the check. Also dropped as equivalent, not caught and not breaks: a guard (`isw is not null`) that `in (isw, isw - 1)` already makes redundant, and a column added to a `GROUP BY` that adds nothing.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot). **The imported notices that differ from their number and are not dated after their upload day are not repaired** (at most 268 of them; the answer describes them, and that is the next step, built from what it prints). **The one-day shift is not explained**, so no importer or page was changed for it, and a register uploaded tomorrow would be read as the old one was
(Part 89's pooled evidence and Part 96's count of unreadable dates are what protect it today). The five-row deduction case is not changed: it needs its real dates from the register. A stamp that is wrong while its notice date is right is not repaired (the rule moves a stamp only with its notice). Recoveries on a repaired notice since its real date are only as old as the payments still in the book (`received_payments` keeps two weeks); the next `fold_notice_payments` brings in what it can.

## Part 99 — A list of the staff without a bank account number: zone, team, staff name (RUN-ME-069)

> "I also need a list of all staff without bank account numbers / 3 columns - by zone (1st and primary), team, staff name / So that I send it and demand them in Whatsapp group / Include even those with no zone" — the owner, 17 Nov 2026

**What it is.** A read-only list, `db/RUN-ME-069-staff-without-bank-account-read-only.sql` (pasted in full in the chat the moment it was checked), for the owner to run in the SQL editor and send. A chat cannot run SQL, so it cannot hand over the list itself, only the query.

**Where the data is.** HR's registry, `staff_registry` (Part 49; `db/RUN-ME-044`): `name`, `role`, `zone`, `account`, `status`, all text. **The registry keeps no team column.** The team is what follows the role, `Field Officer - CHAMWINO`, which is how every staff script writes it (`role_word - team_text`,
`db/TEMPLATE-staff-changes-from-gmo.sql`); a head-office staff (Part 53) has a department for a zone and no team.

**The choices, said to the owner in the answer and written in the file's header:**
- **No bank account number** = the ACCOUNTS cell is empty, blank, has **no digit** in it (`N/A`, `NONE`, `ON PROCESS`, `-`, `HAINA`: placeholders a sheet import stores as text, `accountCell`), or its digits are all zeros. **An account with digits counts as given, however short it looks** (a digit-count threshold would be a guess; a list of accounts that look too short is offered, not built). **Only the ACCOUNTS cell is read**: a number typed into the bank-name cell counts as missing.
- **Active staff only.** A staff switched to Inactive has left; one word (`true` to `false`, on the line marked `CHANGE`) lists them too. The status is read as the portal reads it (capitals, blanks off).
- **Zone first and primary**, then team, then name, **in an explicit order (`collate "C"`)**, so the list is the same whatever the database's default order: the live book's en_US order ignores spaces and punctuation (`LAKEVIEW` before `LAKE ZONE`), a C order does not.
- **A staff with no zone is listed**, as `NO ZONE`, after the last zone (the registry's zone is a plain column: no join to the teams table, which would have dropped them). A staff with no team shows `-`. Zone, team and name are read as the registry writes them (runs of blanks as one, capitals): the same staff filed twice (two records) is listed twice, because a script never merges two staff records on a name alone.
- **Three columns and nothing else:** no account, phone, NIDA, bank or ID is printed (a test pins that the file does not even read them).

**Cost.** One pass over the registry (a few thousand rows at most): **0.75 s on a registry of 100,000 staff, a hundred times the live one**; a 30-second ceiling; nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no code that runs for a user changed (`BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged).

**Checked, on a PostgreSQL made from the real schema.** `tools/db-checks/staff-without-account.mjs`: the whole of `db/schema.sql`; 703 staff with accounts of every kind (real digits with leading zeros, letters and digits, digits with spaces and dashes, a short one, empty, blank, `N/A`, `NONE`, `ON PROCESS`, a dash, `HAINA`, only zeros, only letters), zones (filed, lower case, runs of blanks, none, empty, blank, a department, two whose order depends on how a database sorts spaces),
roles (with a team, with two dashes, with none, a dash and no team, lower case, extra blanks), statuses (Active, Inactive, inactive, with blanks), names (extra blanks, lower case, a tab), and a staff filed twice. **The list equals a model written again in JavaScript, row for row and in order, in two databases:** one that sorts like C and one whose default order ignores spaces and punctuation as the live book's does (this machine has no en_US; ICU's
`en-u-ka-shifted` is the stand-in, and the check first proves the two databases really do sort that pair differently). The other switch (Inactive included) does the same; the registry is byte-identical afterwards; an empty registry and one where everybody has an account give no row and no error; **24 of 24 deliberate breaks of the file each change the list**.
`test/staff-without-account.test.mjs` (9 tests; **22 of 22 deliberate breaks of the pins caught**, run against a baseline that passes) pins one table and no write, the three columns, the rule for an account, the switch and the status, the staff with no zone, the explicit order, how the zone, team and name are read, the columns against the schema, and the kept check.
**Two mistakes of mine the check found, said plainly.** (1) The fixture's strides shared a factor with the lists they walked (a stride of 5 over twenty zones used four of them): no staff had no zone, so five breaks passed; made coprime, they are caught. (2) A mutation run of the pins was first read as "22 of 22 caught" while the baseline itself failed (an end-of-text pattern): every mutant "failed" because the file did; the script now refuses to run on a baseline that does not pass.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot), so the number of staff on the list is not known. Accounts that have digits but look too short or wrong are treated as given. A number typed into the bank-name cell is read as missing. The list is a snapshot: it says nothing of who answered the WhatsApp group; the owner runs it again.

**What the owner has to do.** Run it (pasted in the chat) and send the three columns.

## Part 101 — The details the owner brings are the latest: the staff update by staff ID that replaces what the registry holds (`db/TEMPLATE-staff-update-by-id.sql`)

> "So you can see some names have been better updated and some info should be filled into their columns if missing or replace if existing since the provided is latest." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026, with the morning's staff answer pasted under it.

**What was true before.** Every staff script this repository kept changed the registry the careful way: PLACE and NEW fill only what is EMPTY, a NEW that finds the person changes nothing, and a name is never re-spelt (the owner's order of 11 Nov, "dont correct names using the gmo data i bring unless its new staff"; Parts 48 and 49). That is right for a list of names from a GMO, which carries nothing the registry does not already hold as well. It is wrong for a form the person filled in or a reply a GMO sends for a named person: the registry's spelling is the one a GMO typed first, and the form's is the person's own. The morning's ten replies were filed that way (PLACE fills the empty boxes) and the answer showed names in the registry spelt shorter, or another way, than the forms.

**The order, and how it is read.** The details the owner brings (a form, or an account and a name relayed from a GMO) are the latest: **fill a box that is empty, replace a box that holds something else, names included.** It is read as applying to a form or a reply the owner relays for a person the registry already holds. **A bare list of names from a GMO, with no details, still never renames anybody**: the 11 Nov order stands for those. The owner was told this once, and can object.

**The template.** One row for each person. The staff is found by **staff ID AND the name the registry carries now** (the answer of the PLACE or NEW script prints the ID), so a mistyped ID cannot change somebody else: a row whose ID is not in the registry says NO STAFF WITH THAT ID, one whose ID carries another name prints that name, and nothing changes. **Fifteen boxes:** name, phone, second phone, bank, account, NIDA, TIN, NSSF, birth date, residence, start date (the registry's REG-DATE), and the two relatives each with the number beside them. For each box the row gives, the file works out one of **filled** (the registry's box was empty), **replaced** (it held something else), **same** (the same number written another way: a phone with or without its 0 or its 255, a NIDA with or without dashes, capitals or not; nothing is written), **cleared** (only a relative's number, below) or **none** (the row leaves the box null: **never touched, never emptied**; "nil", "on process", "--" and "hana" are written as null). Only a filled, replaced or cleared box is written. **The role, the zone, the status and the staff ID are never touched**: they are the MOVE and PLACE scripts' work, and a role the registry already holds in more detail than a form's wording stays.
**The guards** the owner's earlier orders and the registry's own rules put in. A **NIDA that is not twenty digits is never written** (it could replace a good one; the row says how many digits it had). **The birth date is the NIDA's** (its first eight digits, as the staff form reads it), else the form's, and **it is never set beside a NIDA it was not read from**: if the registry's own NIDA gives another date than the form's, the form's date is not written and the row says so. **A relative's number is written beside the name it came with**; if another person replaces the name and no number comes with them, the old number (somebody else's) is cleared, and the row says so. A name the update takes that **another staff already carries** is printed (LOOK), not blocked: a script never merges two staff records on a name alone (the house rule).
**Before anything is changed** each row about to change is copied to `staff_registry_update_before` (the very columns the update can write, under the label on the line marked CHANGE; row-level security on and no policy, so it is not readable through the public API); the three lines at the foot, with their dashes taken off, put every one of them back from that copy; the copies stay, so the undo can be run again; **a second run changes nothing and says so.** **It prints no value:** ten columns, each box by its NAME, never a phone, an account, a NIDA, a TIN, an NSSF or an address.
**Cost.** The staff registry only (a few thousand rows; the list is a few dozen); **4.8 to 5.6 s on a registry of 50,000, ten times the live one**; a 5-second lock limit, a 60-second ceiling, the compiler off; nothing on `/api/upload`, nothing on `/api/call`; no front-end file, so `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` are unchanged.

**Checked, on a PostgreSQL made from the real schema.** `tools/db-checks/staff-update.mjs` builds the table from the whole of `db/schema.sql` (never one declared by hand: the lesson of Part 90) and runs the template **as written** with only its list replaced: 96 generated staff with every box in every state (empty, the same number written another way, another value, junk; a row that gives the box and a row that leaves it null; a NIDA that is good, not a day, 22 digits, none; relatives who are none, the same person with or without a number, another person with or without one), two decoys carrying a name some rows send, and 300 other staff the list never names. It passes only when **every column of every staff equals a model written again in JavaScript**, the staff nobody named are byte-identical, every printed line equals the model's field by field, the before-images hold exactly the rows changed with what they held, no printed line holds a value, **a second run changes nothing, the undo puts the whole registry back byte for byte**, and a registry of 50,000 is answered in seconds. It then **breaks the file on purpose 58 ways** (the ID alone finds the person; a box that holds something is never replaced; a box the row leaves null is emptied; a name, a phone, a NIDA, a TIN, an NSSF, a residence or a guarantor compared as typed; a phone's 255 prefix not dropped at any one of the eight places a phone is read; a 22-digit NIDA written; the birth date written beside a NIDA it was not read from; a relative's old number left beside another person; the role or the status written; the before-image not taken, taken again, or short of a column; the copies readable through the public API; the answer wrong, printing a value, or silent about a NIDA it refused) and **all 58 change the outcome**. `test/staff-update-template.test.mjs` is the guard in `npm test` (Node cannot run SQL): 10 pins (it names nobody; it writes only the registry and its copies; the fifteen boxes whole, as a table; the guard by ID and name; the NIDA and birth-date guards; the before-image columns equal the update's and the undo's; no value printed; a phone read exactly as the staff template reads it, in **all eight places**; the notes; what the kept check still does), and **85 of 85 deliberate breaks of the pins are caught**.

**Mistakes of mine the check found, said plainly.** (1) The first fixture built phones that began 255, which the file's own reading drops again, so every second run still said UPDATED: a fault of the fixture (a real mobile number starts with 6 or 7), not of the file. (2) The fixture had nobody for whom the registry already held everything, so "nothing to change" was never asked, and nobody whose form's birth date disagreed with the registry's own NIDA; both were added, with a count of every kind of row before a break is believed. (3) The runner for the breaks that must FAIL never ran the broken file (a short-circuit): it counted a break as caught because it was never run. (4) One break edited only the insert's column list, and the insert has more expressions than that: it is a two-site edit. (5) **Two of the pins matched the check's header comment rather than its code, and a phone pin looked at the first of eight places**: a mutation run of the pins found three of 42 uncaught (two were my own mutations landing on a comment, one a real hole). The pins now read the check's code with its header stripped and the phone in all eight places, the registry's own readings are pinned too, and the run is 85 of 85. (6) The fixture's relatives' numbers never carried the 255 prefix, so a break of their reading could not show; it does now, and the check holds 16 more breaks (58 in all) for the registry-side readings.

**The first batch: three forms of 17 Nov, 13:09 to 13:13.** They came relayed from the WhatsApp group. **All three people were already in the registry:** two officers of the Mara zone, added on 11 Nov from a list of names (Field Officer, no team, no details: they were on the no-account list of that morning), and an officer of the South West zone, added on 13 Nov in the Lindi batch (a phone and a bank filed, nothing else). ## Part 104 — The swapped dates of each customer's last-known deck row, put right in place (RUN-ME-071)

> "Repair everything that's wrong brother I can't be perfect to detect every where dates are wrong ... When we finish disb dates ..." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026; and, 16 Nov: "Don't clean owner role, recycling leader & cycle for 'cleared' customers at expected defaulters because the disb date still gives us where to place them for the 3 columns - we need those 3 filled for followup purposes".

**What is wrong.** Four deck rows in five carry a Disb, Expire and Chronic date with the day and the month swapped (the old importer; Part 84). A customer who is no longer on any deck is shown on the Expected Defaulters tab as CLEARED from **their last-known row** (RUN-ME-055's function, Part 71: the newest current row of the team's loan number), and that row's Disb date is what places them on a cycle day, a recycling leader and a week. Those rows are spread over every day since August. Putting them right the day-by-day way (RUN-ME-060 over every day, about two million rows) is the long road to the same place.

**What the file does (`db/RUN-ME-071-repair-swapped-last-known-deck-dates.sql`, pasted in full in the chat).** It changes the Disb, Expire and Chronic dates of **a customer's last-known row and of no other row**, by **exactly RUN-ME-060's rule** (the loan system's own pattern: a loan expires 91 days after it was disbursed and turns chronic 14 days after it expires; DAYS ELAPSED is the days from the disbursement to the deck's day, less 0 to 3; a row is changed only when its dates as stored do not fit and exactly one reading of them fits; nothing is guessed). **A last-known row** is a CURRENT row for which no newer current row of the same team and loan number exists, on any day (a row of the same day counts as newer when it was written later: a day uploaded twice): the choice RUN-ME-055's function makes, and a pin compares the two. An initial row, a row that is not its customer's newest, Last trans date and everything else are never touched; a customer still on the latest deck has a newest row that was written right. The first lines name the window (the whole range since August, to begin with: 1 Aug to 15 Nov) and `max_rows` (50,000; **0 counts and changes nothing**). Its own log table (`defaulter_last_known_repair_log`: not RUN-ME-060's, which RUN-ME-066 reads: rows put right here are not days put right), the undo at the foot, 3-second lock limit, 50-second ceiling that rolls it all back, and the answer says how many last-known rows the window held, how many do not fit, how many have one reading, how many were repaired, how many are still to do and how many were left alone. **Never at the same moment as RUN-ME-060 or 066, or during an upload** (they write the same table).

**CORRECTED IN PART 106: this form of the file TIMED OUT ON THE LIVE BOOK ("upstream timeout"), and the figures in the next paragraph were measured on a book held in memory and laid out customer after customer; they are not a promise about the live book. The file is now run one day at a time (Part 106).**

**Cost, measured (of the first form).** It reads the current rows of the window (through the `snapshot_date` index) and probes the `(ref, snapshot_date)` index once for each row that does not fit; it writes only the rows it changes (the customers who left). **On a book of 2.44 million rows with the real table's indexes: one month in 1.5 s, the whole range counted in 1.8 s** (10,001 last-known rows in the month, 8,134 repaired). The live book is bigger and slower than the test machine; the ceiling of 50 seconds rolls a run that is cut off back whole, and a shorter window is the answer. Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked, on a PostgreSQL made from the real schema.** `tools/db-checks/last-known-repair.mjs` builds the book the way the old importer left it (swapped wherever both numbers were twelve or under, except the uploads that came right and every upload from 16 Nov) with 728 customers: left on every day of the window, still on the latest deck, **left with only an INITIAL row on their last day** (the current file dropped them that evening), **days uploaded twice** (the later batch is the newest), **the same loan number in two teams**, moved loans (an expiry moved by the days a swap moves a disbursement), loans whose DAYS ELAPSED says nothing true, no chronic date, no DAYS ELAPSED. It passes only when **every row of the table equals a model of the rule written again in JavaScript** after a run over the window (and after small runs of 40 rows, and after a narrow window), the answer's numbers equal the model's, a second run changes nothing, a count (`max_rows` 0) changes nothing, the file's own undo puts every row back byte for byte, the log holds exactly the rows repaired, no initial row, no row that is not its customer's newest and no customer still on the latest deck was touched; and **14 deliberate breaks of the file all change the outcome** (no test of a newer row; an initial row counted as newer; the type of the candidate not asked; the team not part of the customer; the tie of one day uploaded twice broken wrongly in three ways; the window not asked or ending where it starts; the witness of DAYS ELAPSED dropped; the twelfth not a swappable day; the limit not kept; the log not kept; the Chronic date not written). One mutation is not listed and why: `count(*) = 1` to `>= 1` cannot change a book, since two different readings cannot both fit with DAYS ELAPSED as a witness (a swap moves a date by at least 27 days and the witness allows 3). `test/last-known-repair.test.mjs` (6 tests in `npm test`) pins what Node can see: the file writes only the three dates and its own log, the limits, the choice of a last-known row against RUN-ME-055's, **the text of RUN-ME-060's rule word for word** (the exchange, the pattern, the one reading, the guard of the write: two copies of one rule drift), the answer's columns, and what the kept check still does; **21 of 21 deliberate breaks of the pins are caught**.

**Mistakes of mine the check found, said plainly.** (1) The first run of the check ran the file outside one transaction, so `set local` did nothing and the file's own limits were not the limits it ran under; it now runs as the SQL editor sends it, `begin` and `commit` around the file. (2) Three of fifteen breaks were not caught at first: one was an equivalent mutant (above), one ignored a limit that only a small `max_rows` shows (the signature now runs a limit of 7 first), and one was malformed (the broken file did not run, which is not a caught break: the check counts it as a failure of the check). (3) The first timing book held 1.2 million rows, not the two million asked for; it holds 2.44 million now.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book (a chat cannot): the answer's numbers are the owner's to paste, and how many customers have left is not known. A customer's earlier rows (every day before the last) are NOT repaired: they are what RUN-ME-060 over the days is for, and nothing on the Expected Defaulters tab reads them. The Expected sheet's dates, the decks' `due_date` and the other registers are not touched (Part 103).

**What the owner had to do (of the first form; superseded by Part 106).** Run RUN-ME-071 as pasted (50,000 rows a run) until `still_to_do_run_again` says 0, **never at the same moment as 060, 066 or an upload**; `max_rows` 0 counts first. If a run is cut off with a statement timeout it changed nothing: narrow the two dates to a month. Then look at the Expected Defaulters tab: the cleared customers' Disb date, owner role, recycling leader and cycle are the real ones (the tab remembers its answer for about 90 seconds).
