## Part 106 — RUN-ME-071 timed out on the live book; it now runs one day at a time, with the clock on (17 Nov)

> "071 / Error: SQL query ran into an upstream timeout / You can either optimize your query, or increase the statement timeout or connect to your database directly." — the owner, 17 Nov 2026, on the file of Part 104.

**What happened.** The first form of `db/RUN-ME-071-repair-swapped-last-known-deck-dates.sql` asked the database, in ONE statement, to look at every current row of the window (about 1.1 million rows since August) and to ask of each whether a newer row of the same customer exists. On the test book that took 4.3 seconds because the book was held in memory; the statement reads the deck table end to end (measured afterwards on a book of 2.27 million rows, 84,000 pages: **172,196 pages touched**, twice the table), and on the live book (disk reads, other work, a smaller machine) it ran past what the SQL editor waits for. The editor said "upstream timeout", not "statement timeout", so it gave up BEFORE the file's own 50-second ceiling: the database may have gone on and committed, and the owner could not tell. A read-only check was handed over at once (the number of rows in `defaulter_last_known_repair_log`, 0 or no table meaning it rolled back, and whether a query that names the log is still running); its answer is the owner's to paste (section 8 of `CHAT.md`).

**The claim that was wrong, said plainly.** Part 104 and the file's header said the whole range took 2 seconds (1.8 s counted). That was a measurement of a cache and of a layout (the old timing book wrote its rows customer after customer, so one day's rows were scattered over the whole table and the planner read the table in one pass), put in a header as if it held on the live book. A time on a cached test machine is not a bound on anything. Corrected where it stood (Part 104) and in the file.

**What the file does now.** One day at a time, NEWEST day first (the customers cleared lately are the ones the Expected Defaulters tab shows), in a `do` block with a clock: after a day is finished, another is started only while `lk_seconds` (10) have not passed, so a run always does at least one day and stops a few seconds past the clock at most. For a day D: `v_next` is the next day that has a current deck at all; `nx` is who is on that deck; `gone` is D's current rows of customers who are NOT on it (the cheap test: a customer on the next deck is not at the end of their run); `lk` looks up each of those rows once in the `(ref, snapshot_date)` index with `snapshot_date >= D` and `limit 1` (a `left join lateral`: it cannot be turned into a hash join over the table) and keeps those with no newer current row of the same team and loan number (a row of the same day counts when written later): **the same definition as before and as RUN-ME-055's function, now found by a few hundred lookups a day instead of a pass over the book.** From there the chain is RUN-ME-060's rule word for word (`cand`, `one`, `take`, `lg`, `upd`: pinned against 060's text). **Every finished day is written down** (`defaulter_last_known_repair_days`, primary key the day, RLS on: two runs at the same moment cannot both write a day), so the owner runs THE SAME TEXT AGAIN until the answer says `FINISHED`; the answer says the days done in this run, the oldest day done, the last-known rows, those not fitting, those with one reading, those repaired, those left alone, the days still to do and what to do next. The first lines name the window (1 Aug to 15 Nov), the clock and `lk_apply` (`'no'` counts and writes nothing, not even the days). `statement_timeout` is **30 s** (the first form had 50), so the database cuts a stuck script off by itself, with a clean "canceling statement due to statement timeout" and nothing changed, before the editor gives up; `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` (every day is planned for its own two dates) and `enable_seqscan = off` (a day is read through the day index, never by reading the table). The undo (commented, at the foot) restores the dates from the log and clears the days.

**Cost, measured in PAGES, which do not depend on what is cached.** On a book of 2.27 million rows laid out day after day, the way uploads lay it out (84,000 table pages, the real table's other indexes): **a one-day run touches 3,300 to 5,900 pages** (3.9% of the table; the busiest day of the two books measured), 10,400 when it also writes 230 rows (the writes keep seven indexes; the live table has two more); **the same run on half the book touches the same pages** (3,678 against 3,274); with the test of the next deck taken out it touches 74,988 (23 times as many); the first form touched 172,196. **The whole range, counted day by day, took 3 to 5 seconds on the test machine, cached; the live seconds are not known and the number of runs the owner will need cannot be said until the first answer.** Its numbers equal the first form's on the same book (31,268 last-known rows, 19,685 not fitting, 19,685 with one reading). Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`; no front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked, on a PostgreSQL made from the real schema** (`tools/db-checks/last-known-repair.mjs`, rewritten; `test/last-known-repair.test.mjs`, 8 pins). The book now also has customers who **left and came back** (33, away 1 to 3 deck days: their row before the gap is not the last and the next deck does not name it: only the exact lookup stops it being repaired), **a day on which a whole team is missing from the decks**, **Sundays with no deck**, the same loan number in two teams, days uploaded twice; the check refuses to pass unless the book holds enough of each trap (19 returners' rows, 58 older rows of a day uploaded twice, 17 twin repairs). It passes only when: one run over the window equals the model row by row and writes down, for every one of the 76 days, the model's numbers; a second run does no day and says `FINISHED`; **runs of one day each (a clock of zero), newest first, end where one big run ends**; **a database made slow on purpose (a sleep a day) with a clock of one second does 2 to 6 days, finishes the day in hand and says to run again, and the next run carries on to the same end**; **a run cut off by the database's own limit changes nothing**; a count changes and writes nothing; a narrow window writes down only its days; the undo restores every row byte for byte; and **22 of 22 deliberate breaks of the file change the outcome**, plus the clock removed (a slow run then does every day) and the next-deck test removed (23 times the pages). It then lays a 2.27-million-row book and counts the pages (`pg_stat_get_xact_blocks_fetched`, per transaction, table and indexes) of a one-day run, of the same run on half the book, and of the broken one. A mutation run of the pins (71 breaks of the file and of the check) found **5 weak at first and all 71 are caught now**.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first form: it was timed on a book held in memory, laid out customer after customer, and the check compared answers, never pages; **a check of a statement's cost counts pages, on a book laid out the way uploads lay it out, and says what it did not measure** (section 7 of `CHAT.md`). (2) In the new check: the break "a count changes the book" was not caught because the count ran after the apply had done every day (nothing left to change: the count now runs first); the day measured was picked by a fixed offset and landed on a quiet day of a fixture whose leavers clustered on a few days of the week (lives now from a hash, the day the busiest of the middle of the book); the half book was made with a plain `vacuum`, which does not give a table's front back (`vacuum full`); one cast was wrong. (3) In the pins: five of 65 mutations were not caught at first (the days table's primary key was not pinned; three pins matched a comment of the check, one a name used in several places): the pins read the check's code with its comments removed, and the lesson of Part 101 held again.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book; the live seconds a day, and so the number of runs, are not known. A day re-uploaded after it was written down is not looked at again (`delete from public.defaulter_last_known_repair_days where day = ...` makes it be looked at). A customer's earlier rows are NOT repaired (Part 104); the Expected sheet's dates, the decks' `due_date` and the other registers are not touched (Part 103). Why the live editor gave up before 50 seconds is not known (its limit is not published): the run is built to stay well inside any plausible one (10 s of days and a 30 s cut-off), not to a number known.

**What the owner has to do.** Paste the answer of the read-only check (rows in the log); run the new text as pasted (**the same text again until `what_next` says `FINISHED`**, never at the same moment as 060, 066 or an upload); paste the first answer. ## Part 108 — RUN-ME-071 goes team by team (the day-by-day form cost about 3 seconds a day live); the owner's answers of 17 Nov evening read

> "Days still to do is reducing 2 or 3 per run.. Ill go for to long bro" — the owner, 17 Nov 2026, under the first answer of the day-by-day form (`days_done_in_this_run` 3, `oldest_day_done` 2026-11-13, `last_known_rows` 238, `of_them_not_fitting` 0, `days_still_to_do` 104).

**What the live book said.** The second form (Part 106) ran, and did **3 days in its 10-second clock**: about 3 seconds a day on the live book where the test machine takes 0.05. A day is its own 10,600 current rows; on the test book they lay together (400 pages), and **on the live table they do not** (rows are written, replaced and moved by uploads, sweeps and the repairs themselves), so a day is thousands of pages fetched from disk. 104 days at 3 a run is 35 runs. The three days it did (13 to 15 Nov) had nothing to repair: `060` had put them right. The clock was honest; the unit of work was too dear. **The check had counted pages, but on a book whose days lay together: a flattering layout.**

**What the file does now: team by team, and never reads a day.** For each team of the teams table (and then the rows that name none) it walks the team's loan numbers through the `(team, loan number)` index one at a time (`idx_def_snap_team_ref`, RUN-ME-055: an index-only walk, no row is read) and asks the `(loan number, day)` index, for each, for the **newest current row** of that customer (`order by snapshot_date desc, created_at desc limit 1`): the last-known row, the choice RUN-ME-055's function makes. Those rows go to a temporary table; the ones that lie in the window go through **RUN-ME-060's rule word for word** (unchanged text, pinned against 060's). The progress is written per team (`defaulter_last_known_repair_teams`, primary key the team, with the window it was done for: **a team done for a wider window is not done again; for a narrower one it is**), the clock (`lk_seconds`, now 15) is read after each team, and **the answer says `seconds_this_run`**, so the live cost of a team is read, not guessed. The file stops with a plain message and changes nothing when `idx_def_snap_team_ref` is missing. The old table of days (three rows) is no longer used. Everything else is as before: `statement_timeout` 30 s, a 3-second lock, `lk_apply 'no'` counts, the undo (and `delete from ..._teams`) at the foot, never at the same moment as 060 or 066.

**Two settings and one expression keep the look to a row or two, and the first plan I read showed why.** The first draft of the look took **54 table pages per loan number** (nine times the day-by-day form's total on a book whose days lie together, and ten times what it should): the planner chose a bitmap heap scan that collected all 53 rows of the loan number and sorted them. `enable_bitmapscan = off` makes it walk the index entries backward and stop at the newest day (4.7 thousand buffers for 710 loan numbers instead of 39 thousand); and the team must be compared as `(s.team || '') = v_team`, because compared plainly the planner chooses the `(team, loan number)` index and reads every row of the loan number again. Both are pinned, and **both are broken on purpose** in the kept check: either one back and the run touches 2,267,599 table pages (the whole table, fifteen times).

**Measured, in pages, on a book of 2.27 million rows with EVERY ROW IN A RANDOM PLACE** (84,032 table pages; one day's 10,649 rows lie on 10,048 pages: the worst layout, which is what the live table may be): **the whole window touches 151,674 table pages and 256,222 index pages for 42,123 loan numbers (3.6 table pages each; 4.5 on half the book: a loan number costs no more on a bigger book); one team 2,560 pages for 715 loan numbers.** The day-by-day form on the same book: 2,158,553 table pages (**14 times as many**). On this machine, whole window counted, cold (the database restarted and the OS cache dropped): **4.5 s against 14.9 s** (hot 1.4 against 10.9); the live disk is slower than this one, so the pages are the number to trust, and **the live seconds are not known**. Its answers equal the day-by-day form's on the same book (31,371 last-known rows, 19,863 not fitting, each with one reading). **What to expect, and only as an expectation:** 85 or so teams of about 500 loan numbers each, each a few hundred to a thousand page fetches: a team is a fraction of a second to a second or two live, so a run of 15 seconds does ten to forty teams and the whole book is two to six runs, against thirty-five.

## Part 109 — The Advance report's blank accounts: the probe's answer read; a call agent is linked to the registry by an exact name; RUN-ME-072, RUN-ME-073 and a link template (17 Nov)

> No words came with it: the owner pasted the answer of the read-only probe of Part 107 (19 requests that print no account: 14 with a staff ID, 5 Customer Service names with none). It was read as the answer to "the missing account numbers at advance salary tabs automatically fill themselves? ... finance manager is pulling that report and needs the column filled" (Part 102).

**What the answer says.** **The 14 with a staff ID are all in the registry, all Active Field Officers (Mwanza 5, Mara 3, South West 2, and North, Western, Dar North and North Coast one each), and the registry holds NO account number and NO bank name for any of them.** No line said "THE REGISTRY HAS A REAL ACCOUNT", the line that would have shown a fault of the report: **the report is right**, it prints blank because there is nothing to print, and Part 102's rule holds. The accounts come from the staff; when HR's registry holds one, the report fills itself, with no step. **The 5 Customer Service names:** two are in the registry, one Active record each, under a LONGER name that carries both words of the roster's name (CALL AGENT, HQ - CUSTOMER SERVICE, each with a real account); three are in no record under any spelling that carries all the words of the name.

**Why the two were not linked, read in the code.** A Customer Service code is one shared login that picks names off the call-agents roster (Settings, Call agents; the table `call_agents`, `user_id` and `names`, one roster row holding one or several names separated by commas or semicolons). `advRequestPage` gives a roster name its registry row, and so its staff ID and account, **only when `K(roster name)` equals `K(registry name)`**: `K` is trim and upper-case and nothing else, so a different spelling, one more name, or two blanks where the other has one does not match, and an Inactive record is not offered. `advRequest` looks the picked name up with `ilike` (the same test, capitals aside) and, on a miss, files the request with `staff_id: null`, `account: null` and the role CUSTOMER SERVICE: the design says so ("a roster name with no registry row: the name is the identity"). `advReport` reads the registry by `K(r.staff_id)`, so a request with no staff ID has **nothing to join**, however well the registry knows the person. **The Leave request tab matches the roster by the same two lines of code**, so one alignment of the spellings serves both desks. **The question Part 107 left to the owner, matching a request with no staff ID to the registry by its exact name, is answered and withdrawn: it would have changed none of the five** (two differ by a word, three are not there).

**What was built: three files, no code that runs for a user changed, nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`, no `BUILD`.**
- **`db/RUN-ME-072-advance-report-blank-accounts-read-only.sql`** (read-only): for a window (the days a request was SUBMITTED, UTC days to the last millisecond, as `advReport` reads them; November by default) and a state (Approved by default, as the report's; `ALL` or one state), **one row for each person the report prints with no account**: the first three columns are RUN-ME-069's (ZONE, TEAM, STAFF NAME; the same sort, in an explicit `collate "C"` order with a tie-break), the demand list for the WhatsApp group; then REQUESTS, TZS and WHY. **Blank is the report's own rule**: the request's copy is not an account AND the registry's is not, "not an account" being `hasAccount` in `parse.js` (no digit other than zero), the registry joined by `K(staff_id)`. WHY says "the registry has no account for this staff: ask them for it" (and "and the registry says INACTIVE"), "the request has no staff ID: its name is not in the registry spelled exactly so (RUN-ME-073)" (zone `NO STAFF ID ON THE REQUEST`), or "the staff ID on the request is in no registry record". No account, phone, bank or NIDA is printed. About 0.3 s; a 20-second ceiling.
- **`db/RUN-ME-073-call-agents-roster-vs-registry-read-only.sql`** (read-only): one row for each name on the roster, the names the tab does NOT find first. **"The tab finds it" is the tab's own test** (the same letters and blanks, capitals and the cell's ends aside, against an Active record). A name found shows the staff ID(s) and whether the registry has a real account and a bank name. A name not found shows the **Active records that carry every word of it** (the same person under a longer or reordered name, or with other blanks: tagged "the same words: only the blanks differ") **and the Active records of the customer service department that share one word with it** (another spelling), and chooses nobody; and how many requests are filed under the name with no staff ID.
- **`db/TEMPLATE-link-advance-requests-to-staff.sql`** (the one that writes): one row for each person, the name as the roster spells it and the staff ID of the registry record the owner says is the same person. It writes the **STAFF ID and nothing else** on the requests of that name that have none (the amount, state, zone and every other column stay), **only when**: the staff ID is empty; the request's name is the roster name (capitals and blanks aside); the ID typed is an ACTIVE record that carries EVERY WORD of the name; and it is the ONLY Active record that does (the script never chooses between two people). The answer says, for each name, what it did and **the registry's own spelling**, so that the owner can see who was linked and type that spelling into the roster; every request changed is in `advance_requests_link_log` with the staff ID it had (private: RLS on); a second run changes nothing; the undo is at the foot. The template's two sample rows name nobody (no staff name or ID is committed); **the owner's two rows were filled in the chat.** The report then prints the registry's account, bank and phone for those requests; **a NEXT request from the same name is filed with no staff ID again until the roster spells the name as the registry does.**

**Checked** (`tools/db-checks/advance-blanks.mjs`, run by hand on a PostgreSQL over the whole of `db/schema.sql`; `call_agents` is declared by hand because no SQL file of the repository creates it, and a pin keeps its two columns tied to what the portal reads and writes). Every answer equals **a model written again in JavaScript, row by row and in order**: 072 over four windows and states on 260 random requests of 70 staff (the boundary instants of the window, staff IDs padded and in lower case, IDs in no record, requests with no ID, Inactive staff, accounts of every kind); 073 over a roster of every kind (found by the tab, found twice, the same words with other blanks, a longer name, one word in common inside and outside the department, a name on two roster rows, empty cells, a tab); the link in seven situations (normal; two Active records carry the words; the record is Inactive; the ID typed is another person's; no record; another person who shares one word; nothing to link), with a second run (nothing changes), the log, **the undo (every staff ID back as it was, including the empty and blank ones)** and **a check that nothing but the staff ID of a request changed**; and the report's own rule for what it prints (the linked requests print the registry's account, the unlinked one still prints blank). **15 of 15 deliberate breaks of 072, 11 of 11 of 073 and 11 of 11 of the template change an answer.** `test/advance-blanks.test.mjs` (11 pins, run by `npm test`) ties the files to the code they imitate (`hasAccount`, `advAccountOf_`, the report's join and window, the tab's `K` and the roster's split, the two places that match a roster name, the columns of `db/schema.sql`) and to what they promise (read-only; the template sets only `staff_id`; no private column is printed; no staff ID but the two samples); **81 of 81 deliberate breaks of the pins, the check and the code they imitate were caught** (after the first run found six pins too weak: a pin that matched a clause after an `or`, one that read a JavaScript comment, one that matched the first of two places, and three that were tied to one of four reads).

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first draft of 073 collapsed the blanks inside a name before comparing: the tab does not, so "MARY  M" against "MARY M" would have read as found when the tab finds neither; read against `K` before the first run, now mirrored exactly. (2) The first check passed with five breaks uncaught for want of a fixture row of the kind each needs (the window's first instant was a random request that was not Approved; no roster name was in the registry with one word in common outside the department; no record with a real account and no bank; the same name on two roster rows was not there twice), and one break pattern had gone stale when the file was changed: found by reading which breaks the answers did not change (section 7). (3) The link's log first kept no old value, so its undo would have set an empty or blank staff ID to null instead of back; found while writing what the undo must equal. (4) Three of the first eleven pins were wrong (one read the copy with its comments stripped, one matched the next clause's comma, one a capital letter).

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book. **The three call agents who are in no registry record are not added**: they need their details forms (a NEW with role CALL AGENT and zone HQ - CUSTOMER SERVICE, the department the registry already files such people under). **The roster is not corrected**: Settings, Call agents is the owner's screen, and the link's answer prints the spelling to type. The 14 accounts are the staff's to give (the report then fills itself). **A request tab that finds the registry row by every word of a name when exactly one Active record carries them is offered, not built**: it is a new matching rule beside "a script never merges two staff records on a name alone" and the owner's order of 14 Nov never to fix the system by making up a rule, so it waits for a yes. The 13 accounts with no bank name (Part 107) are not touched by any of this.

**What the owner has to do.** Run the link (their two rows are filled in the chat) and paste its answer; run `RUN-ME-072` (the first three columns of its answer are the list to send; it changes nothing) and, if a name looks wrong, `RUN-ME-073`; type the registry's spelling into Settings, Call agents; send the details forms of the three call agents who are in no record.

**Three scripts, handed over in the chat (not committed: they carry names, staff IDs and accounts), tested on a PostgreSQL over the whole of `db/schema.sql`.**
- **D, the accounts.** One row for each person of the list. **With a staff ID** the person is found by that ID AND the name the registry carries now; **with none**, by their name, and only when exactly ONE ACTIVE record carries exactly that name (capitals, blanks and marks such as an apostrophe aside). Then the update template's own engine (the same CTEs, kept, with two lines changed: the name key drops an apostrophe, and the guard reads that key): **a box the row gives is FILLED if it was empty, REPLACED if it held something else, "same" if it holds it; a box it leaves null is never touched; the role, zone and status are never touched**; a copy of every row about to change is kept under a label for the undo. **A person who is not found is never guessed at**: if the registry holds somebody close (the same account on another record, or two words of the name the same or one letter apart) the row says NOT FOUND and **lists** them with their staff ID and the registry's spelling and changes nothing; **if nobody is close and a zone named as the registry files it is already filed, the person is ADDED** (role `CALL AGENT`, zone `HQ - CUSTOMER SERVICE`, Active, the next staff ID past every number in use, the details sent); two Active records of one name, or one Inactive record alone, are never touched and the row says so; a name listed twice counts once. **A bank is never guessed from an account number** (Part 107): four accounts came with none, and the answer says so. The form of the officer whose script of Part 107 was never run is folded in as one more row (his staff ID read off the earlier probe; the ID-and-name guard would refuse a wrong one).
- **C2, the link by registry name.** For each person, the name a request carries and the name the registry carries now: the staff ID is written on the requests of that name that have none, only to **the only Active record of the registry name**, and only if **a word of the request's name is the same as, or one letter apart from, a word of it** (a guard against a typing slip, since the owner names the pair). Nothing but the staff ID of a request is written; a log keeps the old value; undo at the foot.
- **E, the roster.** Each roster name that the registry spells another way is replaced, wherever it stands in a roster row, by **the registry's own spelling**, and only if exactly one Active record carries the new name (so it is run after D); a row is rewritten only if one of its names changed; the `user_id` (the CREATED BY the loans are counted by) and every other name stay; a copy of each row changed; undo at the foot. After it the tab finds those names, and the next request from them is filed with a staff ID.

**Why not the main template's PLACE for the nine who are probably in the registry.** A PLACE row with no role says nothing about the role, and the template then writes the role's FIRST WORDS back (`new_role` strips everything from the first " - "): a found person with the role `CALL AGENT - ASSISTANT SUPERVISOR` would have become `CALL AGENT`. Read in the template before it was used; the by-ID engine never touches a role.

**Checked** (the checks are kept, with made-up people only: `tools/db-checks/staff-accounts-by-name.mjs` for D and `tools/db-checks/staff-accounts-link-and-roster.mjs` for C2 and E; see the addendum below). **D:** every answer and the registry afterwards equal **a model written again in JavaScript** in four scenarios (a realistic list of twenty rows of every kind: added, updated with a typed ID in lower case with a blank, a blank inside a registry name, a name with a mark, an Inactive record alone, two Active records, close records by the same account and by words one letter apart, a name listed twice, an ID in no record, an ID that carries another name, a rename; no zone filed; marks in a name; a registry of 5,000 staff in 0.27 s); a second run adds and updates nobody; the undo restores every staff byte for byte and removes the staff added; and **the registry D leaves is the one `TEMPLATE-staff-update-by-id.sql` leaves for the same rows with the same IDs (full forms, a refused row, a name replaced)**. **23 of 23 deliberate breaks of D change an answer.** **C2:** a model in six situations, a second run, the undo, nothing but the staff ID changed; **9 of 9** breaks (a tenth, the second guard of the write, is an equivalent mutant because the choice of rows already holds it, and was dropped). **E:** a model over a roster of every kind (names on one or several rows, separated by commas and semicolons, a tab, a name twice in a row, blanks inside a name, an empty roster), a second run, the undo and the copies; **11 of 11** breaks.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first plan was the main template's PLACE for everyone; reading its role line before building on it found the suffix loss above. (2) The first runs of the check failed on three things in the check, not in the scripts: psql's output was trimmed, which dropped the trailing empty columns of the last line; the undo of E, read back by the check from the file's own comment lines, lost its `where` because that line was indented one blank less than the others (every roster row would have been set to the names of one row had an owner un-commented it by hand with a slip: the layout of the three undo lines is now the same); a break that only tests a guard repeated in the write was an equivalent mutant and was dropped, said above. (3) The candidates first took any record that shared an account or a word with the name, which listed too many; two words the same or one letter apart is the rule, as the main template's name-by-name rule shows only the strongest.

The **13 who still have no account** are the staff's to give, and the bank of four accounts that came without one is not known. Whether that change belongs in the template (a switch on the line marked CHANGE, default 'no') is offered, not built: it is a one-person case, and the template's rule stays that a person with somebody close is listed, never added.

**RUN-ME-071: the owner ran the old text, and it changed nothing.** The failure pasted was `ERROR: 57014: canceling statement due to statement timeout`, and its context names the steps of the text that ran (`nx`, `gone`, `lk`, `v_next`): **the day-by-day form of #737**, not the team-by-team form of #739 that replaced the file (the current file holds none of those steps: counted). The team-by-team text (238 lines) was pasted in full again, with 072 and 073, the same hour. **Two lessons.** (1) **An SQL editor tab keeps the text it had**: a new form of a file is pasted in a NEW tab, and the answer says so. (2) **An error's context lines name the steps of the text that ran**: they are read before saying which form it was.

**The templates are kept** (the engines would otherwise be lost with the chat that wrote them): `db/TEMPLATE-staff-accounts-by-name.sql` (D), `db/TEMPLATE-link-advance-requests-by-registry-name.sql` (C2) and `db/TEMPLATE-call-agents-roster-to-registry.sql` (E). **Checked.** The checks build the registry from the whole of `db/schema.sql` (the one column the file does not create, `teams.zone`, is declared and said; `call_agents`, in no SQL file, is declared the way the portal reads and writes it) with made-up people, run each template as written, and fail when it is broken. **D:** four scenarios, a registry of 5,000 staff in 0.3 s on the test machine, a second run, the undo from the file's own comment lines, the same registry as the by-ID template on full forms, **23 of 23** deliberate breaks. **C2 and E: 9 of 9 and 11 of 11.** `test/staff-accounts-templates.test.mjs` (12 pins; **73 of 73** deliberate breaks of the templates, the checks and the premises caught by the pins) pins what each template may write (the update sets the fifteen boxes and who and when, never the role, zone, status or ID), every guard in front of a write, that no bank is named in the code, the copy and the undo under one label, the shared engine, that the request tab's rule is still the one the roster template makes true (`K` is trim and capitals, the roster is split on commas and semicolons, the portal saves `user_id`, `names` and `updated_at`), the checks themselves (the whole schema, the breaks, a scratch database made and dropped) and that nothing real is in any of them (plain ASCII).

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The check, converted from the chat's scratch folder into a kept one, built its scratch database after its first query: it had passed in the chat only because the database already existed there, and it failed on the first clean run (found by running it as the kept check, before it was committed). ## Part 110, addendum 2 — the one-person script reached the editor cut at 20,000 characters; two small scripts (17 Nov, evening)

> The owner pasted, with no words, the answers of 060 and 066 (Part 108, addendum 3) and the failure of the one-person yes-or-no script of addendum 1: "Failed to run sql query: ERROR: 42601: unterminated quoted string at or near "'NOT ADDED: no z ... LINE 254", and "I've not continued to 4th". Nothing in this addendum names a person, a staff ID or an account.

**What the error says.** The dashboard adds three comment lines of its own (source, user, date) after the text its editor holds, so the text ended where the error's token begins: inside the literal `'NOT ADDED: no z`, on line 254. **The first 20,000 characters of the text as sent end exactly there** (19,967 characters above that line, then 33 of it), the lines above are the text's own (line 254 of the text is that very line), and **cutting the text at 20,000 characters and sending it as one query to a PostgreSQL gives the same error, word for word.** The cut text still held the placeholder, so the word had not been written. **The whole text is parsed before any statement of it runs, so a cut text can only fail, never do half of the work: nothing was run and nothing was changed** (a text that does not parse never starts).

**What is not known.** What cut the paste at 20,000 characters: the owner's scripts of 30,000 characters and more have run before. The error also shows a long run of blanks in front of `else`, which the text does not hold (it has twelve), so something between the chat and the editor changes what is pasted. An editor that adds the indentation of the line above to each new line would do it (SQL does not read blanks: the text with every line indented a little more than the one above still answers the same); that was not confirmed, and it does not explain a cut at exactly 20,000 characters of the original.

**What was done about it: not "run it again", because the next paste could be cut the same way.** (1) The person's script is **two small blocks, one for each answer to the question the owner was asked** (A: she is the PMO record; B: she is a different person), **4,605 and 2,400 characters** where the general engine, with one row, is 23,615: a script for one person does not need the machinery for five hundred, and there is no word to write any more. (2) **Every line starts at the left edge**: nothing for an indentation to pile up on. (3) **Each ends with an END line** the owner can look for in the editor. (4) 072 and 073, which sat at the bottom of the same long message, were pasted again in the same form (no comment lines, flush-left: 2,964 and 3,049 characters; each answers exactly what the full file answers on a made-up book, row for row and in the same order).

**The two scripts.** **A** (the same person): the record is found by staff ID AND name (the name it carries, or the new one), its name replaced by the list's, its bank and account filled or replaced (case and blanks aside: the same values written another way write nothing), **never its role, zone or status**; **it refuses when ANOTHER record already carries the new name** (a script never makes two records of one name: Part 105); the old row is copied first, once (a later run keeps the first copy); undo at the foot. **B** (a different person): added as `CALL AGENT` in the department's filed spelling of `HQ - CUSTOMER SERVICE`, with the next staff ID by the template's own rule (the larger of the count and the highest number, plus one), the bank and the account; **it refuses when ANY record, Active or not, carries the name** (marks and blanks aside); undo at the foot. **Each refuses what the other did**, so running both cannot make two of her.

**Checked** on a PostgreSQL made from the whole of `db/schema.sql` (the one column the file does not create, `teams.zone`, declared), each text sent as ONE simple query as the dashboard sends it: **48 checks** (every box written and every box that must not change, every other row byte for byte, the words of the answer, a second run, the undo, the copy; and, for each script, the states of the registry that matter: no such ID, an ID that carries another name, a different record that carries the old name, B run first and A run first, a different bank and account, the same values written another way, an Inactive record, no zone filed, the name already there even Inactive, in lower case with blanks run together, and 5,004 staff in 53 ms); **cut texts: A and B cut at every line and at every 61st character (215 and 118 points): a cut text either errors and changes nothing, or ends on a whole statement; never a partial change**; the text with every line indented a little more than the one above answers and writes the same; and the old text cut at 20,000 characters fails with the owner's own words. **27 deliberate breaks** (a missing guard, a wrong literal, the role written, the first copy overwritten, a copy not taken, an undo that restores nothing, a refusal that still says UPDATED or ADDED, a name compared without collapsing blanks...), **each caught by a failing check**; a break that made the SQL invalid or changed nothing would have been counted as not caught (there was none). The two scripts are **not committed**: they carry a person's name, staff ID and account (the engine they were made from is: `db/TEMPLATE-staff-accounts-by-name.sql`); they are not kept as a template either (they are small and specific), so a chat that meets the same question again builds them again from this description.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first one-person script was the general engine with one row in it, 23,615 characters, far more than the job needed; and it had been tested as text and never as text that has travelled to an editor. A limit I could not see made the owner lose a round. (2) The first runs of the new checks failed for reasons of the checks, not of the scripts (the old text was cut after its placeholder had been replaced, so its error differed; the answer's boxes were indexed one off; the registry's JSON as two programs format it was compared as text; an expected staff ID one too low, because the template numbers from the count plus one when the count is above the highest number; comparisons that included timestamps every reset renews); each failure was read before anything was changed, and the scripts were not touched. (3) The first form of the cut-text check took its "nothing changed" copy from an earlier reset, so every cut looked like a partial change, and a check that reports a partial change on every input proves nothing: it was fixed before the break run, which is the run that shows a check can fail on a real fault.

**Cost.** None to the system: words only; no code, no `BUILD` bump, nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book from here. **Neither A nor B has been run**: which of the two is the owner's to say (B is the safer when unsure: a duplicate can be switched off, a rename of the wrong person is worse; both have an undo). The answers of `RUN-ME-072` and `RUN-ME-073` run again are not in. What cuts a paste at 20,000 characters is not known: **every block the owner is asked to paste stays under 10,000 characters, flush-left, with an END line** (CHAT.md section 7).
