## Part 110, addendum 4 — the first of the 13 replies: a one-row accounts script that finds the person by the name the registry carries now (17 Nov, night)

> The owner pasted, with no words, one staff's reply to the message for the WhatsApp group of addendum 3: an account number, a name spelt in full, and a zone typed with a letter missing. Nothing in this addendum names a person, a staff ID, an account or a team.

**What was read.** The 072 answer lists exactly one request from the zone the reply names (addendum 3), and the reply's name carries both words of the registry's name for that person (the first spelt with a variant) and a surname the registry does not hold. So the reply is read as that person's, by two words of the name and the zone; the script's answer prints the registry's old name and the staff ID it found, so the owner reads which person was touched, and the undo is at the foot. **What is written, by the order of 17 Nov** ("the provided is latest", Part 101): the name is replaced by the reply's and the account is filled. **The bank was not given**: it is left as it is, the answer says "not given", and nothing is guessed from the number (Part 107: an account of eleven digits that starts with 10 is CRDB's on most of the book and not on all of it, and a wrong bank on the report the finance manager pulls is worse than a blank).

**Why a new script.** The by-name accounts template (D, `db/TEMPLATE-staff-accounts-by-name.sql`) is about 25,000 characters with its comments stripped, and every block the owner pastes stays under 10,000 (CHAT.md section 7, addendum 2). The update template needs a staff ID, and the 072 list prints zone, team and name, not an ID. The script is **one statement of 6,693 characters for one row** (thirteen rows are 7,596: the other twelve replies are added to the same text as they come), flush-left, plain ASCII, with an END line and the undo at the foot, behind the usual `set local` lines (a 5-second lock wait, a 60-second statement limit, the compiler off).

**What it does, row by row.** (1) It finds the staff: a record that is not Inactive whose name (upper-cased, marks and blanks aside) is the one the registry carries now or the reply's (so a second run still finds them), in the zone the list printed (letters and digits only) and with a role that carries the team's word. (2) It writes the name (upper-case, blanks run together), the bank only when the row has one (upper-case) and the account only when the row has one (an account of digits, dots, blanks and dashes is written as digits, anything else as the text given, upper-case); **never the role, zone or status, never an emptied box**; a name the registry already holds in another case or with other blanks, and a bank or account that differs only in case or surrounding blanks, write nothing. (3) It refuses, changing nothing, and says why on the row: NOT FOUND (and lists the records that carry the old name elsewhere, with status, zone and role), MORE THAN ONE (both IDs), ANOTHER RECORD ALREADY CARRIES THE NEW NAME (any record, Inactive too: a script never makes two records of one name, Part 105), LISTED TWICE (a staff on two rows: only the first is written). (4) It copies the old row first, once for each label, into `staff_registry_update_before` (the update template's table, the same DDL), so the copy is the very first state however many times an edited text is run, and the undo at the foot puts back every staff the label copied. A second run of the same text changes nothing.

**Checked** on a PostgreSQL made from the whole of `db/schema.sql` (the one column the file does not create, `teams.zone`, declared), each text sent as one simple query as the dashboard sends it: **33 checks** (the shape: under 10,000 characters for one row and for thirteen, no line starts with a blank, plain ASCII, the END line; a normal run; a second run; a second run of an EDITED text, which keeps the first copy and whose undo goes back to the very first state; the undo; the states of the registry: two records of the name, the wrong zone, the wrong team, another record carrying the new name, an Inactive record carrying it, a different bank and account replaced, a bank not given kept, an account typed with blanks and dashes, case and blanks in the registry, the same name written another way, an apostrophe in the name; four rows in one text, each its own case); **320 cut points (every line and every 61st character): 279 refused with an error, 15 ran without touching a staff, 26 ran to the end: no partial change**; the text with every line indented a little more than the one above answers and writes the same; **72 to 84 ms on 5,005 staff**; and **23 of 23 deliberate breaks of the text each caught by a failing check** (the Inactive record counted as a match, no zone asked, no team asked, only the old name looked for, the clash guard gone, an Inactive clash let through, a staff listed twice written twice, more than one match written anyway, no copy, the first copy not kept, every staff updated, the role, the zone and the status written, a bank not given emptying the bank, an account kept as typed, a name not upper-cased, a name compared as typed, an account always a change, the answer saying CHANGED, an undo that does not restore the account, the list of the same name elsewhere gone, a copy holding a wrong name). A break that fails only by an SQL error is reported apart and is not counted as caught.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The script itself needed no change after its first full run; every fault the break runs found was in the harness. (2) **The first break run caught nothing in the scenarios that built their own text**: they called the generator directly, so the break was never in the text they sent, and three breaks passed unseen (a staff listed twice written twice, the first copy not kept, an account kept as typed). The scenarios now all take their text from the broken copy, and the run was started again from the beginning. (3) A break that made the script fail with an SQL error crashed the harness instead of failing a check (the next scenario read a copy that was never made); every SQL error is now a failed check, and one that is nothing but an SQL error is reported apart. (4) The first set of scenarios did not show a break that only a second, different run or an Inactive record shows: four scenarios were added after reading what the first breaks left uncaught (an edited second run, a bank not given while the registry holds one, the same name written another way, an Inactive record carrying the new name).

**Cost.** None to the system: words only; no code, no `BUILD` bump, nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was run on the live book from here; its answer is not in. The bank is not known (the staff say it: it is filled by staff ID, or in the next row of the same text). The other twelve replies have not come. **The filled script and the engine that makes it carry a name and an account and are not committed**; a chat that needs the engine again builds it from this description (the one thing to keep from the mistakes above: every scenario takes its text from the broken copy), or the owner says yes and it is kept as a template with a check and pins (CHAT.md section 8).

**What the owner has to do.** Run the script (the last line in the editor must read `END OF THE SCRIPT`; if it does not, nothing is run and the chat is told), paste its answer, and paste each further reply as it comes.

## Part 111 — A demand notice's rule of 2 DC does not apply at D.S 11-12 (20 Nov)

> "The rule of 2 installments shouldnt apply for DS 11-12 because there cant be two there" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026, in the same hour as a request for the SQL that deletes duplicate demand notices and a screenshot of the Postgres errors ("when you finish: postgress war please").

**The rule that was there.** The Legal tab's New-notice drawer serves a customer only at 2 DC and above: the owner's own order ("a demand notice cant be generated for an expected/defaulter not from 2 DC and above ... we only apply these measures when a customer defaults 2 DC+ at demand creation", the comment of `LEGAL_MIN_DC` in `api/_lib/portal-core.js`). The deck's D.C (`missedDc_`, the count of installments the customer has defaulted on) decides, in three places that must never disagree: `legalPreview` (`eligible`, so the drawer withholds the button and says the DC), `legalFind` (the pick list marks the line red before a tap) and the guard at the top of `addDemandNotice` (refused anyway, so a stale screen cannot slip one through). Reprints of letters already served are not gated.

**Why it needed a hole.** D.S is paid-of-target (the handbook's glossary: `11-12` is eleven paid of the twelve due; the loan system writes it with a dash or a slash) and a loan has twelve installments. At 11-12 only the last installment can be missing: D.C is at most 1 and can never reach 2. Held to the rule, such a customer could never be served, however long the finished loan stood unpaid. At 10-11 the same is not true (a twelfth installment can still fall due and make two), so the rule stands for them.

**What changed.** One question, written once: `legalEligible_(d)` is `legalDcWaived_(d) || D.C >= LEGAL_MIN_DC`, and `legalDcWaived_` reads D.S with `dsParts` (`api/_lib/call-core.js`, the reader the phone reads D.S with: one or two digits, a dash or a slash, spaces aside) and is true exactly when paid is 11 and target is 12. The D.C is not asked when it is waived: the rule is not theirs, and a deck row with no D.C at all is served. The preview answers `eligible` and `dcWaived`; the pick list answers `eligible` on every line, and the Legal module (`public/mod/legal.js`) reads it (`var low = !r.eligible`) instead of comparing DC with the rule itself, which was a second copy of the rule in the browser; the drawer says, in Swahili and English, that the rule does not apply and why; the guard refuses with the same words as before.

**What did not change.** (1) The rule for every other D.S, and for a row with no D.S. (2) **The fine's own rule.** `legalFine` gives no fine for a single missed payment on a loan that has not expired (`missed < 2 && !expired`, the handbook's Legal fines section): the same number two, a different rule, and the owner did not name it. At D.S 11-12 it means a notice served before the loan expires (91 days after disbursement) reads a fine of 0; after the expiry the fine runs as always. Whether the fine should start earlier for them is the owner's to say (CHAT.md section 8). (3) The restructuring offer, which reads the same D.C with its own minimum (`RESTRUCTURE_MIN_DC`, 4).

**Cost.** None to the system: no read added anywhere, a regex on one string per customer; nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call` (`dsParts` is a named import in `portal-core.js`; `call-core.js` is not touched); `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged. A front-end change: `BUILD 2026-11-20-a` (a page older than the server reloads itself past the cache).

**Checked.** `test/portal.test.mjs`, one new test through the real dispatch: D.S 11-12 at DC 1 is served (`eligible`, `dcWaived`) and the letter is issued; the slash form, spaces around the dash and a row with no D.C likewise; 10-11, 9-10, 8-9, 11-11, 12-12, 1-12, 11-13, an empty D.S, `n/a` and no D.S at all are refused as before, with the old words; 9-12 at DC 3 and 10-12 at DC 2 as before; the pick list says `eligible` per line. `test/pages.test.mjs`: the drawer's pin (the list reads the server's answer and no longer compares DC itself; the drawer says why at D.S 11-12). **13 of 13 deliberate breaks of the code and of the drawer each turn a test red** (waived for nobody, waived at 10-11, the target not asked, the paid count not asked, the guard or the preview or the pick list asking the DC alone, the preview not saying why, a waived row that still needs a DC, the rule dropped for everybody, the drawer deciding the rule itself, the drawer not saying why). `npm test`: 1,777 pass.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing was seen on the live screen. The fine at D.S 11-12 is as it was (above). A customer at 10-11 who the owner thinks should also be waived is the owner's to say: the rule is waived where it can never be met, not where it merely is not met yet.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing: the Legal tab picks the change up when the page reloads (the `BUILD` moved).

## Part 112 — Duplicate demand notices by ref no: `db/RUN-ME-074` (20 Nov)

> "SQL to delete duplicate demand notices by ref no" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026, the first of three requests of that morning (the others: Part 111, and "postgress war"). The SQL was pasted in the chat the moment it was checked (CHAT.md section 2, 14 Nov); the owner ran it and pasted the answer. This Part keeps the file, its check and its pins.

**What a notice's ref is, and what a duplicate is.** `demand_notices.ref` is the customer's loan reference, the key the owner has always replaced by (`replaceNoticesByRef` in `api/upload.js`: an upload of the register replaces the earlier uploaded notices of the same ref or Kumb.Na. and never touches an app-made one). A notice's own number, the Kumb.Na. (`notice_id`), is unique by an index, so two notices with one ref are two letters for one customer. Two ways they arise are in the code: the officer presses Issue again because the print did not appear (the comment in `legalPreview` records that the register once showed one customer served six times on one day; the drawer now says "Already served today" and offers the reprint first, and a second letter is a decision, `servedToday`), and a register line sits beside an app-made notice for the same customer. The owner's data does not say which made these 93. The file calls two notices duplicates when they share a ref (blanks trimmed, any case) and, in the mode that was sent, a notice date.

**What it does.** One statement (a `WITH` of six steps, so a notice is never deleted without its copy and a failure rolls all of it back), behind a 5-second lock limit, a 60-second ceiling and the compiler off. It reads `demand_notices` once, ranks each group by notice date, issue time, whether the notice carries a Kumb.Na. (one with a number first) and id, **keeps the first**, copies every other notice whole as jsonb (its stored letter and upload stamp included) to `public.demand_notices_removed` (private: row-level security on, no policy) under the label `DUPLICATE NOTICES 20 NOV (SQL)` with the id of the notice that stands, and deletes it. A blank or null ref is never grouped. **The word on the CHANGE line:** `DAY` (as sent) groups by ref and day; `REF` groups by ref alone, so a customer served again a week later loses that second notice too; any other word is refused (the answer says `NOTHING DONE`, nothing is removed or copied). The undo, in the last comment lines, reads the copies back with the table's own type (`jsonb_populate_record(null::public.demand_notices, ...)`) and does not fail on a row that is already back (`on conflict do nothing`). Nothing else is touched.

**Why DAY.** The code already says it: "The same person can be served more than once; the reference is what must stay unique" (`db/migrations/2026-07-26-demand-notice-id.sql`), and a second notice a week later is a second legal letter. Across days the screens disagree on which notice speaks for a customer: the tab's tiles read each customer at their EARLIEST notice (`noticeTiles_`: "the largest, since it looks back furthest"), the dashboard card and the lawyers' board at their LATEST (`legalFold_`). So removing the other days' notices is a decision about which one stands, and the file does not take it silently: it counts them (`refs_served_on_more_than_one_day`) and leaves them. `REF` keeps the first notice of each ref; keeping the last is not built.

**The answer, and what it says.** One row: the word used, `DONE`, notices with a ref, refs with repeats, notices removed, notices left, refs served on more than one day. **The owner ran it as DAY on 20 Nov: `DAY | DONE | 1127 | 60 | 93 | 1034 | 48`**: 1,127 notices carried a ref; 60 refs had a same-day repeat; 93 notices were removed (8%); 1,034 are left; 48 refs were served on more than one day and kept every notice. Running `REF` would remove at least 48 more (one for each such ref, and more where a ref was served on three days or more); that is the owner's to say.

**What it does not touch.** No payment, no deck, no other register. **The recoveries ledger** (`notice_payment_ledger`, one row for each ref, notice date and payment: `RUN-ME-041a`) is not written: in DAY a removed repeat shares its (ref, day) with the notice that stands, so every ledger key still has a notice behind it, and `legalFold_` (which reads a ledger row only under a notice the register holds) counts what it counted. **REF is different, and was not tested:** a later-day notice's ledger rows would sit under a notice the register no longer holds, and the cards would stop reading them; the same payments also sit under the earlier notice's date (the ledger holds every payment on or after each notice's date, by the way 041a builds it), which is read in the code, so the card's sums should not move. The register's tiles (`noticeTiles_`) take, for each customer, the notice with the largest drop, and that may be a later one, so a tile can move under REF; not measured. **A numbering note:** `nextNoticeId` gives a new notice the number after the highest suffix left (`HMCL/<initials>/<dd>/<mm>/<yyyy>-2`), so after a repeat with the highest suffix is removed that number can be given again to a later notice of the same person on the same day; the undo then skips that one notice (`on conflict do nothing`) instead of failing.

**Cost.** None to the system: a file the owner runs once, about 1,100 rows; 686 ms for 112,000 notices on the test machine, where 30,000 were removed and copied (the live book held 1,127 with a ref). No code that runs for a user, nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`, no `BUILD` change.

**Checked.** `tools/db-checks/duplicate-notices.mjs` (run by hand: `PGHOST=/var/run/postgresql PGUSER=postgres node tools/db-checks/duplicate-notices.mjs`, 1 minute 20 seconds) builds a PostgreSQL from the whole of `db/schema.sql` and the two real migrations that add `notice_id` and the upload stamp, with a fixture that knows the truth (three same-day repeats; a ref served on two days; one ref written three ways; blank and null refs; two notices at the same instant, one with a Kumb.Na.; notices with no date; a removed notice with a stored letter and an upload stamp; singletons; two refs repeated on one day; a ledger that must come out as it went in) and passes only when: the notices left equal a model written again in JavaScript in both modes and for DAY followed by REF; the answer's numbers equal the model's; every removed notice is in the copy whole with the id of the notice that stands; a second run writes nothing; the undo restores the table byte for byte (after DAY, after REF, and after DAY then REF); a refused or empty word removes nothing; a book with nothing to remove and an empty book answer `DONE` with zeros; **the text cut at 150 places (every line and every 53rd character) either fails or finishes: 96 refused with an error, 38 ran without touching a notice, 16 ran to the end, no partial change**; the same text with every line indented answers the same; **112,000 notices (a hundred times the live book) are answered as the model says**; and **21 of 21 deliberate breaks of the file each fail a check** (the day ignored in DAY, the day always used, the last issued standing, every notice of a group deleted, a blank ref grouped two ways, the ref compared in its own case or with its blanks, the word not validated, no copy, a copy of the id alone, a delete with no join, a copy under another label or naming the wrong notice as the one that stands, an undo asking for another label, a partition that forgets the ref, no Kumb.Na. tie-break, a notice with no date read first, `last_value` for `first_value`, and two wrong answer counts; an SQL error alone does not count as caught). `test/duplicate-notices.test.mjs` pins the lines that make it safe (nine pins; **41 of 41 breaks of the pins caught**). `npm test`: 1,786 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The file entered the repository inside #749's commit, before its check and pins existed: a `git add -A` took the untracked file in, the PR body said so, and the owner had already run the text. (2) The check first claimed a book "a hundred times the live one" on 12,000 notices, about ten times; found when its numbers were read back for this Part, and the book is now 112,000. (3) The mutation run of the pins found one pin too loose (a copy narrowed by a `where false` got past it, because the pin did not anchor the end of the copy), tightened before the pins went in. (4) A first draft of the docs said "five steps" for a statement of six, and named a screen's function from memory: every function named here was read in the code first.

**Not done, said plainly.** `REF` was not run. A Kumb.Na. of a removed repeat can be reused (above). Repeats in the other registers (complaints, restructures, deductions) were not looked at: their uploads already replace by their own keys. Nothing was seen on the live book beyond the owner's answer.

**What the owner has to do.** Say whether one notice per ref, whatever the day, is wanted (change `DAY` to `REF` on the CHANGE line and run the file again); otherwise nothing. To see what was removed: `select notice->>'ref', notice->>'notice_id', notice->>'notice_date', kept_id from public.demand_notices_removed order by 1, 3;`

## Part 113 — No second demand notice while the last one is not cleared (20 Nov)

> "Avoid duplicate demand notices - one cant create a second when the last one is not yet cleared" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026, the day the register's repeats were removed (Part 112), and, a few minutes later, asked what is then allowed: "so one can create demand for the same ref no if the existing is cleared and the new one is 2dc+ or ds 11/12".

**The rule that was there.** Nothing stopped a second letter. The migration that gave a notice its number says it outright ("The same person can be served more than once; the reference is what must stay unique"), and `legalPreview` only WARNED when a notice was already served today ("a second letter is still possible, but it is now a decision"). What that allowed is in Part 112: one customer served six times on one day (the officer pressing Issue again each time the print did not appear), 60 customers with a same-day repeat, 48 served on several days.

**The rule now: two questions, both must pass.** (1) **Is a letter allowed at all:** the customer is at 2 DC and above, or at D.S 11-12 (`legalEligible_`, Part 111, unchanged, asked first and on its own: a customer who has cleared but is below the rule is refused by THAT rule, in its own words). (2) **Does an earlier notice stand in the way:** the customer's LAST notice (`legalServed_`: any date, whether the app issued it or the register's upload brought it, found by the customer's REF#) is not cleared (`legalOpenNotice_`). Both are asked by the preview (`openNotice`, null when nothing stands in the way) and again by `addDemandNotice`, so a stale screen cannot slip one through; a reprint of a letter already issued is never gated.

**What "cleared" means.** The register's own word and its own test: `noticeCleared_`, the customer is off the deck or owes nothing (the State column's "Amemaliza / Cleared", which the tab and the guard now share as one function). **It is applied to the time since the notice, not only to today**, because the owner's second message describes exactly the case today's reading cannot see: a customer served, who then cleared, and is in default again. Today they are back on the deck owing, so today's reading calls their old notice not cleared for ever and they could never be served again. So a notice is cleared if the customer owes nothing today, or if on ANY day a defaulters deck was uploaded after the notice (`defaulterDeckDays`: `deck_totals_days`, the calendar the dashboard already reads, cached a minute) the customer was off that day's current deck or stood on it owing nothing (their own rows, `defaulter_snapshots` by REF# and day, the `(ref, snapshot_date)` index). A customer who stood on every deck since the notice has not cleared. The days considered end at the deck the customer is being read from (with today's file not yet in, yesterday's).

**What it costs.** Nothing for a customer with no notice (the usual case: the first question short-circuits, no read is added). For one who has a notice: one read of their own deck rows since it and the cached calendar. The guard rides in the same round of reads as the number, the teams, the brand and the officer's phone, so creation waits no longer. Creation is an officer's act, a few a day: nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`, and `test/speed.test.mjs` is unchanged. The drawer's Issue button is off from the press until the server has answered (back on after a refusal), which is what stops the pressing that made six letters.

**What it cannot know, said once.** A day whose deck was uploaded but never built into the calendar is not a day the customer could have cleared on: a missed record reads as "did not clear", the safe side. A team missing from one day's file reads as cleared that day, as it does everywhere else (the whole-book rule, RUN-ME-032). With no calendar at all (RUN-ME-022 not run, or the table empty) today's reading stands. Two officers issuing for one customer within the same second can both pass (the guard reads before it writes): the button now stops the one officer, a database rule for two is not built. The pick list does not mark customers who have an open notice (a read per search). A notice backdated by the officer is judged from the date they typed.

**Checked.** `test/portal.test.mjs`, two new tests through the real dispatch. First: no notice, then issued; the notice in the way named by the preview and refused on the same day, a week later, by another officer and with no preview ever looked at, nothing filed; the reprint still works; another customer unaffected; a notice that came from the register's upload weeks ago stands in the way of ITS customer; owing nothing lets the customer through and the tab reads that notice as Cleared on the same row; and source pins that the tab and the guard ask ONE `noticeCleared_`. Second: stood on every deck since (held); off the deck on one day a deck was uploaded (allowed, and the new notice then stands in the way of a third); the same absence on a day with no deck (held); no calendar, an empty one, the table missing (held); a settled row on the deck (cleared that day); cleared but below the DC rule (refused by the DC rule, not by the old notice); cleared at D.S 11-12 (allowed); today's file not yet in (the day after the deck being read does not count). Three older tests that issued two notices to one customer were rewritten to a customer with no notice (the reference still counts up, `-2`, for a DIFFERENT customer whose initials give the same number: that is what the suffix is for). `test/pages.test.mjs`: the drawer's pins. **22 of 22 deliberate breaks of the code and of the drawer each turn a test red** (the guard gone, a customer who owes nothing blocked, the history never finding a gap, a day after the deck counting, the notice day counting, no calendar read as cleared, a settled row not clearing, another customer read, the calendar not asked, the notices read for another ref, the preview not naming the notice, cleared only below zero, the refusal not naming the notice, the tab's copy of the test, a non-400 refusal, the DC rule no longer first; the drawer: the button drawn regardless, a press repeatable, the button staying off after a refusal, the reprint opening the wrong notice, no words, the server's answer ignored). `npm test`: 1,788 pass. `BUILD 2026-11-20-b` (the Legal module changed).

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first build read "cleared" as today's reading alone (the customer is on the deck owing, so any earlier notice stands in the way): it passed its own tests and would have barred every customer who cleared and fell back into default from ever being served again; the owner's second message, sent while it was being built, said what is allowed, and the rule was rebuilt on the time since the notice. (2) Two breaks were not caught at first: the drawer test sliced the page source from `lgIssue` to the end of EVERY module (`lgPrint` no longer exists), so another module's text satisfied a pin (a weakness older than this change, now bound to the Legal module); and the fake database answers a table it was not given with empty rows, so the no-calendar path was never taken until a test named the table as missing (`missingTables`). (3) A first draft of the break list had a break that replaced text found once and changed nothing a test reads: counted, not believed.

**Not done, said plainly.** The fine's own rule (Part 111). A database rule against two officers issuing for one customer in the same second. A mark on the pick list for customers who already have an open notice. Nothing was seen on the live screen: a notice served before today is judged by the deck calendar of the live book, which a chat cannot read.

**What the owner has to do.** Nothing: the Legal tab picks the change up when the page reloads (the `BUILD` moved). To try it: open New notice on a customer who already has a notice and still owes: the screen names that notice and offers its download instead of the button.

## Part 114 — The Postgres war: what the logs say, RUN-ME-075 ran, and the ghost lookup keeps the last good list when the database refuses it (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026, with the Supabase logs card: 478,172 requests at 99.1% success, and Postgres 2,594 log events of which 2,078 errors in 24 hours, following working hours.

**What was ruled out first.** The first idea was that a migration the live book lacks makes the app's optional-column probes (`expFoldRead` and `deckColsFor` in `snapshot-totals.js`, `readRows_` in `imprest.js`, `advColMissing_` in `portal-core.js`) log one Postgres error each time. The owner ran the catalog read of the sixteen columns the code asks for: **16 of 16 present.** Refuted for every probe named. Nothing to run, and no chat proposes it again.

**What the logs say.** The owner found the Logs pages (the project's address ending `/logs/postgres-logs` and `/logs/edge-logs`; the two Explorer queries of the first hand-over were run in the SQL editor by mistake and answered `42P01`: `postgres_logs` and `edge_logs` exist only in Supabase's log store) and pasted both lists. **Postgres, the 100 newest rows (12:01 to 12:13 East Africa time, 20 Nov): 93 are `canceling statement due to statement timeout`**; 4 were the owner's own two mistaken queries; 3 were routine checkpoint lines. Not one is a missing column, a duplicate key or a bad value. About 7 to 8 a minute at midday, in bursts of 5 or 6 within 3 seconds. **API Gateway, the 100 newest rows (13 seconds): every one is 200, 201 or 204 except one, `POST /rest/v1/rpc/defaulter_ghost_rows`, which answered 500** (RUN-ME-055; Parts 71 and 76). One sample: a suspect, not a finding. All of it comes from the app's own server (supabase-js, role `service_role`, AWS us-east-1). The expanded rows carried access codes and customer numbers: none is repeated here, and the owner was asked once not to paste raw rows.

**Why that function is the suspect (read in the code and measured on a test book; not seen on the live one).** (1) It is asked for by every server instance, for every team set the instance serves, once every 90 seconds of use (`GHOST_TTL_MS`); on Vercel each instance has a cache of its own. (2) The app's budgets (`GHOST_BUDGET_MS` 800 ms on the phone, `GHOST_REPORT_BUDGET_MS` 5 s on the reports) stop the app WAITING, not the database: the statement runs on until the limit of the role that runs it (**corrected in Part 115: through PostgREST the function's own `set statement_timeout = '800ms'` IS enforced**; this Part first said it does not cancel a longer call, from a direct SQL session with no limit of its own where a 1.85 second call succeeded, which is not how the app calls it). (3) Its cost grows with the teams in the set times the customers each team has ever had and no longer has (a team's walk) and, in the first text, with candidates times the refs on today's deck (`ref <> all (array)`): measured on a test book with real churn (1.7 million current rows, 92 teams, about 800 departed customers a team) the first text took 45 ms for one team, 311 ms for ten and 3.7 seconds for all 92 (an unrestricted admin), warm and in memory; the live book is bigger and on disk. (4) One failed gateway call in a sample of 100 in 13 seconds is the size the timeouts per minute would give if this function were most of them (about 1.7 expected): consistent, not proof.

**RUN-ME-075 (#754) ran.** The same function, the same name and answers, cheaper: the check against the known refs became a hashed anti-join and each candidate asks the `(ref, day)` index for its one newest current row (17 ms, 178 ms and 1.75 seconds on the same book; identical rows on 600 random books except which of two rows with the very same timestamp is called the latest, which the first text left unspecified too). The owner ran it at about 12:50 East Africa time and pasted its last line, `defaulter_ghost_rows`: the editor sends a script as one statement, so an error anywhere would have shown instead, and the new body is live. **Its effect on the timeouts is NOT known yet.** The owner was handed two read-only measurements in the chat: (1) in the **Logs Explorer**, the count of `statement timeout` rows per minute for the last hour (7 to 8 a minute before; a fall after the minute it ran says this function was the main source, no fall says it was not); (2) in the **SQL editor**, from `pg_stat_statements`, the twelve statements that cost the database most, the twelve with the worst single run, and this function's own line (normalised text, no customer data; it counts statements that finish, not the ones a timeout cancels, so it names the heavy shapes). The second was run on a scratch PostgreSQL that loads the extension, as one statement, before it was handed over.

**A correction to what #754 said, found the same afternoon by counting pages, as section 7 of CHAT.md says a check must.** #754 said the cheaper text "halves the cost"; it had timed milliseconds on a warm book held in memory. Counted in buffers touched, on a book laid out the worst way (every row in a random place; 848,000 deck rows, 20 teams, 110 days of history for each customer, about 200 departed customers a team asked for), the first text and the cheaper one touch the SAME pages (hits and reads together): 16,032 and 16,027 for one team, 72,896 and 72,891 for five, 297,974 and 297,972 for twenty. What it saves is CPU only (30.5 to 21.9 ms, 149 to 83 ms, 463 to 306 ms warm: 1.4 to 1.8 times quicker), because both texts have to read EVERY row of every departed customer to find its newest current row: the planner reads the `(team, ref)` index for all of a customer's rows, initial and current, every day it was on a deck, and keeps the newest (`explain` of the lookup: 14 rows read, 7 removed by the type filter, a top-1 sort). The `(ref, day)` index that #754's header says each candidate asks is not the one the planner chooses, since neither the type nor the team is in it. On the live book, which is on disk and holds up to 110 days of rows for a customer, the pages are what cost: **RUN-ME-075 alone is not expected to take the timeouts away, and a chat must not read "no fall after RUN-ME-075" as "this function was not the source".** What does cut the pages is an index that holds a (team, ref)'s newest CURRENT row in one place: a partial index on `(team, ref, snapshot_date desc, created_at desc) where snapshot_type = 'current'` takes the same call from 16,027 to 2,681 buffers for one team, from 72,891 to 11,832 for five and from 297,972 to 46,712 for twenty (6 to 6.4 times fewer), and 21.9 to 6.7 ms, 82.6 to 24.7 ms and 306 to 118 ms warm (the first text profits from it too: 16,032 to 9,341 for one team). **It costs the upload:** inserting a deck day of 20,000 rows (10,000 of them current) took 595 ms without it and 714 ms with it (median of ten interleaved runs: +119 ms, +20%, on a test table with five other indexes; the live table has more, so the share is smaller and the absolute cost about the same: some 12 microseconds for each current row). It is offered with those numbers and not run: CLAUDE.md section 1 puts a reason beside anything the upload pays for, and the owner decides (CHAT.md section 8).

**What the app did when the database refused, and no longer does (`api/_lib/expdf.js`, `readGhosts_` and `ghostRowsFor_`).** A read of the ghost list that failed (a statement timeout is the usual way) threw away what the last good read had found and answered nothing for the next five minutes (`GHOST_MISSING_TTL_MS`): every customer who had left the book vanished from the Exp.Def lists and the phone's list for five minutes at a time, for whoever that server instance and team set served. That is the thing the owner ordered against on 13, 15 and 16 Nov ("they should stay there", "i expect that customer in initial never to get lost"). A read that was only late at the end of its budget did the same: the caller got nothing while the cache held the last good list. **Now** the failure, the pause after it and the late read all hand out the last good list, however old (never made up: it is only older, and `ghostRowsFor_` still takes out every ref today's own deck names); where there has never been a good read behind it (RUN-ME-055 not run, a server instance that has just started, or the very first read failing) the answer is nothing, as before; the five-minute pause is unchanged, because it is what stops a function that times out from being run, and timing out, over and over. Found beside it and fixed with it: the cache entry used to be written after the read started, so a read that failed the moment it was asked for had its memory overwritten by a settled promise and the instance asked for nothing, and answered nothing, until it was restarted. The real client cannot fail that way (its builder answers later), so this changes nothing live; the new test reproduces it on the code as it was.

**Cost.** None. No read added and no round trip changed (`test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged and green); nothing on `/api/upload`; on `/api/call` arithmetic on a list the instance already holds (the list was already cached; it is now also kept through a failure instead of being dropped). No front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked.** `test/ghost-lookup.test.mjs`: seven tests on a fake clock (a good answer is kept 90 seconds; a refusal keeps the last good list; the pause holds and ends at five minutes; a late read answers the last good list, is not waited for, and lands in the cache for the next caller; with no good read the answer is nothing; a ref today's deck names is never a ghost in a stand-in list; one team set's failure does not touch another's; a read that fails at once is remembered; what is asked of the database is unchanged). **Five of the seven fail on the code as it was** (the two that pass are the behaviours that did not change). **18 of 18 deliberate breaks of the code each turn a test red** (the pause handing out nothing, the memo dropping the list, a refused read answering nothing to its waiters, the budget fallback empty, no pause, the stand-in keyed another way, the old write order, the known refs not taken out, a good answer never fresh, never stored, a stand-in always empty, no pause set, a pause of 30 seconds, a life of 30 and of 300 seconds, one entry for every team set, the known refs not sent, another function asked for). `npm test`: 1,795 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first form of the late-read test held the read with a promise that settles only when the test releases it, and the budget's own timer is unref'd, so with nothing else holding the event loop open the runner ended the test under it ("Promise resolution is still pending but the event loop has already resolved") and cancelled the six tests after it; the repository's own earlier comment (`test/portal.test.mjs`, the budget test) says exactly this and I met it anyway: the read now answers after a real delay. (2) I started the full test run inside a background subshell of a command that was itself run in the background: the completion notice was the wrapper's, at once, and its log had no totals yet; the run finished minutes later (1,795 pass). Read the totals, not the notice.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **The 1,000-row cap, probable and NOT MEASURED.** `readGhosts_` calls `db.rpc` bare. PostgREST caps a function that returns a set exactly as it caps a table (the repository's own note above `rpcAll` in `api/_lib/supabase.js`; paging such a function re-runs it for every page), and the project keeps the default of 1,000 rows unless its API settings say otherwise (not looked at). So a viewer whose teams hold more than 1,000 departed customers in all (a manager, a GMO or an admin, probably; one team, probably not) receives the first 1,000, the teams in the order asked and each by ref, and loses the rest without a word: the same thing the owner ordered against. The cure is a design (a function that answers one value, under a new name so that a book without it says "no answer yet"; or the question asked for a few teams at a time), not a patch, and what a viewer should see when there are more than a screen can use is the owner's to say. (2) **How often it runs.** A longer life for a good list is the next lever: ten minutes instead of ninety seconds is 6.7 times fewer runs, and the list changes only when a deck upload drops customers, once or twice a day, so the price is a list up to ten minutes older after the morning upload. Not pulled: there is no evidence yet that it is needed once RUN-ME-075 is in. (3) **The region** (CHAT.md section 8): not changed, because it moves every function, the upload and the call app included. (4) A kept check and pins for `db/RUN-ME-075`, and its header comment says each candidate asks the `(ref, day)` index for its newest row, which the correction above shows it does not (its measurements were made in a chat's scratch folder, which goes with the chat). (5) Nothing live was seen: whether the timeouts fell after RUN-ME-075 is not known. (6) The portal's other heavy screens and the call app's other reads were not looked at: no statement text says which.

**What the owner has to do.** Run the two measurements pasted in the chat and paste the answers (counts and normalised statement text only); say yes or no to moving the Vercel functions next to the database, and confirm in Supabase (Project Settings, General) that its region is Ireland.

## Part 114, addendum — RUN-ME-076, the partial index that cuts the ghost lookup's pages; the kept check and pins for it and for RUN-ME-075 (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. The pages were counted the same afternoon, after the correction above.

**What counting pages found, on three books** (buffers touched, hits and reads together; every row of every book in a random place, the worst layout a table can have).
(1) A book of 848,000 deck rows, 20 teams, 110 days of history for each customer: RUN-ME-075 and the first text touch the same pages (16,032 and 16,027 for one team; 297,974 and 297,972 for twenty).
(2) The kept check's own book (60 teams of 100 customers, none more than about 2% of the table, as on the live book's 90 teams; about 500,000 rows): for four teams with 110 days of history and 400 departed customers asked for, the first text and the new one both touch 28,000 to 39,000 pages (the book is random, so the figure moves from run to run); **with the index the new one touches about 2,850 every time (10 to 14 times fewer) and the first text 23,000 to 34,000, which it hardly helps: it is the pair, RUN-ME-075 with RUN-ME-076, that reads about ten times fewer.** The lookup of one customer's newest current row costs 4.0 pages whether the customer stood on the decks 30 days or 110 (without the index 14.7 against 67.7: it grows with the history).
(3) A book of eight teams, the first form of the check: the first text read 8,414 pages against the new one's 70,724, because for a team that was an eighth of the table the planner read the whole table in one pass, which no live call does. A timing book's number of teams decides the plan it measures; the check's book has sixty.

**`db/RUN-ME-076-defaulter-snapshots-current-last-index.sql`: one index, on the current rows only, offered and NOT RUN.** `create index concurrently if not exists idx_def_snap_current_last on defaulter_snapshots (team, ref, snapshot_date desc, created_at desc) where snapshot_type = 'current'`. It makes a customer's newest current row one index descent and one row. It changes no row and nothing in the app; it builds without blocking the upload (CONCURRENTLY, run alone, as RUN-ME-054 and RUN-ME-055 were); its undo is one `drop index concurrently`. **What it costs the upload, written beside it because `/api/upload` writes this table (CLAUDE.md section 1):** every CURRENT row an upload inserts also writes one entry here (initial rows do not: it is partial). A deck day of 20,000 rows, 10,000 of them current, inserted in 595 ms without it and 714 ms with it (median of ten interleaved runs on the 848,000-row table: +119 ms, +20%, about 12 microseconds for each current row); six runs of the kept check, on a smaller book, gave +0% to +21%: noisy, of the order of ten percent. The live table has more indexes (two trigram ones among them), so the share is smaller and the absolute cost about the same; the cost is spread over the upload's slices (a 2,000-row slice: about 24 ms). The index is about 55 MB on the live table. **Whether to run it is the owner's.**

**What is kept, and what it holds.** `tools/db-checks/ghost-rows-cheaper.mjs`, on a PostgreSQL made from the whole real `db/schema.sql`, with the first text of the function (RUN-ME-055 section 3) installed beside the new one: (1) the answers: the new function, the first text and a model written again in JavaScript return the same rows on 250 random books (a seeded generator) and eleven hand-made cases (a customer in two teams; a customer with initial rows only; a newest row that is an initial one; a day uploaded twice; two rows with the very same day and time, of which exactly one comes back; an empty team list; a team with no rows; known refs matched exactly, not by case or blank; a team asked twice answers twice; and the two inputs the app never sends, a NULL known list and a NULL inside it, pinned to what they do: the first text answers nothing, the new one every candidate); (2) the pages, as above, asserted only where they do not depend on the plan the planner picks for the first text; (3) the index file as a file (its statement runs alone as one statement, builds the definition it says and is valid, is harmless when run again, the planner names it for the lookup with no Sort node, section 2 says valid, the undo drops it); (4) the cost of inserting a deck day with and without it, printed, and never more than double; (5) **21 of 21 deliberate breaks of the two files each make a check fail** (the known refs ignored or inverted; the old comparison against the array; initial rows or another team's row as the answer; the oldest row; the earlier upload of a day; two rows a customer; only the first team; the walk from the last ref; the day of today; the balance dropped; status and ds swapped; the lookup not tied to the candidate; an index that is not partial, is for initial rows, lacks `created_at`, starts with the ref, does not say `desc`, has another name, or fails when run twice). `test/ghost-rows-cheaper.test.mjs` (11 pins, in `npm test`): **the hash of the function that RAN**, so the repository cannot say the owner ran something else; the same name, arguments and columns as the first text; the lines that make it what it is; each file a block the owner can paste (under 10,000 characters, flush-left, plain ASCII, ending with its END line); nothing destructive; the index statement exactly; what the file says it costs; the kept check's own contents; and that this Part and CHAT.md name RUN-ME-076. **29 of 29 deliberate breaks of the pins, the two files and the check each turn a pin red.** RUN-ME-075's header was corrected to say what counting pages showed (its function text is unchanged: same hash).

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) #754 said the cheaper function "halves the cost" from milliseconds on a warm book held in memory, after CHAT.md section 7 had said twice that a cost is counted in pages on a worst-layout book. (2) The first form of the kept check used a book of eight teams and reported the first text eight times cheaper: the planner read the whole table for it. (3) The check's first run said both functions returned nothing on every book, because its result key was `k0` and the lookup `0`; it was found because the first text disagreed with the model too. (4) A first assertion said the cheaper function must read no more pages than the first text: it does (1.00) on one book and up to 1.3 times as many on another, so it is printed and not asserted. (5) Three breaks of the index file named text that also stands in the header, so they were "not in the file exactly once": the check refuses such a break and says so (that is how they were found).

**Not done, said plainly.** RUN-ME-076 was not run (the owner decides); nothing live was seen, so how many pages the live lookup reads, and whether the timeouts fall, is not known. The walk over a team's refs still costs about three buffers for each distinct ref it has ever had (an index descent each) and is the next cost once the index is in: not touched. The 1,000-row cap, the refresh rate and the region are as Part 114 left them.

**What the owner has to do.** Decide whether to run RUN-ME-076 (the statement and its check are pasted in the chat; select only the statement and run it alone), and paste the two measurements asked for in Part 114.

## Part 115 — The Postgres war, matter 1: the day's called numbers as one small answer (`db/RUN-ME-077`), what the owner's `pg_stat_statements` say, and the 800 ms limit that IS enforced (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. Two pastes came after the question of Part 114, with no words: the twelve heaviest statements from `pg_stat_statements` (SQL editor; normalised text, no customer data) and the check of the index of RUN-ME-076.

**What the heaviest statements say (read off the owner's paste; the paste itself is not kept here).** The twelve heaviest by total time add up to 323,938 seconds. In order (calls, seconds, mean, worst, share of the twelve): (1) the call app's `select phone, duration from call_logs where call_date = today`: 272,573 calls, 87,148 s, 320 ms, 7,991 ms, **27%**; (2) a read of `call_logs` by `officer, team, duration, portfolio …` (by its column list and the code, the dashboard's week of call logs, `officerBoardsUncached` in `api/_lib/portal-core.js`): 121,746 calls, 70,285 s, 577 ms, 7,654 ms, 22%; (3) a window function called with `p_from` only (by its argument, `expected_phone_window`, the call app's phone index): 149,469 calls, 50,631 s, 339 ms, 5,538 ms, 16%; (4) a window function called with `p_from, p_to, p_teams, p_lookback`: 174,991 calls, 40,290 s, 230 ms, 7,662 ms, 12%; then the follow-up list (197,252 calls, 85 ms), the phones' call-log inserts (832,000 calls, 16 ms each: the sacred path's own write, not touched), three reads of the Expected sheet and the decks, and three of `loans` (each 1.5% to 5%). **Four statements are 77% of the twelve.** By worst single run: the first five are the owner's own repair scripts (RUN-ME-060, 066 and 071: 15 to 38 seconds, run by hand in the SQL editor), and then seven statements of the app sit at 7.9 to 8.0 seconds, **the role's own limit of about 8 seconds cutting the slow ones off**: the call-log read above, the `p_dates, p_teams, p_lookback` window function (560 calls, mean 2.7 s), two reads of the decks (637 and 115 calls, means 3.3 and 4.1 s), two of the Expected sheet (130 and 3 calls) and the four-argument window function (1,677 calls, mean 1.0 s). **The ghost function: 12,793 calls, 3,075 s (about 1% of the twelve), mean 240 ms, worst exactly 800 ms.** A share is of the twelve heaviest put together; the database's whole time is not known, and `pg_stat_statements` does not record a statement that is cancelled, so the cancelled calls are in none of these numbers.

**A correction of what #754, Part 114, RUN-ME-055's comment and CHAT.md section 8 said: the function's own limit IS enforced through PostgREST.** They said that `set statement_timeout = '800ms'` on `defaulter_ghost_rows` does not cancel a longer call (a 1.85 second call succeeded in a direct `psql` session with no limit of its own). That is true of a call made directly in SQL, where the statement's clock is armed before the function's body runs, and it is not how the app calls it. PostgREST **hoists** a function's own `statement_timeout` into the request's transaction (`db-hoisted-tx-settings`, on by default for `statement_timeout`) before the call starts, so every call through the API is cancelled at 800 ms. The paste shows it: this function's worst recorded run is exactly 800 ms, where statements with no limit of their own reach 7.9 to 8.0 seconds, and 93 of the 100 newest Postgres log rows were `canceling statement due to statement timeout`. **So the timeouts of the ghost lookup are its own 800 ms limit, not the role's, and a lookup that needs more than 800 ms (a manager, a GMO or an admin holding many teams, probably) is cancelled every time it runs**, which is the same loss of cleared customers #755 softened. The cure that fits is the one #756 offers: fewer pages per lookup (RUN-ME-076's partial index, 6 to 14 times fewer) so that the biggest viewer's call fits under 800 ms. A longer limit for the reports (a second function with its own, which PostgREST would also enforce) was not built and is the owner's to say, because the lookup is shared with the phone, whose budget is 800 ms. The claim is corrected in place in Part 114, in CHAT.md section 8 and in RUN-ME-055's comment (the function text of RUN-ME-055 and RUN-ME-075 is unchanged: same hash).

**The index of RUN-ME-076.** The owner's earlier paste showed it built, valid, **126 MB**: about twice the 55 MB expected from the test book, so the live table holds about twice the current rows assumed (the cost to the upload is per row inserted, so it is not doubled by this). That paste ended with a second "Success. No rows returned" that could have been the undo, so the owner was asked for one line (it returns one row if the index stands). The answer was **two bare "Success. No rows returned"**, read as: the check found no row, and the create line (given for that case) was then run and succeeded, so **the index is probably in place again; this was not seen**, and the check is asked again (one row, `valid = true`). Whether the timeouts fell is not known (the per-minute count is still wanted).

**Matter 1, what was built: the call app's called-today read becomes one small database answer.** Under every officer's list the app asks "which numbers were rung today for longer than a dial attempt" (`calledTodaySet`, `api/_lib/call-core.js`, kept half a minute per server instance). It read the whole company's calls of the day, in pages of ten thousand: `fetchAll` adds the table's key as the last `ORDER BY` (`pageKeyFor`: `call_logs` → `id`), and each page re-runs the whole query with a larger offset, so a day of 20,000 calls was read and sorted three times. **`db/RUN-ME-077` adds `called_phones_today(p_day, p_min)`**: one jsonb value `{"phones": [...]}` of the day's distinct numbers whose call lasted longer than `p_min`, so there is no paging, no row cap and no sort by id. The app asks it first (`calledPhonesFromDb_`) and applies `pnorm` to what comes back as it always did, in one place (the SQL never normalises, so a number rung from another handset still ticks the same customer). **Where the function is not installed, throws, or answers a shape it does not make, the read is the old one, page by page, unchanged, and the failure is remembered for five minutes** (the same pause the ghost lookup and `expected_phone_window` use): never a failed list, and never nobody ticked. An officer's own new call still ticks at once (`noteCalledToday`, unchanged).

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** Reads added to `/api/upload`: none. To `/api/call`: none in the steady state; the function **replaces** the day's read (one round trip where there were ceil(N/10,000)+1, three for a day of 20,000 calls).
