## Part 116 — The Postgres war, matter 2: the dashboard's and the Presentation's call board as one small answer (`db/RUN-ME-078`) (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. The second heaviest statement of their `pg_stat_statements` paste (Part 115): `select officer, team, duration, portfolio ... from call_logs` for the whole week, **121,746 statements, 70,285 s in all, 577 ms each, 7,654 ms at worst, 22% of the twelve heaviest put together.**

**What the read was.** `officerBoardsUncached` (`api/_lib/portal-core.js`, behind the Dashboard and the Presentation, kept a minute per viewer's scope) read every call of the week (all teams for an admin), the eight columns the call boards draw, in pages of ten thousand: `fetchAll` adds the table's key as the last `ORDER BY`, each page runs the whole query again with a larger offset, so a week of 140,000 calls is fifteen statements, each reading and sorting the week by id. The rows were then added up in JavaScript into one line of figures per officer for the week and one for today (`callBoard`: `callRollupRows` and `callTotals`). The statements are probably about eight thousand board builds in the window of the paste (121,746 divided by fifteen): an inference, not a count.

**What was found while reading it: the board has never counted by category.** Its query does not select the `category` column, so `categoryOf` sees none and every portfolio call is one kind on the board. Ripoti and the Calls tab count through `call_report_rollup` (RUN-ME-042), which does split a portfolio call into EXPECTED, DEFAULTER and UNCATEGORIZED, so **a number rung under two categories on one day by one officer is one call on the board and two on Ripoti.** It is rare (a number is classified once by the phone index at the time of the call), it was there before this change, and it is **not changed**: a function that counted by category would have moved figures people are judged on the day it was switched on. The new function ignores category too, a test and a kept-check break pin it, and the owner can say whether the board should follow Ripoti (section 8 of CHAT.md).

**What was built.** `db/RUN-ME-078` adds `call_board_rollup(p_from, p_to, p_day, p_teams)`: the same adding up, inside the database, answered as ONE jsonb value `{"w": [...], "t": [...]}` (the week and the day), one object per officer **name** (the board is drawn by the name each call was filed under, not by `user_id`), in the order the officers first appear (the smallest `id`, the order the rows were always read in), with the eight figures `callTotals` gives and the first non-empty team the officer's calls were filed under. No paging, no row cap. The rules it keeps, each pinned and broken on purpose: a number rung is one call a day however often it was dialled (one line for each number an officer rang on a day, team and portfolio flag, then counted); talk time is portfolio talk time and the other is apart; a number is reached if any call to it connected; customers are distinct refs (or numbers) of portfolio calls; a team that is null and one that is empty are one team (`callRollupRows` joins them in a key); a blank officer is `(unknown)`; an officer is trimmed of every character JavaScript's `trim()` removes (written as escapes: the vertical tab is `\x0b`, `\v` would be the letter v); an outcome is matched without regard to case and blanks; the viewer's teams are matched exactly against the list `onTeams` always sent (`teamMatchList`). Only `service_role` may call it; it has no limit of its own (PostgREST would enforce one on every call, Part 115); the undo is one `drop function`.

**The app.** `boardRowsFromLogs` (`api/_lib/call-core.js`) is now the one definition of a board's lines from call rows, and the fall-back: it is what the screen computed inline before, moved out unchanged in effect. `callBoardSource_` (`portal-core.js`) asks the function first, with the viewer's team list or none for an admin, and **where the function is missing, throws or answers a shape it does not make, the read is the old one (the same eight columns, the same `.in()`), added up by `boardRowsFromLogs`, and the failure is remembered for five minutes**: never an empty board (heavier than before only for as long as a function that TIMES OUT takes to time out: Part 119). A viewer who holds no teams sees nobody's calls (the old read dropped every row), so nothing is read or asked for them. `portal-core.js` no longer imports `callRollupRows` or `callTotals`: one definition of the counting rule, in one place.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call` (this is a portal screen). On the portal the function REPLACES the week's read: one round trip where a week of 140,000 calls took fifteen. Before RUN-ME-078 is run, one cheap failed call every five minutes for each server instance (PostgREST answers an unknown function from its own schema cache, so it should reach neither Postgres nor its log), and the un-migrated budget of the Officer boards in `test/speed.test.mjs` moves by that one trip: measured on the speed test's fixture, the Officer boards take 26 trips before this change, 27 un-migrated and 21 with the function installed (the same as before: it replaces the one read); the budgets are unchanged (their ceilings, 53 and 33, are far over all of these) and the migrated world of the test now includes the function, as it includes every migration. **Measured** by `tools/db-checks/call-board-rollup.mjs` on a PostgreSQL made from the whole real schema (with Supabase's default grants and the two other `call_logs` indexes the repository's migrations make), on 800,000 call-log rows (forty days of 20,000; 300 officers; 40 teams), the old read's fifteen statements in the exact shape the app sent (`order by id asc limit 10000 offset ...`) against the function, in buffers touched, warm: rows of a day together on the table, 279,451 pages, 2.5 s and 20.9 MB against 3,236 pages, 0.68 s and 104 KB; every row in a random place (the worst layout), 2,436,420 pages, 3.8 s and 20.9 MB against 14,616 pages, 0.66 s and 104 KB. **That is 86 to 167 times fewer pages, 3.7 to 5.8 times less database time and 205 times fewer bytes. The live numbers are NOT known** (the live table is bigger and on disk; the owner has not run the file yet). The first form of the function copied today's rows through the big aggregates a second time and sorted twice with a spill to disk (1.3 seconds on the test book); one grouping by number, then the counts, and today's figures taken from the week's groups took it to about 0.7 s: measured with `explain (analyze)`, kept because the check proves the answer is unchanged.

**Checked.** (1) **THE OLD CODE AS YARDSTICK** (`test/call-board-rollup.test.mjs`): the screen's code as it stood before this change is kept in the test word for word, and the boards the new path makes are compared with it on 250 random books (officers padded and cased every way, null and empty teams, redials, ties on calls, phone users who are and are not on the board), for the admin and for a viewer with teams, from the rows and with the function: **2,000 boards, equal in every line, every figure and the order of ties.** The refactor is live the moment this deploys, before RUN-ME-078 is run, so this is the test that matters first. (2) `tools/db-checks/call-board-rollup.mjs`: the function against the production `boardRowsFromLogs` on 150 random books and six parameter sets each (admin, a viewer with teams, a day past the window, an empty team list, an empty window), exactly and in order; the cost in two layouts (printed; the function must read fewer pages, take less time and send a twentieth of the bytes, and the week must be read through an index); the file as a file (twice as one text, who may call it, the landing line, the undo); **28 of 28 deliberate breaks of the file each make a check fail.** The scratch table drops the two check constraints the real `call_logs` has on `outcome` and `category`, on purpose, so that the generator can write the variants a book without them could hold. (3) Fifteen more tests through the real portal dispatch: the same boards from either source and no read of `call_logs` when the function answers; category is ignored; a viewer's team list reaches the database exactly as the `.in()` sent it; no teams, no read; a missing, throwing or wrong-shaped function falls back; the five-minute pause; 1,200 officers are 1,200 lines; ties keep the order officers first appear. (4) **68 of 68 deliberate breaks of the tests' targets each turn a test red.** `npm test`: 1,838 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The tool I write files with turned the unicode escapes I typed for the no-break space, the line and paragraph separators, the ideographic space and the byte-order mark (in the SQL file and in the kept check) into the characters themselves: invisible, and exactly what section 7 of CHAT.md says a paste can mangle. Found by scanning my new files for anything outside plain text before committing; rewritten as escapes, and the pin demands plain ASCII. (2) The first form of the check wrote outcomes and categories the real table's check constraints forbid; its first run said so. (3) The first form of the yardstick forgot the exact `.in()` the screen also puts on the phone users, and reported a difference that was the harness's, not the code's. (4) A first full run of the check crashed at its first deliberate break because the break's text assumed the file was indented; a break whose text is missing is now reported as one, never a crash. (5) The first form of the function was correct and twice as slow as it needed to be (above).

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **RUN-ME-078 has not been run**: until it is, the Dashboard and the Presentation add the week up in JavaScript exactly as before (through `boardRowsFromLogs`), and the live saving is not known. (2) The board still ignores category and so differs from Ripoti on the rare number rung under two categories in a day (above). (3) Other readers of `call_logs` were not touched: the Exp.Def report's calls of the week (`api/_lib/expdf.js`), the calls report's fall-back, an officer's own day (`call-core.js`); none is in the heaviest twelve. (4) Matters 3 and 4 are untouched and come one at a time: the two calendar-window functions (149,469 and 174,991 calls) and the follow-up list. A phone index rebuilt for every server instance every five minutes, and a longer life for a good list, are the levers there; the number of reads is instances times refreshes, not only their cost. (5) A review by a second reader was **Not read by a second reader before the merge**: the old screen code kept as a yardstick, the PostgreSQL check and the mutation runs stand in for one, and CHAT.md section 7 says to merge first and have one reader read it after, when nothing is owed to the owner. That reader reads the merged change; what it finds is recorded in the next entry, and a finding is checked by hand on the test database before it is called real..

**What the owner has to do.** Run `db/RUN-ME-078` (pasted in the chat) in a NEW SQL editor tab: its last line before the END line answers two numbers (the officers with calls this week and today). Then, in a few hours, the combined `pg_stat_statements` query the owner was given: the old week read's `calls` should stop growing and a line for `call_board_rollup` should show its own small mean.

## Part 117 — The Postgres war, matter 3a: the phone index reads six columns of an expected sheet, not thirty (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. On the call app's own path: "UPLOADING and CALL APP should NEVER GO DOWN neither SLOW DOWN" (CLAUDE.md section 1).

**What was read.** The phone index (`phoneIndexCompute`, `api/_lib/call-core.js`) is what `/api/call`'s sync asks to tell whether a number is a customer's or a guarantor's. Every warm server instance builds it on its own clock (every five minutes) and again after every upload, and the first sync on a cold instance waits for it. It reads five things; two of them are today's and tomorrow's expected sheet (`latestSnapshot` on `repayment_snapshots`), **every column of every row, all teams, about thirty columns: the amounts, the dates, the branch, the zone** — though the index uses six of them: `ref, full_name, contact, guarantor_name, guarantor_contact, team` (`add(r.contact, r.full_name, r.ref, r.team, ...)` and `add(r.guarantor_contact, r.guarantor_name, r.ref, r.team, ...)`; `latestSnapshot` adds the two columns that decide which upload wins, `upload_batch` and `created_at`, itself). The comment above those lines said "The phone index needs names and numbers, nothing else" and narrowed only the register read beside them; `latestSnapshot`'s own note says narrowing is opt-in per caller because it is shared (an earlier attempt to narrow it for everyone put customers on phones with no name), and this caller had never opted in.

**What changed.** The two calls pass `columns: PHONE_INDEX_SHEET_COLS` (the six). Same rows, same index. No read added or removed.

**Measured** on a scratch book made from the whole real schema (14 days of two sheet types, 10,000 rows a sheet, every column filled the way a sheet fills them), the sheet read in the shape PostgREST sends it (`order by id limit 10000`), warm: **98 to 137 ms and 7.8 MB with every column; 60 to 64 ms and 2.65 MB with the six**: about 45% less database time and three times fewer bytes for each sheet; two sheets for each index build. **What that is on the live book is NOT known:** the owner's paste ranks `repayment_snapshots.*` reads seventh and ninth (43,069 and 29,393 statements, 12,610 and 6,750 s in all), but other screens read the same table the same way, so which of those statements are the phone index's cannot be told from the paste; the egress saved is the bytes times the number of builds.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/call`: no read added, none removed, two reads ask for fewer columns (less to build, less to send, a shorter wait for the first sync of a cold instance). `/api/upload`: nothing. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged and green. No front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked.** The existing call tests covered four of the six columns: dropping `guarantor_name` or `guarantor_contact` from the list failed nothing, so a guarantor lost from the index would have gone unseen (found by dropping each column in turn before the change was kept). Two tests were added to `test/call.test.mjs`: one pins the exact list each sheet read asks for and that no read takes every column; one syncs the numbers of a customer and a guarantor on today's sheet and on tomorrow's and checks the match, the name, the ref and the category each comes back with. **Each of the six columns dropped on purpose now fails 2 to 10 tests, and putting every column back fails 1.** `npm test`: 1,840 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** None found by the tests; the one thing the change nearly rested on was a belief that the existing tests would catch a missing column, and two of six would not have.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) The index's other two heavy reads are untouched: `expected_phone_window` (149,469 statements, 50,631 s, 16% of the twelve heaviest, the two-week distinct of customers) and the whole follow-up register (197,252 statements, 16,852 s), which is the register the index needs in full. (2) **The number of builds is the lever, not only their cost**: the figures above are statements, and a build runs once for each warm instance every five minutes and again after each upload, so the statements are (instances) times (refreshes); on a host that starts many short-lived instances each one builds its own. Ways to cut the count are architecture and the owner's to choose: one long-lived process (the own server, section 5 of CHAT.md, builds it once for everybody), a copy shared between instances through the database, or a longer life for a good index (it is rebuilt on every upload anyway, so five minutes is a safety net, not a freshness rule). None was built or measured. (3) The live saving is not measured.

## Part 118 — The Postgres war, matter 3b: the phone index is read in two parts and built once (20 Nov)

> "when you finish: postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026.

**What the index was.** `phoneIndex` (`api/_lib/call-core.js`; what `/api/call`'s sync asks to tell a customer's number from a guarantor's, and what the phone's search reads) was ONE thing: five reads (the follow-up register; today's sheet and tomorrow's sheet, each a date and its rows; the two-week window `expected_phone_window`; the numbered comments), seven statements in all, kept per server instance against the key `today + DATA_VERSION + NEW_NUMBER_VERSION` and for five minutes, and thrown away whole when ANY of those moved. The owner's `pg_stat_statements` (Parts 115 to 117) rank two of its reads high: the window is the third heaviest statement in the book (149,469 runs, 50,631 s, 339 ms each) and the register read the fifth (197,252 runs, 16,852 s).

**What was found by reading it.** The two stamps do not mean the same thing. `DATA_VERSION` moves when something is UPLOADED, and the register, the sheets and the window are what an upload changes. `NEW_NUMBER_VERSION` moves when an officer records an "Ana namba nyingine", and only the numbered comments change. Yet one recorded number made every warm server instance read the whole book again to learn one number (the code's own note says "a handful a day": nothing measures how many it really is). And a server instance that is handed several syncs at once, with the cache empty or past its five minutes, ran the same reads once for each of them.

**What was built.** The index is read in two parts, each kept for the same five minutes as before: the LISTS (the four big reads) against today and `DATA_VERSION`, the NUMBERED COMMENTS (one small read) against `NEW_NUMBER_VERSION`; the index is made again from the two, by arithmetic and no database, when either has changed (`phoneIndexLists`, `phoneNumberRows`, `phoneIndexBuild`). And a read is shared: the first sync to find a part missing asks, the others in flight wait for that answer (`phonePart_`); a read that FAILS is forgotten at once, and the failure of an older read never throws away a newer one. Both parts are started together, as the five reads always were. `phoneIndex(db, nowMs, dataVersion, numberVersion)` is exported, and takes the two stamps apart where it took them joined in one string.

**What did not change.** The index is byte for byte what the old code made from the same rows. The five minutes. Every key. The first sync after an upload, and the first after a recorded number, sees it. A served index costs no read and is the same object (the phone's search keeps an index of it). The ONE difference, only toward fewer reads: a rebuild forced by a recorded number no longer also reads the lists again, so a change to the register or the sheets that moved NO stamp (the admin button that restores the register from the deck is the only one the code has) is seen at the lists' own five-minute mark and no longer also at the next recorded number.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/call`: no read added anywhere. A cold instance reads what it always read (7). A recorded number: ONE small read where there were seven, for every warm instance. Syncs in flight together: one set of reads where there were as many as there were syncs. A served index: none. `/api/upload`: nothing. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged and green. Memory: the raw lists are kept beside the index now (about as much again as the index: ten to twenty megabytes for a book of ten thousand customers, ESTIMATED, not measured). No front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked.** `test/phone-index.test.mjs` (17 tests). THE OLD CODE IS THE YARDSTICK: its compute is kept in the test word for word, and the index the new code makes is compared with it, key by key and in insertion order (the phone's search lists customers in that order), over 120 random books (numbers written five ways and colliding on purpose, two weeks of sheets, a day older than the window, a second upload of a day, a sheet ahead, comments with and without numbers), over 30 books on a database without the window function, and over 60 random sequences of 40 events (uploads that change the register and a sheet and move the stamp, recorded numbers, the clock up to nearly seven minutes, midnight): 2,400 syncs, each compared with the index the OLD code would make from the book as it is then. The reads are counted: a cold index is 7 statements; a served one 0; a recorded number 1; an upload 6; five minutes 7; midnight rebuilds the lists; twelve syncs at once are one build; nine at once on a new number stamp are one read; a failed build is told to every waiter and not kept; the failure of an older build leaves a newer one alone; a clock that jumps backwards is not trusted; a change that moved no stamp is seen at the five-minute mark; the two parts start together. **20 of 20 deliberate breaks** (a key that carries the other stamp, the comments keyed by the upload stamp, a read not shared, a failure kept, an older failure clearing a newer build, the five minutes never ending, a clock trusted backwards, midnight missing from the key, the build never reused, two customer lists added in the other order, the numbered comments or the guarantors left out, the window from the future or a day short, the two parts asked one after the other, a build dated at the epoch, a read that stays "in flight" for ever, the register first again, both callers passing the stamps joined or one of them missing) each turn at least one test red. `npm test`: 1,857 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first failure test counted reads as if the reader asked once; it retries a transient timeout, so it saw three and said so. (2) The first pin of the two callers cut each call at its first closing bracket and found three where there are two. (3) The first test of the older failure built its counter after the cache had been filled, and the cache is kept against the client: a new client is a new cache and it saw a cold index. All three were the tests', found at their first run, not the code's.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **The live saving is not known**: it depends on what makes the instances rebuild today (recorded numbers, the five minutes, cold starts), and the owner's statistics cannot tell them apart. Where recorded numbers dominate it is large, where the five minutes dominate it is small. (2) **The five minutes are unchanged.** A longer life for the lists once their upload has had time to finish (the stamp is the upload's own millisecond clock, and the register is written just AFTER the stamp moves) is the next matter and a freshness decision: see the next entry. (3) **A cold instance still pays the whole index**: only a copy shared through the database, or one long-lived process, cuts that; architecture, the owner's. (4) The window and the register statements cost what they cost; their own plans were not changed. (5) Nothing live was seen.

## Part 119 — The second reader of #759: what it checked, what it found, what was changed and what was not (20 Nov)

> "please never stop until whats asked is done." / "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026.

**The reader.** CHAT.md section 7 says merge first and have a change read after, one reader at a time and nothing owed to the owner meanwhile. #759 (the call board as one database answer, `db/RUN-ME-078`) was merged without a second reader, and one was started on it afterwards. It worked in its own scratch PostgreSQL 16 from `db/schema.sql` and the repository's file, touched neither the repository nor git, did not run `npm test` or the kept check, and reported at the end. **Its findings were checked by hand before any was called real** (section 7).

**What it tried, and found nothing.** (1) The blanks: all 1,114,110 code points, the 25 that JavaScript's `trim()` removes against the ones the function's `btrim` removes: the same set. (2) A differential fuzz of about 2,000 books against six parameter sets (the admin; team lists with commas, quotes, an apostrophe, a backslash, blanks, a no-break space, case and trailing-space variants; a day outside the window; an empty list), on a C.UTF-8 table and again on an ICU-collated one, sparse and dense; officers padded with all 25 blanks, `(unknown)`, numbers, `null`, `undefined`; teams null, empty and blank; phones null, empty and in Arabic digits; durations past 2^31: **0 differences**, and a dense 6,000-row book equal. The id order is the same comparator on both sides. (3) The whole `officerBoards` screen in three modes (the portal before #759; the portal after it with no function; the portal after it with the REAL SQL function behind the call), 220 books by 8 viewers (the admin, one team, two teams in two spellings, a team with a trailing blank, a list with blanks in it, an empty list): **1,664 boards, 0 differences**, and instrumented: no function is one failed attempt and one read of `call_logs`, the function answering is no read at all. (4) Every failure of the function (an error, a throw, `null`, a wrong shape) falls back and pauses: never a blank board and never a hang beyond what the screen's other fourteen reads would be.

**Found and CHECKED BY HAND: one real flaw, fixed.** `callBoard` keys the officers on a plain object through `bucket()`, which read `if (!map[key])`. An officer's name is free text typed at registration; for a name every object already has (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`) the map's value was not empty, so the board was handed `Object.prototype` itself and wrote the officer's team onto it. **Reproduced through the real screen with one logged call under the name `__proto__`: afterwards `({}).team` read `KONGOWE` for every object in the server process until it restarted, and the officer was on no board.** (The board before #759 threw for such a name, so the Dashboard failed for everyone whose scope held that officer: a loud fault. After #759 it was silent, and wrote.) `bucket()` now looks for the key among the map's OWN properties and makes it with `defineProperty`, which gives `__proto__` a property of its own instead of setting the map's prototype; for every other key the property is the same one an assignment made, in the same order, so the 30 other callers of `bucket()` (staff names from Teams & Staff, upper-cased keys) are unchanged and no longer able to meet the same thing.

**Found, small, fixed.** The function's answer was believed if two of its figures passed `Number.isFinite(Number(x))`, and `Number(null)` is 0: a row with a null figure passed. All eight figures a board draws must now BE numbers (and the name text); anything else is a wrong shape and the board is read the old way. The function this repository ships coalesces every figure, so nothing live changes.

**Found, a claim of mine that was false, corrected (not the code).** #759 said the fall-back was "never heavier than before". A function that is MISSING answers at once from PostgREST's schema cache, and that is the usual case. One that TIMES OUT is waited for until the role's limit (about eight seconds, the function sets none of its own: Part 115) and only then is the old read made: one wait for each server instance, then nothing for five minutes, and the requests that start during the wait wait with it. Worst case about eight seconds plus the old read, inside the client's 45 and the host's 60. The pause is for the whole PROCESS, not one scope: if only the all-teams admin's call times out, every smaller scope is read the old way for the five minutes too. **Not changed**, because the old read is the heavier of the two and would meet the same slow database: a budget that abandoned the function sooner would send more load to the database exactly when it is struggling. The sentence is corrected in the code's comment, in `db/RUN-ME-078`'s header (a comment line: the function is not touched) and in Part 116.

**Recorded and NOT changed: two differences between the SQL and the JavaScript that no live row can reach.** (a) An outcome spelt `mißed`: JavaScript's `toUpperCase` makes `MISSED`, PostgreSQL's libc `upper()` leaves the `ß`, so the SQL counts it connected and the JavaScript does not. Not reachable: `call_logs_outcome_check` (`db/schema.sql`) and the sync's whitelist refuse any outcome but the four. (b) `callRollupRows` joins its group key with an unescaped control character: two officers whose typed names carry that character can fall into one group in JavaScript where the SQL keeps them apart (the SQL is the exact one). `callRollupRows` is shared by Ripoti, the Calls tab and the phone's own summary, so it was not touched for a case that needs a control character typed into a name. Also noted, not acted on: the old paged read could count a row twice if the phones inserted between its pages (an inference, not reproduced; the function reads one snapshot); a function answer scales with distinct officer NAMES, not calls (about 19 MB for 100,000 distinct names; the live book has about 300).

**What the reader could not check.** The live function's text (only the repository's file was tested: the owner pasted this file and it answered `382 | 285`, so what ran is the file; comparing `pg_get_functiondef` is optional), real PostgREST (that the bare `{w, t}` object comes back as it does here, the live role's timeout), the live collation (`en_US.UTF-8`, which the reader could not install: C.UTF-8 and ICU were tried and the `ß` case is assumed to follow glibc), and live timings.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/upload`, `/api/call`: nothing. The portal: `bucket()` makes one own-property test and, for a key it has not seen, a `defineProperty`, where it made one read and an assignment: nothing a person could notice, and no read of the database. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged. No front-end file: `BUILD` and `CALL_BUILD` unchanged.

**Checked.** Two tests in `test/call-board-rollup.test.mjs`, **both red on the code as merged and green on the fix**: five names every object has (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`) are on both boards, from the rows and from the function, with their calls and team, and nothing is written onto `Object.prototype` (the test removes `team` from it afterwards whatever happened, so a failure cannot leave the runner polluted); and each of the eight figures as a null, as a string and as missing, a row with no name and a name that is a number, are wrong shapes read the old way, while a whole row is believed. **7 of 7 deliberate breaks** (the assignment back; own-property test with plain assignment, where `__proto__` sets the prototype and the officer is lost; `defineProperty` with the lookup through the prototype chain; the check believing a null; the check on two figures only; one figure forgotten; the name forgotten) each turn a test red; the last was missed at first, because the strict figures had made the old no-name test pass for another reason, and the test was strengthened. `npm test` green.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) "Never heavier than before" was false for a timeout: said in a code comment, a SQL header, Part 116 and the PR body, and not checked against the case that matters. (2) The pollution was reachable from the day #759 merged: the reader found it, I did not, and #759 went in with a mutation run of its own tests and no second reader. (3) The no-name test lost its force when the shape check became strict, and the mutation run found it.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) `callRollupRows`' group key and the `ß` case (above). (2) The five-minute pause is for the process, not the scope. (3) Nothing live was seen: the owner ran `db/RUN-ME-078` (it answered 382 officers this week and 285 today) and has not yet said whether the boards or the statements look different.

## Part 120 — The Postgres war, matter 3c: the phone index's lists live thirty minutes once their upload has settled (20 Nov)

> "please never stop until whats asked is done." / "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026.

**Where matter 3b left it (Part 118).** The index's four big reads (the register, today's and tomorrow's sheet, the two-week window `expected_phone_window`: the third heaviest statement of the owner's `pg_stat_statements`, 149,469 runs and 50,631 s) were kept for five minutes by every warm server instance whatever happened, and read again when DATA_VERSION moved. Nothing says how many of the live rebuilds are the five minutes, how many are uploads, how many are recorded numbers (matter 3b) and how many are cold instances. Matter 3c is for the first.

**Why it was five minutes.** The code's own note says so: "a backstop for a deployment whose DATA_VERSION never moves". And one more thing it does not say: `api/upload.js` stamps DATA_VERSION on the LAST slice, after the sheets are written, and the register (`writeFollowupFromDeck`) is written just AFTER the stamp, in the same request. A rebuild at the stamp can hold a register that is not finished, and the five minutes are what put it right.

**What was built.** The stamp is read as a clock as well. It is the upload's own `Date.now()`. A lists build made at least ten minutes after it (`PHONE_INDEX_SETTLE_MS`: the host stops an upload at sixty seconds) is SETTLED: it holds everything that upload wrote, and it is kept thirty minutes (`PHONE_INDEX_SETTLED_TTL_MS`) instead of five. A build made sooner is unsettled and lives five minutes, exactly as before; so after an upload an instance builds at its next sync, again five minutes on, again five minutes later (the first build made ten minutes after the stamp), and then every thirty minutes. A stamp that is not a millisecond clock (empty on a book never uploaded to, a label, a number below 10^12, one from the future) never settles and keeps the five minutes. The numbered comments are not touched: five minutes, and a recorded number re-reads them at once (Part 118). A new stamp rebuilds the lists on the very next sync, settled or not.

**What it rests on, and what was found.** Every writer of what the lists hold must move a stamp, or the longer life is a staleness nobody sees. Read, not assumed: an upload moves DATA_VERSION (the last slice; every upload type reaches it, the only early return being a file with no rows); the call app's and the portal's comment writers move NEW_NUMBER_VERSION; **two did not, and now do**: the admin button that restores the register from the deck (`rebuildFollowup` writes customers' numbers and guarantors' and moved nothing the phones watch) now moves DATA_VERSION, and the old `/api/followup` endpoint (no caller in the repository) moves NEW_NUMBER_VERSION when it records a number. `followupClean` writes no number. `test/phone-index.test.mjs` reads the sources and fails when a file that writes `new_number` does not name NEW_NUMBER_VERSION, when `rebuildFollowup` stops moving DATA_VERSION after it writes, or when an upload stops stamping on its last slice.

**The price, written down.** A change made BY HAND in the database that moves no stamp (an SQL script that edits a number in the register or a sheet) reaches a phone's index after thirty minutes where it reached it after five. When it matters, after the script, in a new tab: `update settings set value = (extract(epoch from now()) * 1000)::bigint::text where key = 'DATA_VERSION';` (tested on a scratch database: it writes a 13-digit millisecond clock). Every instance then rebuilds at its next sync, and every handset fetches its figures once.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/call`: no read added anywhere; reads fewer. An instance that is quiet and settled builds the lists twice an hour where it built them twelve times; after an upload it builds them three or four times in the first forty minutes where it built them eight. `/api/upload`: nothing. The admin restore adds one write of one row to a button used a few times in its life. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged. No front-end file.

**Checked.** Eleven tests in `test/phone-index.test.mjs` (27 in all) and one in `test/portal.test.mjs`: a settled build is kept thirty minutes and the comments five; an unsettled one five, and the sequence after an upload; the settle point is exactly ten minutes (one millisecond before is unsettled); six stamps that are not clocks never settle; an upload's new stamp rebuilds at once and the new build is unsettled; a recorded number on a settled index is one read; a change that moved no stamp is seen at thirty minutes and not at twenty-nine (the price, pinned); the settled index equals the old code's on 30 random books; the sources. **15 of 15 deliberate breaks** each turn a test red (the settled life five minutes or an hour; every build settled or none; no settle margin or five minutes; an exclusive settle point; a tiny or an empty stamp counted as a clock; the comments also kept thirty minutes; the lists not told the stamp; the five minutes gone; the stamp moved before the register is written; the restore or the old endpoint no longer moving a stamp). `npm test` green.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The first break of the old endpoint changed my own comment, not the code, and was "missed": a break that is not a break (found when the miss was read; aimed at the code and caught). (2) The restore's stamp was first written `if (added + restored > 0)`, a condition that cannot be false where it stands (a register with nothing to do returns above): a branch no test could reach, removed.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **A cold instance still pays the whole index**, and so does the first sync after every upload: only a copy shared through the database, or one long-lived process, cuts that (architecture, the owner's). (2) The live saving is NOT known. (3) The window's and the register's own statements cost what they cost. (4) Nothing live was seen.

**Read.**

1. **Matters 1 to 3c did what they were built for, where it can be seen.** The new called-today answer takes 31 ms where the old read took 320 ms on average and 8 s at worst; the ghost lookup takes 86 ms a run where it took 240 (about 2.8 times cheaper per run, a sample of 709) and never passes its own 800 ms; the phones' inserts are unchanged. **The database is not saturated on average:** the statements in the table add up to about 1,945 s of database time in the window (and about 100 s more for the two new functions, whose totals cannot be cut to the window), in 13,405 s of clock, about 15% of one core's worth. It is a lower bound (a statement outside the twelve heaviest of each ranking is not in it), not a load figure.
2. **The old reads are still running as often as the new answers, and that is the largest single block of measured time.** The only readers of those two exact statement shapes in the code are the fall-backs (`api/_lib/call-core.js` `calledTodaySet`; `api/_lib/portal-core.js` `callBoardSource_`: a search of every `call_logs` read in `api/`, the same shape appears nowhere else), so the old called-today read ran 389 times beside 386 runs of the new answer, and the old week read 810 times (a board is about fourteen of those statements: roughly 58 boards, an inference) beside 31 runs of the rollup. **Together 917 s of the 1,945 s, 47% of the listed time in the window (44% if the two new functions' whole totals are added to the time).** When the small answer fails once the app switches to the heavy read for five minutes (`CALLED_FN_PAUSE_MS`, `CALL_BOARD_PAUSE_MS`), which is exactly when the database is already struggling. **Why the small answer fails is not known:** a failed statement is not in these figures. Three causes would each fit and none can be told from the other here: a statement timeout (the rollup takes 3 s on average and 5.5 s at worst, against a role limit of about 8 s, where the scratch book took 0.7 s: the live table is colder); a wait for a connection when the PostgREST pool is full of slow reads (the Postgres log shows bursts of 5 or 6 timeouts within 3 seconds, which looks like several slow statements ending together); a network error between the host and Supabase.
3. **What `pg_stat_statements` cannot name:** the statements behind the 7 to 8 timeouts a minute that the Logs showed at midday. The statements with a worst single run near 8 s (7,996, 7,992, 7,991, 7,970, 7,959, 7,890, 7,885 ms) are mostly NOT running now: five of the seven did not run at all in the window.
4. **Two corrections.** (i) The statement with 560 runs, 2,659 ms on average and 7,996 ms at worst, declared as `(p_dates, p_teams, p_lookback)`, did not run once in the window and **is declared in no file of the repository**: it is an older function the book still holds. An index on `contact` costs the upload a little on every deck row it writes (CLAUDE.md section 1, Part 114's measurement of the same kind), so it is a matter to measure before it is offered, not one to build now.

**What was handed over (in the chat, pasted in full).** Two queries for Supabase, **Logs, Logs Explorer** (the project's address ending `/logs/explorer`; time range "Last 24 hours"; not the SQL editor): (a) the API Gateway's answers of 500 and above, by method, path and status (`edge_logs`), which names the endpoint or table that fails and how often; (b) the Postgres log's `statement timeout` rows grouped by the statement text (`postgres_logs`, `parsed.query`, cut at 200 characters, runs of blanks as one), which names the statements the table above cannot. Neither prints a name, a number or an amount. If `parsed.query` is not a field of that log the second says so, and the fall-back is to open one timeout row in Logs, Postgres and paste its `query` line only.
