## Part 121 — The access codes hold the latest leader of each team, and Teams & Staff follows them: `leadersSync` (20 Nov)

> "The access codes hold the latest staff / leader per team, so unless not there, will be set aty teams and staff but teams and staff (Wafanyakazi / Staff — by person and its Orodha / List of team's leaders) must always update the leaders as from settings (Misimbo ya kuingia / Access codes)" · "and that should affect all the current teams and staff nav data right away" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026.

**What was already there (read before anything was built, section 2's rule: a surprising result is read against the rule that already governs it).** (1) `saveAccessCode` carried the ONE code just saved across to the sheet (`syncStaffFromCode`, "an access code and the teams table are one fact kept in two places": a role that is a column, an explicit team list, nobody else's name touched), for the roles whose name IS a column (GMO, MANAGER, OPM, RECOVERY, CREDIT ANALYST ...). (2) The boards read the sheet with the codes LAID OVER IT for three units (`overlayCodes_`: RECOVER..., EXPECT.../EARLY..., collection), never written back. (3) The Teams & Staff list filled a blank collection or legal officer from the code that holds the team, and a typed name won. (4) Who held what is recorded around every save (`holders.js`). **What was missing:** nothing carried ALL the codes, so every code edited by any other road (an upload of the codes sheet, a hand edit, a code saved before the rule existed) left the sheet and the codes saying different things, and the rotation, the phone, the SMS lists and both Teams & Staff screens read the STORED sheet; the by-person and the leaders list never showed the codes; and two definitions of "which column does this role name" existed (the exact names for the save, the words for the overlay), so a "PMO RECOVERY" code laid itself over every board and was never written to the sheet, and a team dropped from it stayed on the sheet to re-assert itself.

**What was built.** (a) **ONE rule for the column** (`leaderColumnOf_`): the exact names and aliases, else the words RECOVER/EXPECT/EARLY; the collection officer is left out on purpose (their teams live on the code, and the list fills the column from it). (b) **The plan** (`api/_lib/leaders-sync.js`, pure): which cells of the stored sheet the codes change, which they keep and why, which they cannot decide. (c) **`leadersSync`** (write; preview with `{preview:true}`) reads the stored teams and the codes (never the code values: they are passwords), plans, writes the cells (grouped by the keys each row carries: PostgREST turns a missing key into NULL, which on a conflict BLANKS the cell), keeps the way back in the settings table (`LEADERS_SYNC_LOG`, written BEFORE the first cell; no access code in it) and answers what it changed, kept, could not decide and noticed; **`leadersSyncUndo`** puts back every cell the last sync changed that still holds what it wrote. Both are audited, refused to a view-only code at the one door, behind the Teams & Staff tab, and recorded in the history of who held what. (d) **It runs** when somebody asks, when `saveAccessCode` has saved a code (the whole sync, after the one code's own: quiet on failure, the code is saved either way), and **as the Teams & Staff screen opens**: the screen asks a READ first (`leadersCheck`: what differs, nothing written, open to a view-only admin too, never in the audit log or the history of who held what) and asks the WRITE (`leadersSync`) only for a code that may change things and only when the check found a cell out of line, and BEFORE it reads the list, so what is on it is current the moment it is looked at; a book that agrees costs two small reads on open and leaves no trace, where a write on every open would have put a line in the audit log and six reads of the history each time. A card at the top says what happened, with Sync now and Undo (a view-only admin is shown what differs and offered nothing to press). (e) The list's collection and legal officer now come from the code that names the team over a typed name (a team no code names keeps its row). (f) `/api/me` tells the page when a code is view-only, so the screen never asks the write of a code the server would refuse (and write the refusal in the audit log at every open). `BUILD 2026-11-20-c`.

**The rules, and what each stops.** (1) **A cell no code names keeps what Teams & Staff says** ("unless not there"): a code never clears anybody; a person dropped from a code is taken off by `saveAccessCode` at the moment of the save (it knows who the code used to be), never by a sweep that cannot. (2) A code names a cell only when it holds the team EXPLICITLY and its role is a column; a code with no team list means every team and is nobody's portfolio (writing it through would make one person the GMO of every team); a role that is no column (ADMIN, MANAGEMENT ...) names nothing and is counted, so it can be told. (3) **Two codes of one role that name DIFFERENT people on one team change nothing and are reported**: which of them leads is a person's to say, and "a rule that has to choose is a guess"; the same person under two spellings is one claimant, and two different people who share a first name are never merged (`holders.js` `looseSame` and `canonNames`, the rule the history already uses). (4) **The same person is never re-spelt SHORTER**: a code that says MARY where the sheet says MARY SAMPLE keeps the sheet's fuller name and the cell is told (so the code's name can be made the full one: the leader's own list matches by the code's spelling); a code that spells the person fuller upgrades the sheet. (5) **A new leader does not inherit the last one's number or staff ID**: they get the ones the same person already has beside that role on another team, else none, which the screen shows in red and which is true. (6) Only the columns the book has are written. (7) The plan does not depend on the order the database returns the rows (a sorted copy). Seven columns only (OPM, recovery, GMO, manager, credit, expected, bike).

**What the owner will see.** The first time an admin opens Teams & Staff after the deploy (or saves any access code), every leader cell a code names is brought into line, and the card lists each one (team, role, was, now). **That moves customers between leaders' lists wherever a code names somebody other than the sheet did, in the rotation, the reports, the commission boards and the phone: it is what the order says, and the card and `team_holders` are the record.** (Part 122: as first built, Undo was written again by the screen's own next look and never stuck; it now holds the cells it puts back.) Cells two codes dispute, names kept longer on the sheet, and leaders whose own code does not hold teams the sheet gives them are listed and left.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/upload` and `/api/call`: nothing (the phone reads the stored leaders it always read, which now follow the codes; its own memo ages out as before). The portal: opening Teams & Staff as an admin reads the teams and the codes (the screen reads both anyway) and one settings row, and writes only the cells that differ; saving a code does the same; no screen that is not Teams & Staff changes. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged but for the two names added to its list of writers.

**Checked.** `test/leaders-sync.test.mjs` (34 tests: 19 on the plan, 15 through the real door and the screen's sources), `tools/browser-checks/portal-leaders-sync.mjs` (a real Chromium on the real `public/app.html` and `public/mod/admin.js`: 31 points, among them that the check is asked first and the write only when it found a difference, that the screen WAITS for the sync (a stub that answers it late shows a stale list to a screen that does not), a leader named `<img onerror=...>` drawn as characters, a view-only code shown what differs and never asked to write, a settled book offering no Undo), and the three existing tests the rule touched (the typed-name-wins test of the list, the writers list, the read-only wall's list). **34 of 34 deliberate breaks** (the plan: a cell no code names processed, an all-teams code claiming every team, two people on one cell decided, the same person not recognised, a shorter spelling re-spelt, a new leader keeping the last one's number, an upgrade losing the number, two spellings not folded, a column the book lacks sent, the caller's scope ignored, the order of the rows, the writes not grouped, the way back losing the number and ID; the door: the word rule dropped, the way back not written first, an undo that overwrites a later change, a save that no longer runs the sync, a non-admin let in, one batch for every group, a preview that writes, the typed collection officer winning again, the tab gate, the audit list, the history list; the check: it writes, it is audited, it is recorded in the history; the screen: a view-only code asked to write, a write on every open, the list read before the sync, a name put into the page raw, the remembered list not dropped, the buttons not wired, `/api/me` without `readOnly`) each turn a test or the browser check red. `npm test` green.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) The save already had its own column rule and the first plan left it beside the new one: two definitions of one rule (now one). (2) The test of the all-teams code asserted only that no cell changed, and passed with a break that made two such codes claim every team (they were in conflict, so nothing changed): it now asserts the conflicts too. (3) One of my breaks of the screen's order was no break (the request left in the same order whichever way I wrote it) and was "missed": the check now has the sync answer late and shows a stale list to a screen that does not wait.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **Nothing live was seen**: the live book's first sync may change many cells and some of them may not be what the owner expected; the card is the review and Undo is the way back. (2) A code changed by an upload of the codes sheet or by hand reaches the sheet at the next open of Teams & Staff or the next save, not at that moment. (3) Two codes naming two people on one team are reported, never decided (the overlay of the three PMO units still lets the LAST code win on its own cells: unchanged, and no longer reachable once the sheet carries the cell). (4) A sheet name longer than its code's stays: the code's name is the owner's to lengthen. (5) Collection and legal officers stay on the code and are filled at read time. (6) The staff registry is not touched. (7) A leader who is on the sheet for teams their own code does not hold is told, not taken off: "unless not there".

## Part 122 — The second reader of #764: what it checked, what it found, what was changed and what was not (20 Nov)

> "please never stop until whats asked is done." and the order of Part 121 — the owner, 20 Nov 2026.

**How it was read.** After #764 merged and was live on both sites (`BUILD 2026-11-20-c`), with nothing owed to the owner, ONE independent reader (the rule of CHAT.md section 7: one at a time, only when nothing is owed, no team) was given the merged commit, the owner's words and the questions, and told to change nothing. It read the plan, the door, the screen and the tests, and ran its own scripts: the real `portalApi` over the repository's fake database, and the real `public/app.html` and `public/mod/admin.js` in one Chromium against the real `portalApi`. **Every finding below was reproduced by hand on the merged code before it was believed** (the reader's scripts were re-run: section 7's rule that a finding is read against the rule that governs it, and that a reproduction shows what the code does and the Part says whether that is wrong).

**What it found, and what was true.**

1. **Undo could not stick (the worst one).** The screen's `render()` after Undo asked `leadersCheck` first, the codes still said what they said, so the check found the same differences and the screen wrote them again: in the real page the calls after the click were `leadersSyncUndo → leadersCheck → leadersSync`, the book ended as it was before the Undo, the card said "3 leaders brought into line" and offered Undo again. Part 121 and CHAT.md called Undo "the way back": **that was false as merged.** The first browser check could not see it: its stub answered the check as "changed" for ever and only counted the Undo call.
2. **Rule 5 (a new person does not inherit the last leader's number and ID) did not hold on the road people use most.** `syncStaffFromCode`, which saves ONE code, wrote the name alone; the sync that follows saw the same name and skipped. A new person saved onto a team showed the previous leader's `gmo_no` and `gmo_id`.
3. **A number lent to a different person.** The number and ID were looked for by `looseSame`, so a bare JOHN on one team matched JOHN BETA on another and handed him JOHN ALPHA's number.
4. **The same person written with an apostrophe, an accent or another alphabet counted as a new person**: `wordsOf` split on anything outside A–Z0–9, so NG'SAMPLE and NGSAMPLE were different words, the cell was "replaced" and the number and ID blanked. (Two symbol-only names, or two different names in another alphabet, were taken for the same person, because both have no words.)
5. **Silence.** (a) The screen swallowed a failed check or sync: the list opened with the old leaders and nothing said so ("say what was not done", CLAUDE.md section 2). (b) `saveAccessCode` returned what the sync did and the form's handler read none of it. (c) A first big sync run by a code save never reached the card: a later open said "every leader agrees" and listed nothing, yet offered an Undo for cells the screen never showed.
6. `leadersCheck` was missing from `READ_FNS`: every open of Teams & Staff, even on a book that agrees, wiped the page's remembered screens.
7. **Smaller, all reproduced:** Undo put back a whole cell (name, number, ID) when only the name still matched, so a number typed since was lost, although the confirm text promised that a changed cell is left alone; Undo indexed the teams by their trimmed name, so a registry with `KONGOWE` and `KONGOWE ` as two rows restored one and answered "2 restored, 0 left"; **a Collection or Legal code with an empty name was shown as the officer's name, and the name is the access code, a password**, in every team it holds, to every viewer of the Teams tab (before #764 only in blank cells; "the code wins" made it every cell); a person with two codes of one role that together hold their teams was listed as "off their code"; a sync cut short by a failure left a log that the next sync overwrote with only the remaining cells, so the first part could no longer be undone; two codes that differ only in capitals wrote a spelling that depended on the order they came in.

**What was changed.**

- **Undo holds (plan rule 8).** Undo writes a HOLD for each cell it puts back — (team, role, the person the code named) — in the settings row `LEADERS_SYNC_HOLDS`, BEFORE the first cell is put back. The plan skips a cell while a code still names that same person there and reports it as `held`; the card lists them; **both roads respect them** (the sync and the save of one code share one matcher, `holdsOn`). A hold ends when no code names that person there any more (the write that sees it — a code save, a code deletion — lets it go) or when the owner presses **Sync now**, which says first that it will write what was undone, and sends `{ releaseHolds: true }`. A check never writes (the holds are read fresh, in the same one read as the log; a read that fails throws, because a look that could not see the holds must not go on to write what they forbid).
- **One rule for a cell that changes hands** (`handsOverPatch`, used by the plan and by the save of one code): the new name, and beside it the number and ID the same person already has on another team — **the same words only** (accents, apostrophes and punctuation aside; never a short form), and **only a value every such cell agrees on** — else nothing. The save road's rows now go in groups by the keys they carry (as the plan's always did).
- **Names:** `wordsOf` drops accents, drops an apostrophe instead of splitting on it, and reads the letters of any alphabet; a name with no words is nobody's "same person" (`same_`). A code that writes the same person with the same words another way (or fuller) now makes the sheet follow it (`respelt`, name only, number and ID stay); a code that writes the person SHORTER is still kept (rule 4). Two spellings with the same words are one claimant, not a conflict. A person's codes are pooled for "off their code".
- **Undo puts a cell back only if everything the sync wrote there is still there** (the log now keeps `wrote` beside `undo`; a log from before this change, with no `wrote`, is undone by the name cell as it was), reads the teams by the spelling the log was written under (twin rows stay two cells), and holds what it put back. A cell that was not put back is not held.
- **A cut-short sync is taken up by the next one:** the log says `done:false` until the last cell is written, and the next sync keeps the first part undoable (each cell keeps what it was BEFORE the first of them touched it); a look with nothing to do closes an unclosed log. One more settings write per sync that changed something.
- **The screen says what happened:** a failed check or sync is a card (the server's own words, as text, with Try again) and the list still opens; the card lists the cells held back and, when this open did not write them, the cells of the last sync (what Undo would put back); saving or deleting an access code says what the sheet did ("N leaders on Teams & Staff brought into line", conflicts, held, or the failure); `leadersCheck` is in `READ_FNS`. `BUILD 2026-11-20-d`.
- **Deleting an access code brings the sheet into line right away** (`deleteAccessCode` runs the sync, quiet on failure): that is how a stale code is put right, two codes stop disputing a team, and a hold on a claim nobody makes any more is let go.
- **A code with no name names nobody** (`portfolioByTeam_`): it is never shown as the Collection or Legal officer.
- **An admin scoped to some teams** neither judges nor lets go of the holds on the teams they may not change (found on a last read of this change: a sync by such an admin would have dropped them).

**Recorded, not changed.**
- **A stale code** (a person who left, code never deleted, still listing teams) is written onto those teams at every open; `access_codes` has no inactive or expiry column (checked against `db/schema.sql` and every migration). The way out is to delete the code, or take the teams off it; **Undo now holds**, so the owner can put the cells back and then fix the code; the first sync's card is the review. Whether a code should be able to be switched off without being deleted is the owner's to say (not built: a new rule).
- **Role words:** "BIKE RECOVERY", "RECOVERY MANAGER" and "EARLY RECOVERY SUPERVISOR" name the Recovery column (the words RECOVER/EXPECT/EARLY the boards' overlay always read), and the sync now writes what the overlay showed. Whether such roles exist live is not known.
- An edit made by hand on Teams & Staff to a cell a code names is written over at the next open: the card says so, and it is the owner's rule.
- The teams memos (15 s, portal and phone) and the phone's role map (60 s) are not dropped by any teams writer, `saveTeam` included: "right away" is within about a minute for the phone, as for every other change of the sheet.
- An explicit Sync now on a book that agrees writes one audit row and runs the history sync twice (the open path does neither): harmless.
- The same fallback `c.name || c.code` exists at other sites (`staffRoster`, the promise and commission boards, the call-agent roster): a blank name is only possible by SQL (the form requires one), they were not touched, and none lays a code over every team the way the Teams list now could.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call` (the reader traced the imports: `call.js` → `call-core.js` imports none of the changed modules; `upload.js` loads the plan as a pure module and calls no holder function). Opening Teams & Staff reads the teams, the codes and ONE settings query (log and holds together; it was a second, later read before: one wave less), and writes only what differs; a sync that changed something writes the log, the cells and the log again (closed). Saving a code reads the holds once more. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged.

**Checked.** `test/leaders-sync.test.mjs`: 57 tests (the 34 of Part 121, all still green, and 23 new: **21 of them fail on the merged code**; the other two guard the compatibility of an old log and a save that survives a failing sync); `tools/browser-checks/portal-leaders-real.mjs` (new: the real page against the real `portalApi`, 41 points; **19 of them fail on the code as merged**) beside the stub check of Part 121 (31 points, still green); **51 of 51 deliberate breaks** each turn a test or the browser check red (three were missed at first and the tests were strengthened: IDs that disagree, a name in another alphabet, a cut-short log merged with a cell written twice). `npm test` green.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) I wrote "Undo is the way back" in Part 121 and CHAT.md and tested it with a stub that could not show that it was not: the first check of a screen asks the SERVER, not a stub that says what the screen hopes to hear. (2) Rule 5 was written on one road and the commonest road was left as it was. (3) I took `looseSame`, built for a history of who held what, as strict enough to hand a person's number over on. (4) The first draft of the holds left the save road writing them back (found while designing the tests, before it shipped). (5) Two of the new tests' own expectations were wrong at first (a number can only be inherited from a cell that already carries the same words as stored), and three breaks were missed (above).

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) Nothing live seen. (2) The first sync's card is still the owner's to review; stale codes are the likeliest surprise. (3) A code changed by an upload or by hand reaches the sheet at the next open or save. (4) Two codes naming two people stay reported, not decided. (5) The staff registry is still not consulted (a person marked Inactive is still written if their code names a team). (6) The reader's list of role words is not checked against the live roles. (7) This change was read by its author and tested; it was not read by a second reader.

## Part 123 — The Postgres war, matter 4: the two fall-backs keep the last good answer for ten minutes instead of making the heavy read (20 Nov)

> "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. From their second `pg_stat_statements` paste (Part 120, addendum): the OLD reads that the two small database answers (RUN-ME-077 and RUN-ME-078) replaced were still running as often as the answers themselves: **917 s, 47% of the listed database time in a window of 3 h 43 min.**

**What it was.** `calledTodaySet` (`api/_lib/call-core.js`, under every officer's list) and `callBoardSource_` (`api/_lib/portal-core.js`, behind the Dashboard and the Presentation) each ask a small database function first and fall back to the heavy read it replaced when it fails, remembering the failure for five minutes (`CALLED_FN_PAUSE_MS`, `CALL_BOARD_PAUSE_MS`). **Every failure was treated alike**, so a single failed call (a statement cancelled at the role's limit, a full connection pool, a network error between the host and Supabase) meant five minutes of the heavy read for that server instance: the day's calls in pages every half minute, or the fifteen statements of a week board each time one was asked. That is the heavy read, made at exactly the moment the database was busy or unreachable.

**What was found, and what is not known.** The paste shows the old called-today read +389 runs (591 ms each) beside 386 runs of the function, and the old week read +810 runs (849 ms each, about 58 boards) beside 31 runs of the rollup. A search of every read of `call_logs` in `api/` finds those two statement shapes in no other place than the fall-backs, so those runs ARE the fall-backs. **Why the small answers fail is not known**: a failed statement is not in `pg_stat_statements`. A timeout (the rollup takes 3.0 s on average and 5.5 s at worst against a limit of about 8 s), a wait for a connection when the PostgREST pool is full of slow reads, and a network error would each fit; the Logs Explorer queries handed over in Part 120's addendum are what tells them apart.

**What was built: one rule, in two places.** `isTransient` (`api/_lib/supabase.js`: the definition of "the database is briefly unreachable" that the reader already retries on: a timeout, a cancelled statement, a full pool, the network, a gateway page) and `STALE_OK_MS` (ten minutes, defined once beside it).

- **[CHANGED in #769, Part 126: "transient" here is now `isBusyFailure`, a stricter test of its own, not the reader's loose retry test `isTransient`.]** **When the small answer fails and the failure is transient, the last good answer stands in for up to ten minutes, and the heavy read is not made.** The ten minutes are counted from when the answer was built; standing in never renews it.
- **Every other case is answered by the old read exactly as before:** a function that is not installed, one that is refused (`permission denied`), one that answers a shape it does not make, a scope or an instance with no good answer, and a failure that has lasted the ten minutes. A fault is not a bad moment: serving a stale answer for a fault would hide it.
- **The called-today set** (`calledTodaySet`): the stand-in is this instance's own entry for today, however it was built (by the function or by the old read after a first failure), and it goes on being added to by the instance's own syncs (`noteCalledToday`: an officer's own new call still ticks at once). **The threshold (`CALL_MIN_SECS`) is not compared:** it is read from the very database that is struggling and a failed read answers the default, so comparing it would send the heavy read exactly when the stand-in is wanted; if the owner changes it meanwhile, for ten minutes the set is the one it was. The failure memory is now `{ at, soft }`.
- **The week boards** (`callBoardFromDb_`): the last good answer is kept for each viewer's scope (the week, today and the teams: the three things the function is asked, so another scope, another day and another week never get this one's) and handed out marked `staleS`, its age in seconds, which the answer of `officerBoards` carries as `callsStaleS` only when the boards are an older answer. Only answers younger than ten minutes are kept when a new one is kept.
- **A failed small answer says why, in the server's own log** (`errWords`, `api/_lib/supabase.js`): one line for each failure (its code and message on one line, cut at 160 characters, and whether a held answer stands in or the old read answers), never on a good answer, and nothing from the five minutes of pause (the function is not asked then): `[call] called_phones_today did not answer: 57014 canceling statement due to statement timeout -- the database was busy or unreachable: ...` and `[boards] call_board_rollup did not answer: ...`. In Vercel: the project's Logs, searched for `did not answer`. Until now the reason was swallowed, and `pg_stat_statements` cannot say it (a cancelled statement is not in it): this is what will tell a timeout from a full pool from the network. The words are the database's own about a call whose arguments are dates, a number and team names: no customer data.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/call`: **no read added; reads fewer.** [CORRECTED the same evening, Part 126: not true of the called-today path while a held set stood in: each list request still made ONE `settings` read (the threshold, read before the function's pause was found out), 55 in 60 requests as the second reader measured it; "reads fewer" held for the heavy table only. Fixed in #769: nothing is read while a held set stands in.] Under a database that keeps failing, twelve minutes of an instance's lists cost ONE read of the day where each refresh cost one (17 refreshes in the test); on a good day nothing changes; a few comparisons and nothing in memory beyond what was already held. `/api/upload`: nothing. Portal: the boards keep one answer per scope for ten minutes (the officers' lines; about 100 KB for 300 officers, ESTIMATED, not measured). `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged. One `console.warn` on a failure path (at most once for each failure), nothing on a good answer. No front-end file, no `BUILD` or `CALL_BUILD` bump.

**What the owner will see.** Nothing on a good day. When the database is briefly unreachable: a call list may show a customer an officer's colleague has just rung as not yet rung, for up to ten minutes (the officer's own calls tick at once), and the Dashboard's and the Presentation's call boards may be up to ten minutes old. **The screen does not draw the age yet**: the answer carries it (`callsStaleS`). **How to see the effect:** in a few hours, the verification query already given: the old called-today read and the old week read should grow far more slowly than before (they were +389 and +810 in 3 h 43 min), and `called_phones_today` and `call_board_rollup` keep their small figures.

**Checked.** Twenty new tests (and the suite keeps its output quiet for the two log tags: `test/fake-db.mjs`): the stand-in for ten minutes (exactly ten minutes is not one), twelve minutes of failure costing one read, five kinds of bad moment (a returned error, a thrown one, a full pool, a gateway page, the network), the faults answered by the old read (not installed, refused, a wrong shape, nothing, a call that throws something that is not a bad moment; the board also in its pause), a cold instance, an officer's own call during the stand-in, yesterday's set (never) and a set built at another threshold (still stands in), a clock that went backwards, a board of another scope or day, a refused answer never kept, what the log line says in each case and that a good answer says nothing, `errWords` (one line, its code, cut at 160), and four source pins. **The new behaviour tests fail on the old source** (6 of the 16 called-today tests and 4 of the 6 board tests; the others pin what did not change: a fault is still answered by the old read, ten minutes exactly is not a stand-in). **39 deliberate breaks (31 of the stand-in and `STALE_OK_MS`, 8 of the log line) each turn a test red; 38 are caught by the behaviour tests alone, and one (the memory pruning of the board) only by its source pin, because the age check at read already refuses an old answer, so pruning cannot be seen from outside.** `npm test`: 1,954 pass.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) Three breaks were first caught by the pin and not by behaviour: a thrown fault (every board test used a returned error), the day in the board's scope key (masked by the age: the first test moved the clock a whole day; the new one builds at 23:55 and asks at 00:02, seven minutes old and still not served), and the pruning (equivalent). The tests were strengthened. (2) Two of the new board tests' own expectations were wrong at first: the answer cache keeps an answer a minute, so a request 41 seconds after one is not a new look; and the five minutes of pause belong to the whole process, so a second scope cannot be built by the function inside the first scope's pause. (3) My break script's pattern for "behaviour tests only" matched the pin test's title and hid a break for a while. (4) **The first form compared the set's threshold with the one just read, which would have sent the heavy read exactly when the settings read had failed in the same stall** (a failed read answers the default): found reading my own diff before the merge, and taken out with its test and pin.

**Not done, said plainly.** (1) **The failures themselves are not cured**: nothing here makes the function fail less often; the Logs Explorer queries name the statements. (2) A request that finds the set or the board expired still WAITS for the failing function (up to the role's limit, about eight seconds) before the stand-in is served; only the heavy read after it is gone. A budget race (as the ghost lookup has) would end that wait, and was not taken here: during a stall it would start another call for each list unless the calls were shared. (3) A cold instance with no set at all still makes the heavy read once. (4) A set built by the old read after a first failure also stands in for the ten minutes. (5) The screen does not say a board is old. (6) Nothing live seen; not read by a second reader.

## Part 124 — How the database is doing: the owner's first health reading (20 Nov, 18:23 East Africa time), and `db/RUN-ME-079` and `db/RUN-ME-080`

> "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. They ran the two Logs Explorer queries of Part 120's addendum in the SQL editor three times and got `42P01: relation "edge_logs" does not exist`, then the same for `postgres_logs`; they ran the health query below and pasted the table it prints.

**Why these two files.** `pg_stat_statements` lists only the statements that FINISHED: a statement cancelled at the role's limit is in none of its figures. The queries handed over to name those statements only exist in Supabase's Logs Explorer, and the owner works in the SQL editor, so they were dropped and what the SQL editor CAN show was built instead, from Postgres's own counters. **`db/RUN-ME-079-database-health-read-only.sql`**: one small table (database size and memory settings, connections, transactions committed and rolled back, cache hit percent, temp files, deadlocks, the limits each API role carries, and the eight biggest tables with how much of each is served from memory). **`db/RUN-ME-080-statements-that-spill-read-only.sql`**: the ten statements that wrote most to temp files and the ten that read most from disk, as Postgres normalises them (`$1`, `$2`: no customer name, number or amount), with DO blocks and other utility statements (the owner's own scripts, whose text can carry what was typed) left out. Both read-only, flush-left, plain ASCII, one statement, an END line, under 10,000 characters (CHAT.md section 7).

**What the owner's answer said** (counters since the cluster began; "counting since" printed n/a, so there is no reset date and no rate yet):

| line | value |
|---|---|
| database size | 2,858 MB |
| `shared_buffers` (a quarter of the compute's RAM) · `effective_cache_size` | 512 MB · 1,536 MB (a 2 GB machine, by inference) |
| connections open · `max_connections` | 26 · 90 |
| transactions committed · rolled back | 27,112,624 · 39,827 (0.147%) |
| cache hit, whole database | 99.76% |
| **temp files written** | **143,120 files, 1,640 GB** |
| deadlocks | 0 |
| role limits | `anon` 3 s; `authenticated` 8 s; **`authenticator` `statement_timeout` 8 s and `lock_timeout` 8 s**; `service_role` none; `postgres` a search path only |
| `defaulter_snapshots` | 1,980 MB: table pages from memory 92.5%, index pages 96.2% |
| `repayment_snapshots` · `call_logs` · `loans` | 473 MB (98.9%, 97.9%) · 182 MB (100%, 99.9%) · 47 MB (100%, 98.6%) |
| `defaulter_date_repair_log` · `defaulter_last_trans_repair_log` | 46 MB (97.8%, 99.6%) · 20 MB (96.4%, 99.7%) |
| `received_payments` · `followup_status` | 23 MB (99.9%, 98.3%) · 19 MB (100%, 99.5%) |

**Read** (inference marked).

1. **Memory is not badly short overall, and one table does not fit.** The cache hit is 99.76% for the whole database; the defaulter decks table is 1.98 GB against 512 MB of `shared_buffers` and is served from memory 92.5% of the time, the lowest of the book: anything that reads across its days (the Legal and Find customer searches, the owner's repair scripts of 16 and 17 Nov) goes to disk. A bigger machine is a decision the owner takes on the price and on this, and **no recommendation is made yet**: if statements are spilling (next), mending them is cheaper than buying memory for them.
2. **The temp files are the surprise: 1,640 GB, about 570 times the size of the whole database.** A statement that sorts or hashes more than its working memory writes temp files and runs several times slower (Part 71's review measured the ghost function's documented worst case, a disk spill, at about seven times slower). **Inference, not known:** the old paged reads (each page re-sorted the week by id: 122,556 statements in the paste of Part 120's addendum) and the heavy functions, much of which the Postgres-war matters of this day (#757 to #767) took away. RUN-ME-080 names the statements; the CURRENT rate is the difference between two runs of RUN-ME-079.
3. **The 8-second wall is Supabase's setting.** The role the app connects through carries `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` of 8 s (the app's `service_role` has none of its own, so by inference it works under that); the worst runs of 7,99x ms in the tables of Parts 115 and 120 agree with that wall. Not changed, not recommended.
4. **Failed requests:** 39,827 rolled back of 27.1 million, 0.147%, since the counters began. The card's 2,078 errors in 24 hours is the same kind of thing seen over a day; the rate needs two runs.
5. **The two repair logs are 66 MB** of undo copies of the date repairs, read by nothing in the app; they can be archived or dropped once the owner is sure the repairs will not be undone. Not urgent, not done.

**Cost.** Words and two read-only SQL files: no code that runs for a user, no `BUILD` bump, nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`.

**Checked.** `test/database-health.test.mjs`: seven pin tests (the form, read-only-ness and what each file reads, what RUN-ME-079 prints and in which order, what it says it is for, the records in these documents). `tools/db-checks/database-health.mjs`, run by hand on a PostgreSQL 16 scratch server (it needs one): RUN-ME-079 answers its rows in order, shows a role's `statement_timeout`, lists the eight biggest of twelve tables biggest first with a size and two percentages, does not count its own statement as running, counts a failed statement as a rollback more and a committed one as a commit more, changes nothing in a table or the catalogue after two runs, and **each of 6 deliberate breaks changes its answer or fails**; RUN-ME-080 names a statement made to spill, with what it wrote to temp and its values as `$1`, leaves out a DO block whatever was typed in it, answers ten rows at most in each ranking, and a break that keeps ONLY the scripts changes its answer.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) I asked for the figures three times through the Logs Explorer, in a place the owner does not work from: their standing order is SQL to paste, and the SQL that runs where they work should have come first. (2) The check's first spilling statement sorted an indexed column, so the planner read the index and nothing spilled; the check said so and the statement was changed.

**Not done, said plainly.** The spilling statements are not named (RUN-ME-080's answer is next); the rate of failed requests and of temp spill is not known (two runs of RUN-ME-079, an hour apart, give it); `work_mem` and its neighbours were not in the first run (a one-line `pg_settings` read was handed over beside RUN-ME-080); whether the compute size is the limit is not concluded; nothing was changed in the book.

## Part 126 — The second reader of #767: what it found, what was changed, and what was not (20 Nov)

> "please never stop until whats asked is done." — the owner, 20 Nov 2026 (CHAT.md section 2); and the rule of section 7: merge first, then one reader, nothing owed.

**The reader** (one, started after #767 had merged and was live; its own scripts on the merged code and a scratch PostgreSQL; the repository untouched) read the two stand-ins of Part 123 and the two SQL files of Part 124. **Every finding was reproduced by hand on the merged code before it was believed** (the reader's scripts, run again; the figures below are theirs, reproduced).

**What was true, and what was changed**

1. **"Reads fewer" was not true of the called-today path while a held set stood in.** `calledTodaySet` read the threshold (`CALL_MIN_SECS`, from `settings`) BEFORE it found out that the function was in its five minutes of pause, so every list request of those five minutes still made one read: 55 in 60 requests (one every 5 s), 271 in 296 (one a second). The heavy read of the table was gone, as claimed; "no read added" was false of these lists, and CLAUDE.md section 1 counts reads on `/api/call`. **Fixed:** the held set is handed out BEFORE anything is read while the pause that follows a busy failure is running: one `settings` read in the whole five minutes (the one before the first failure), then none (the same script again: 1 in 296).
2. **The kind of a failure was read back from memory another list might have overwritten.** `calledPhonesFromDb_` kept `{at, soft}` in a per-database memory and its caller read it back afterwards: when two lists meet different failures in the same instant (one a bad moment, one a fault) the first could read the second's and make the heavy read it was built to avoid. Reproduced by resolving two pending calls in one instant. **Fixed:** the call that saw the failure hands its own kind back (`{ phones, soft }`); the pause hands back the kind of the failure that began it. (The boards' path already used its own local value and was not affected.)
3. **The test for "briefly unreachable" was the loose retry test.** `isTransient` matches words anywhere in a message (it is meant to: a retry that is wrong costs nothing), so `22P02 invalid input syntax for type integer: "15022"` (it holds 502), `42703 column "network_id" does not exist`, `42501 permission denied for schema "timeouts"` and a bug of ours (`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'timeout')`) all stood in for ten minutes under a log line that said the database was busy; and two real bad moments, PostgREST's `PGRST002` (the schema cache) and a refused connection, did not stand in. **Fixed:** a new `isBusyFailure` (`api/_lib/supabase.js`), the stand-ins' own test, its whole definition a table in `test/busy-failure.test.mjs`. When the database NAMED the failure (a SQLSTATE or a PostgREST code) the name decides: busy are 57014 and 55P03 (a cancelled statement, a lock timeout), 40P01 and 40001 (a deadlock, a serialization failure), 57P01 to 57P03 (the server going away or starting), class 53 (no resources, such as no connection left), 08000, 08001, 08003, 08004, 08006 and 08007 (a connection that failed) and PGRST000 to PGRST003 (PostgREST cannot reach the database, the schema cache, the pool); every other code is the database naming a fault. Only with no such code are the words read, and then only the network's and a gateway's, never in a message that is a JavaScript fault of ours. `isTransient`, which decides retries, is unchanged in meaning (pinned).
4. **A failure that cannot be turned into words failed the LIST.** `isTransient`, `errWords` and the catch blocks called `String(...)` on whatever was thrown: a null-prototype object, or an object whose `toString` throws, made the list (and the boards) throw. Not a thing supabase-js does; a sacred path must not depend on that. **Fixed:** `isTransient` and `errWords` are exception-safe (`errWords` says "an error that cannot be read as words"), `isBusyFailure` never throws.
5. **The boards' scope key could collide.** Two team lists became one key when a team NAME held the character the key was joined with (U+0001): a viewer could be handed another scope's kept board. **Fixed:** the key is JSON.
6. **A gap in the tests, not in the code:** a board answer whose rows lack their figures (`{ w: [{ name: 'X' }], t: [] }`) was never tried as "kept". It is refused by the shape check; now pinned: never kept, never what stands in later.
7. **RUN-ME-080 would have leaked a literal.** Its filter was a blacklist of the kinds of statement to leave out (`do|create|alter|...`); Postgres keeps a `CALL`'s text with its arguments, and `call public.p767('SECRET SIX')` came back in the table. It is now a whitelist: only statements that begin SELECT, WITH, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE are listed (Postgres puts `$1` in place of their values). The kept check's DO-block test was vacuous (the block did not spill, so it was in no ranking whatever the filter said): it now uses a DO block and a CALL that really spill to temp, proves Postgres kept their literals, and fails on the first form of the filter. **The owner's run of the first form (18:30 East Africa time, Part 124) carried no literal:** every row is a PostgREST statement with `$1`, and one dashboard introspection query.
8. **RUN-ME-079 could wait behind a lock.** `pg_total_relation_size` takes a lock on every table it measures (and lets it go inside the call): behind a script that holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on one table the reading would hang. Sizes now come from the catalogue's page counts (`relpages` of the table, its TOAST and its indexes: about, as of the last vacuum or analyze). The kept check holds a lock from a second session and the reading must not wait; it fails on the first form. Nothing needs to be run again: the owner's run (18:23) returned.

**Recorded, not changed.**

- **`callsStaleS` is the age of the answer when it was MADE.** `officerBoards` answers are kept for a minute by the answer cache, so a board on a screen can be up to eleven minutes old (the ten, and the minute the cache holds it), and the figure it carries is its age when it was made. Nothing said so.
- **The pause is one for the whole process, per function** (Part 119): one scope's timeout pauses the function for every scope.
- **The retry loops (`runQuery`, `fetchAll`) retry a statement timeout up to three times.** For a statement that is always slow that triples what every request that meets it costs the database, at the moment it is struggling. An open question, **not changed** (it is the reader the whole app uses); to be read against the statements the recorder names (Part 127).

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** `/api/call`: reads fewer, for real this time (one `settings` read in a five-minute stand-in, where there was one for every request); nothing added; the stand-in's test is a few regular expressions on a failure that has already happened. `/api/upload`: nothing. `test/speed.test.mjs` unchanged. No front-end file, no `BUILD` or `CALL_BUILD` bump.

**Checked.** `test/busy-failure.test.mjs` (5 tests: the whole definition, case by case, with 11 things that are not errors and cannot be read); 4 new tests in `test/call.test.mjs` (nothing read while a set stands in; the race, reproduced by two pending calls resolved in one instant; unreadable failures; the reader's misclassified messages, and a fault inside the pause is still read), 4 in `test/call-board-rollup.test.mjs` (rows without figures; the colliding scope key; unreadable failures; the same classification), three source pins updated and made stricter; **14 of 14 deliberate breaks of the code each turn a test red**; the kept check `tools/db-checks/database-health.mjs` on a PostgreSQL 16 scratch server (a lock held by a second session; a DO block and a CALL that really spill); `npm test` green.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** (1) "No read added; reads fewer" (Part 123, #767, the PR body) was never measured with the setting read counted: my tests counted reads of `call_logs` only. (2) I took `isTransient` for the definition of "briefly unreachable" because it already existed: a definition made for retries is not one for hiding a fault. (3) The first form of the lock probe in the kept check looked in `pg_locks` after the call; the size functions release their lock inside the call, so it saw nothing and the check "failed" for the wrong reason: the probe that works holds a lock in a second session and waits. (4) One of my 14 breaks was first "not caught" because my break script filtered the tests by name and skipped the one that covers it.

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing live seen; the figures are the reader's and mine on test databases. The recorder (RUN-ME-081 to 083, run by the owner on 20 Nov) comes next, in its own change.

## Part 127 — The Postgres war, matter 5: the owner's RUN-ME-080 answer read, and the recorder that names the statements nothing else can (`db/RUN-ME-081`, `082`, `083`) (20 Nov)

> "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. They ran `db/RUN-ME-080` and the one-line settings read (about 18:30 East Africa time) and pasted both tables with no words; then ran the recorder (`db/RUN-ME-081`, about 18:53) and its two reads (`082`, `083`) once, seven minutes in, and pasted those too.

**Why a recorder.** `pg_stat_statements` lists only the statements that FINISHED: a statement cancelled at the role's 8-second limit is in none of its figures, and the Logs Explorer queries that would name them went into the SQL editor three times (Part 124). What the database CAN show, from the SQL editor, is the statements that are running NOW. So `RUN-ME-081` makes the database write down, by itself, every 5 seconds, any statement the app sent that has been running for more than 3 seconds (what it is, how long, what it is waiting for), and every minute the failed-request and temp-spill counters. After a working day two read-only files read it back.

**What the first one is** (`db/RUN-ME-081-recorder-of-slow-statements-and-failures.sql`, pasted in full in the chat, run once by the owner: its last line answered `schedule | 3`): `pg_cron` (Supabase's own scheduler; a background worker) runs three jobs: `ops-health-sample` (every minute: the counters of `pg_stat_database`: commits, rollbacks, temp files and bytes, deadlocks, cache blocks, connections, statements running), `ops-slow-sample` (every 5 seconds: one row for each statement that starts `WITH pgrst_source` (what PostgREST builds for the app) that has run longer than 3 seconds, kept up to date while it runs, with its table or function named) and `ops-retention` (3:17 each night: rows older than 14 days, and `pg_cron`'s own log older than 2 days, are deleted). They write only into two small tables of a schema of its own (`ops`, which the API does not expose). **What it records is only what PostgREST built: its text has `$1`, `$2` where values go, so no customer name, number or amount; a statement typed into the SQL editor is never recorded** (the filter is a WHITELIST: the second reader's finding about `RUN-ME-080`'s blacklist, Part 126, does not apply to it). **Undo, alone:** `select cron.unschedule('ops-health-sample'); select cron.unschedule('ops-slow-sample'); select cron.unschedule('ops-retention'); drop schema ops cascade;`.

**The two reads** (read-only, one small table each, no customer data): **`RUN-ME-082`** failed requests, temp spill and how busy, hour by hour in East Africa time (the transactions committed and rolled back in the hour, the rolled-back percent, the temp written, the most connections, the most statements running at once, and how many of the hour's minutes were recorded); **`RUN-ME-083`** the statements that ran longer than 3 seconds, one row for each shape, most often first (how many times, how many were still going after 7 seconds, the longest, what it was usually waiting for, the hours it was seen, and the first 260 characters of its text). **The first answers (about 19:00 East Africa time, seven minutes in): the 18:00 hour 2,083 committed and 2 rolled back (0.096%), 215 MB of temp written in 22 files, at most 26 connections and at most one statement running at once; `083` printed no row: in those seven minutes nothing the app sent ran longer than 3 seconds.** One quiet hour, not a working day: the reading that matters is the owner's tomorrow evening, after a day of work (section 8 of CHAT.md).

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** Nothing in the app changes: `/api/upload` and `/api/call` are untouched, no code that runs for a user is changed, no `BUILD` bump. The database does one small insert a minute and a read of its own session list every 5 seconds (it reads `pg_stat_activity`, which is in memory; it writes a row only when a statement has already run for more than 3 seconds, which on a quiet hour is never).

**What the owner's RUN-ME-080 answer says** (lifetime totals since the counters began; the first form of the file, whose filter leaked nothing here: every row is a PostgREST statement with `$1`, and one dashboard introspection query):

| What the statement is (by its columns and arguments) | Runs | Avg / worst | Written to temp | Read from disk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the old week read of `call_logs` (officer, team, duration ...), the dashboard's and the Presentation's call boards | 122,556 | 579 ms / 7,654 ms | **768 GB** | 17 GB |
| a calendar-window function `(p_from, p_to, p_teams, p_lookback)` | 176,243 | 231 ms / 7,662 ms | 88 GB | 97 GB |
| a read of `defaulter_snapshots` | 13,977 | 339 ms / 3,764 ms | 52 GB | 323 MB |
| a function `(p_dates, p_teams, p_lookback)` (not declared in this repository: an older one) | 560 | 2,659 ms / 7,996 ms | 35 GB | 39 GB |
| a window function `(p_from, p_to, p_teams, p_lookback)` | 921 | 1,338 ms / 7,859 ms | 20 GB | 13 GB |
| a read of `defaulter_snapshots` | 3,726 | 314 ms / 6,184 ms | 18 GB | 13 MB |
| a window function `(p_from, p_to, p_teams, p_lookback)` | 1,677 | 1,032 ms / 7,890 ms | 17 GB | 113 MB |
| the dashboard's own introspection query (`with f as (...)`) | 807 | 202 ms / 1,034 ms | 3,562 MB | 91 MB |

The settings read: `work_mem` 5 MB, `maintenance_work_mem` 128 MB, `temp_file_limit` unlimited, `jit` off, `max_connections` 90, `random_page_cost` 1.1.

**Read** (inference marked).

1. **The old week read is 768 GB of the 1,640 GB written to temp: 47% of everything the database ever spilled.** That is the read `db/RUN-ME-078` replaced on the same day (Part 116): the Dashboard and Presentation boards now come from one small answer, and the old read is the fall-back only. The lifetime total therefore OVERSTATES today's spill: whether the spill has stopped is what the hour-by-hour temp column of `RUN-ME-082` shows over a working day (the 18:00 hour wrote 215 MB in seven minutes: one quiet hour). The top ten statements wrote 1,006 GB, 61% of the total.
2. **Most of the rest is the calendar-window functions** (the three `(p_from, p_to, p_teams, p_lookback)` rows, 125 GB of temp and 110 GB read from disk between them, one of them 176,243 runs) and two reads of `defaulter_snapshots` (70 GB). They are the calendar-window functions and the follow-up list of the list in Part 115 (its numbers were reused since: the phone index took 3a to 3c and the fall-backs took 4), not started: **the recorder will say which of them are the ones that are cancelled at 8 seconds**, which `pg_stat_statements` cannot.
3. **`work_mem` is 5 MB** (the database's own setting; the 8-second limit and the temp limit are Supabase's too). A statement that sorts or hashes more than that writes a temp file and runs several times slower. **A scoped fix exists and is NOT built:** `ALTER FUNCTION ... SET work_mem = '<more>'` for the functions that spill (the first candidate is `call_board_rollup`, which spilled about 47 MB a call on the scratch book: a figure from the scratch book, NOT a live one), so one function gets more memory for its own statements and nothing else changes. It is read from the recorder's data first, then measured on the scratch book, then offered.
4. **Not in the table, and said:** the upload's own write, `INSERT INTO defaulter_snapshots` (8,590 runs, 445 ms on average, 5,279 ms at worst, 32 GB read from disk), and the phones' `INSERT INTO call_logs` (836,870 runs, 16 ms each, 15 GB read). Both are the sacred paths' own writes and are NOT touched. **An open question, not measured:** whether the two trigram indexes of `RUN-ME-054` (the Legal tab's search, 165 MB and 73 MB on the live table) add to the upload's write cost; they were measured for the search, never for the insert.
5. **An open question the recorder can answer: the retry loops.** `runQuery` and `fetchAll` retry a statement that failed with a timeout (the words `canceling statement` are in the retry test): up to three tries. For a statement that always takes more than 8 seconds that triples what every request that meets it costs the database, at the moment it struggles. If so, `RUN-ME-083` shows the same statement three times within a few seconds (its header says how to read it). **Nothing was changed**: the loop is the reader the whole app uses.

**Checked.** `test/recorder.test.mjs` (6 tests: the files are blocks the owner can paste, small and flush-left with their END lines; the setup's three jobs with their schedules; what is recorded and what never is (a whitelist); the two reads; the undo; this record). `tools/db-checks/recorder.mjs`, run by hand on a PostgreSQL 16 scratch server with `pg_cron` (it needs one, and takes about five minutes because it waits for the clock): the setup runs whole as one text and again harmlessly; statements built the way PostgREST builds them (a select, an insert, an rpc) that run past 3 seconds are recorded once each, kept up to date while they run, with their table or function named; a plain select and a DO block with words typed in it are never recorded; the health rows arrive a minute apart; the two reads answer on what was recorded; the nightly cleanup removes what is older than 14 days and keeps the rest; a setup in a database that cannot schedule fails and creates nothing; the undo removes everything; every one of a list of deliberate breaks of the setup makes a check fail (16 checks, all passed on a quiet machine). **It waits for the clock, so it must be run ALONE:** started beside a full `npm test` it recorded two of its three statements (the `pg_cron` worker ran late) and three checks failed; and its first form depended on a row an earlier run had left in a scratch table (`t_x`: `select pg_sleep(14) from t_x` sleeps only if there is a row), so on a clean database it could never have passed: the check's own setup now puts the row there.

**Mistakes of mine, said plainly.** I asked for the Logs Explorer queries in the first place and then three times again, in a place the owner does not work from (Part 124); the recorder is what should have come first. And the first `pg_cron` setting of the scratch server failed to start the server because two preload libraries were quoted as one string (found at the first start, not in the files); and the recorder's kept check had been trusted from one pass: it passed because of what an earlier run had left behind, and it failed the first time it ran on a busy machine (above).

**Not done, said plainly.** Nothing live seen beyond the seven minutes above; the statements cancelled at 8 seconds are still not named (the recorder will, after a working day); the 1,000-row cap of the ghost lookup, the region of the app against the database, the compute size and the two repair logs (66 MB) are the same open items as before (section 8 of CHAT.md).

## Part 127, addendum — the owner's re-runs of the corrected `db/RUN-ME-079` and `db/RUN-ME-080`, 83 and 76 minutes after the first (20 Nov, 19:46 East Africa time)

> "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026. They asked for the text of the two files ("(RUN-ME-080) & (RUN-ME-079) text?"), ran the corrected forms of Part 126 in new tabs at 19:46 and pasted both tables with no words. The first answers were 079 at 18:23 and 080 at about 18:30.

**The two files work on the live book.** 079's table sizes now come from the catalogue's page counts, taken without a lock on any table, and agree with the first run (`defaulter_snapshots` 1,980 MB with 92.5% of its table pages served from memory; the two repair logs 45 and 19 MB, where the exact functions had said 46 and 20). 080's whitelist printed only PostgREST statements and the dashboard's own introspection query. "Counting since" reads `n/a`: the counters have never been reset, so every total is since the database began, not since the app moved.

**A quiet evening, not a working day** (inference marked). In the 83 minutes since the first 079: rolled-back transactions 39,827 → 39,851 (+24; 0.147% of all, unchanged); temp files 143,120 → 143,363 (+243, about 3 a minute: the recorder's 22 files in 7 minutes at 18:00 is the same pace); temp bytes 1,640 → 1,642 GB (about +2 GB: each end is rounded to the GB, so 1 to 3); cache hit 99.76%, unchanged; 21 of 90 connections open and no statement running; no deadlock. So the 1,640 GB since the counters began came from working days, mostly the old week read. ## Part 127, addendum 4 — the upload's page reads, measured on a scratch copy of the deck table: the random uuid primary key is half of them, and a time-ordered id (`db/RUN-ME-085`, offered, NOT run) cuts one day's two decks by 37%

> "postgress war please; and that shouldnt distract efficiency of system operations" — the owner, 20 Nov 2026, and CLAUDE.md section 1: the upload never slows down. Addendum 3 (point 3) found the upload's insert into `defaulter_snapshots` at 1,279 ms a statement over its last 88 runs against 445 ms over its life, cause not known, and promised the measurement of what each index of that table costs a chunk. This is it.

**The scratch book** (`tools/db-checks/upload-index-cost/`, a disposable cluster of its own, about two minutes to build): the real `defaulter_snapshots` (`db/schema.sql`), 2.13 million rows laid out day after day as uploads write them (110 days, an initial and a current deck each, about 9,500 loans on a deck, a loan on the decks 30 to 90 days), and every index the live book has: the primary key, `idx_def_snap_lookup`, `_ref` (ref, snapshot_date), `_batch`, `_date`, RUN-ME-055's `_team_ref`, RUN-ME-054's two trigram indexes and RUN-ME-076's partial index (nine in all). 617 MB of table and 975 MB with its indexes against 400 MB of shared buffers: about the live ratio (live: 1.98 GB against 512 MB). The measurement is a chunk of 1,000 rows (`WRITE_CHUNK_MAX`, `api/upload.js`) inserted as `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL)` of an `INSERT ... SELECT`, ten chunks of an initial deck and ten of a current deck for each configuration, from a cold start (the cluster is restarted so the first chunk finds nothing in memory), with each index's own block counters read before and after every chunk. The unit is **pages read from outside shared memory**, which is what a cold disk is paid in and what the live `shared_blks_read` counts. A configuration is the book with some indexes dropped or the id's default changed: an index's cost is the difference of two.

| Configuration (pages read, ten chunks of 1,000 rows) | initial deck | current deck | one day, both | write-ahead log |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **as now (nine indexes)** | 14,323 | 8,665 | **22,988** | 168 MB |
| **time-ordered id (UUID version 7)** | 8,198 | 6,273 | **14,471 (-37%)** | 118 MB |
| no partial index (RUN-ME-076) | 14,394 | 5,603 | 19,997 (-13%) | 146 MB |
| no trigram indexes (RUN-ME-054) | 14,374 | 5,788 | 20,162 (-12%) | 147 MB |
| both of those gone (the book before 12 Nov) | 14,390 | 2,773 | 17,163 (-25%) | 124 MB |
| time-ordered id, no partial index | 8,198 | 3,251 | 11,449 (-50%) | 95 MB |
| time-ordered id, no trigram indexes | 8,191 | 3,394 | 11,585 (-50%) | 96 MB |
| time-ordered id, neither of the two | 8,191 | 372 | 8,563 (-63%) | 73 MB |
| no `(ref, snapshot_date)` index | 8,499 | 8,639 | 17,138 (-25%) | 124 MB |
| the primary key alone | 6,585 | 2,740 | 9,325 (-59%) | 59 MB |
| rows sorted by team and ref inside the deck | 14,356 | 6,465 | 20,821 (-9%) | 164 MB |

**What it says.**
1. **The table's own id is the biggest single cost.** `id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid()` puts every new row in a random leaf page of the primary key: about 1,000 distinct pages for 1,000 rows on a cold cache, 569 a chunk once the cache is warm, which is **about half of every chunk's reads** (48% of an initial chunk's 1,197 and 45% of a current chunk's 503 on the per-index counters; 616 and 260 to 283 when it is the only index left). A time-ordered id puts every new row at one moving edge of the index (the same property `idx_def_snap_date` has), and its reads drop to nothing: 628 an initial chunk (-48%) and 267 a current chunk (-47%) once warm, 1,842 and 1,621 on the cold first chunk (-35% and -18%), and the write-ahead log 168 to 118 MB a day (each first touch of a page after a checkpoint writes the whole page).
2. **After that the order is:** for an initial deck, `idx_def_snap_ref` (ref, snapshot_date), 510 reads a chunk, 81% of what is left; for a current deck, **RUN-ME-076's partial index** (+223 a chunk once warm, +907 on a cold first chunk: 503 against 280 without it) and **a flush of the two trigram indexes' pending lists** (one chunk in about fifteen reads 650 pages more and takes twice as long; +63 a chunk on average). The indexes that follow the date (lookup, batch, date) cost nothing: they only append.
3. **My own part, said plainly.** RUN-ME-076 was measured on 20 Nov warm, on a CPU basis ("+20% of a deck day"), and its header said so. Counted cold in pages it adds 80% to a current chunk's reads (and a current deck's first chunk reads 1.9 times as much). With RUN-ME-054's two indexes (12 Nov, never measured for the insert) the two are **68% of a current deck's reads** (8,665 against 2,773). I under-measured the cost of an index on the table the upload writes: the lesson of CHAT.md section 7 (count pages, in the worst layout) was written for reads and applies to writes too.
4. **What they buy, so that the trade is seen whole.** RUN-ME-076 took the ghost lookup from 240 ms to 44 ms a run (3,413 runs in 19 hours, each inside the phone's 800 ms budget), and RUN-ME-054 took the Legal customer search from about 3.3 s to about 0.2 s (16 runs in the same hours). At a live disk's 0.5 to 1 ms a read, what they add to a day's current deck is about 3 to 6 seconds; a time-ordered id takes about 4 to 8 seconds off the day's two decks. **Recommended:** the time-ordered id (nothing is lost for it); keep both indexes unless the owner's `RUN-ME-084` shows one of them is read by nothing; decide on the live numbers, never here.
5. **Sorting a deck by team and ref before writing it gains nothing** (-9%, and worse on its own in the later chunks): the three ref-keyed indexes want three different orders and a chunk covers a tenth of the key space either way. Not built, and not to be proposed again without a new reason.
6. **Does it fit the live observation?** The cold first chunk reads 2,000 to 2,900 pages on the scratch book (500 to 1,200 once warm) and the live statement read 1,400 to 4,300 (11 to 34 MB, addendum 3): the same order of magnitude. At 0.5 to 1 ms a page that is the 1.3 s a statement. **An inference, not a proof:** this machine's operating-system cache holds the whole book, so reads are counted and never timed, an index grown by years of inserts is more fragmented than one built in one go, and the live machine has other load. What carries over is the shape: which indexes cost reads, and how many pages more.

**What was built.** `db/RUN-ME-085-time-ordered-ids-for-the-deck-table.sql` (offered, NOT run; 3.3 KB; five statements, flush-left, ends `-- END OF RUN-ME-085`): `set local lock_timeout = '500ms'`, a SQL function `public.hope_uuid_time_ordered()` (a version 7 UUID: the 48-bit millisecond clock first, the version nibble 7, 74 random bits from `gen_random_uuid()`; volatile, so each row gets its own), a `grant execute ... to public` (so the API role can run it on a book that takes new functions from PUBLIC), `alter table public.defaulter_snapshots alter column id set default public.hope_uuid_time_ordered()`, and a select that answers the new default (`hope_uuid_time_ordered()`). **No row is rewritten and nothing else about the table changes**: an existing row keeps its id, the app builds no id (the deck importer sets none and the upload writes the table by plain insert), and ordering by id (the pager's tie-break) stays a total order. **Its cost, written beside it: the ALTER takes the table's heaviest lock for an instant**, so it waits at most 500 ms for it and gives up changing NOTHING (the SQL editor runs a script as one transaction, so the function is not made either); a query that arrives meanwhile waits at most that half second; it is run in a quiet minute, not during an upload, and again if it says "lock timeout". PostgREST reads its schema again in the background (about 0.2 s of work). **Undo, one line, alone:** `alter table public.defaulter_snapshots alter column id set default gen_random_uuid();`. **Checked** (`tools/db-checks/time-ordered-ids.mjs`, a PostgreSQL made from the whole of `db/schema.sql`, a book that takes new functions away from PUBLIC, a plain role standing for the API's): the file runs as one transaction and answers one row; 20,000 ids made in one statement are all version 7, variant 8 to b, within ten seconds of now, never going back, and 200,000 are all different; the API role writes 5,000 rows by default, as PostgREST does (an insert that names its columns, from `json_populate_recordset`), all version 7 and all different, 1,000 consecutive new ids sharing their first sixteen bits where random ones share nothing; the 3,000 old rows keep their ids byte for byte and the table has the same indexes, constraints and columns; with a reader holding the table the file gives up in 0.5 s with "lock timeout" and changes nothing; it can be run again; the undo works; **9 of 9 deliberate breaks each caught for their own reason** (an equivalent mutant, the clock read once per statement instead of per row, was dropped and is said in the check). `test/time-ordered-ids.test.mjs` pins its form, the one table it touches, the half-second wait, that it rewrites nothing, the function's bits, the numbers and the undo line (6 tests). **Kept, so the next chat can measure again:** `tools/db-checks/upload-index-cost/` (`build.sh` and `measure.mjs`, with the cluster's settings in the header: a measurement, not part of `npm test`).

**Mistakes of mine.** The first form of `RUN-ME-085` had an explicit `begin` and `commit`, which no earlier file used (they rely on the editor's single transaction for `set local`); taken out. The kept check's first lock-down fixture used a schema-level default privilege, which can only add to what PostgreSQL grants PUBLIC, so the break that removes the explicit grant was "caught" for the wrong reason (state left over from the break before) until the fixture and the cleaning between breaks were fixed; the break "wrong table" first changed the undo line in the comment instead of the statement. The reader's backend of the lock test went on sleeping, lock and all, after its client was killed, and failed the next run: it is now ended.

**Cost, CLAUDE.md section 1.** Words, one SQL file offered and two measurement tools: nothing in the app changes, `/api/upload` and `/api/call` are untouched, no `BUILD` bump. **If the owner runs `RUN-ME-085`:** the upload's reads fall (the measured saving, by the shape), the call app is touched only by the half second of the lock and the background schema reload, and nothing is lost.

**Not done, said plainly.** `RUN-ME-085` is not run and not decided. The saving in seconds on the live book is NOT known (the shape is measured, the live disk is not). `repayment_snapshots` (the Expected sheet, also written by an upload) has the same random uuid key and the same remedy: unmeasured, so not offered. `call_logs` takes the app's own hashed id and is not touched. No index was dropped or proposed to be dropped; `idx_def_snap_ref` (81% of an initial chunk's remaining reads) and the two new indexes wait for the owner's `RUN-ME-084` (how often anything reads each). The 385 quick failures are still not named.

## Part 128 — The Legal tab's weekly recovery card gets week arrows: last week(s) report is one press away (23 Nov)

> "Legal recovery weekly report at the top right card should have foward and backward arrows so that we get last week(s) reports" — the owner, 23 Nov 2026.

**Which card.** The Legal tab (Demand notices) draws a row of cards that ends, at the top right, with *Imerejeshwa wiki hii / Recovered this week* (`lgRecW`: the week's recovery by the customers served notices, with its Rec % in front); tapping it opens the list of the customers and payments behind it (`legalRecoveriesDrawer_`, the owner's "clickable to show list of the recoveries", Part 26's sibling). **Both were this week's, always**: `demandNotices` and `legalRecoveries` read `weekMondayKey(nowMs)` and nothing else. The dashboard is different: its *Legal recovery* card, its two Legal boards and the board's **[Report]** button (Part 26) all follow the dashboard's own week bar (`weekBar`: ◀ ▶, a date, "Back to this week", the owner's "backward and forward should both work"), so last week's Legal figures were already reachable there. The gap was the Legal tab, so the arrows went there; **if the dashboard's card was the one meant, its arrows are the week bar at the top of the dashboard** (said to the owner in the same message that delivered this).

**What was built.**

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `legalRecoveries(period, weekOf)` (`api/_lib/portal-core.js`) | reads any week: `weekOf` is a date inside it (the dashboard's own rule, `asOfWeek`: any day names its Monday); blank, unreadable (`2026-13-45`, `next week`, a number, an object) or **a week that has not begun** is this week, since nobody has paid in it. `period: 'today'` ignores a week. Answers `weekOf` (the Monday that was read) and `legal`, the card's reading of that week. **Another week is read without the fold** (`fold: mon === thisMon`): the fold copies the live book's payments into the ledger, the tab folded when it opened and every dashboard read folds, so what is filed for a week that has gone is all there is to read: **two trips where this week takes three**. |
| `legalCard_`, `legalSince_` | the ONE object the card is drawn from: `legalTotals_` (the dashboard card's own fold) plus `today`, `mon`, `sun`, `thisWeek` (the forward arrow's ceiling) and `since` (the Monday of the earliest notice in scope: the backward arrow's floor; a notice with no readable date is passed over, never trusted). `demandNotices` builds the tab's card from the same function, so the card on first paint and the card after any arrow press are one shape. |
| `lgWeekCard_(lg)` (`public/app.html`) | draws the card of ONE week: **◀ ▶ in its corner** (two `.lgwkb` buttons, `position:absolute`), forward off at this week, backward off at the first notice, both off without the ledger (the note is shown, escaped); lit (`.kpi.tap.on`) with its own name (*Imerejeshwa wiki iliyopita / Recovered, past week*) and a way home when it is not this week. It carries its own state (`data-mon`, `data-this`, `data-since`) and **inline handlers**: a table search or sort repaints the whole screen from `HEAD` and drops whatever `wireForms()` attached (found while building; see below), so the card does not depend on `wireForms`. |
| `lgWeekPaint_`, `lgWeekGo_`, `lgWeekStep_` | a reading goes on the screen **and into `HEAD`** (between the `<!--lgw-->` markers `VIEWS.legal` writes), so a repaint brings back the week the reader chose and not this one; a press asks `lgWeekAsk_` (answers kept two minutes per week: stepping back and forth asks the server once; a failed read is not kept); **a press made while an answer is still on its way steps from THAT week** (two quick presses are two weeks, not one), **an answer that comes back after the reader moved on is dropped**, a failure is said (`toast`) and leaves the card where it was, not dimmed. |
| `legalRecoveriesDrawer_(period, weekOf)` | the list takes a week: the same ◀ ▶ and a way home at its top (`lgWeekBar_`), the card behind it painted with the week the list is on, and **the week in the title of its Excel / JPG / CSV** so a download of last week's list says whose week it is. A tap on the card opens the week the card is ON (`lgWeekOpen_`). Today's card is unchanged. |
| `public/mod/legal.js` | draws the weekly card through `lgWeekCard_` and forgets what the arrows remembered each time the tab reads the register afresh (so opening the tab shows this week). `BUILD 2026-11-23-a`. |

**Rules kept, so nobody has to look again.** *One definition:* for any week the Legal tab's card equals the dashboard's Legal card for that week (customers, owed, recovered, Rec %): a test asks both for three weeks and compares. *The card is the list's total* (same fold, same scoped notices; a source pin holds that the card is never read off a wider set than the list under it). *Team scope* is unchanged (the database filter, then `scoped()`), for any week. *Nothing on `/api/upload` or `/api/call`.*

**Not changed, said plainly: past weeks are read with TODAY's register.** A customer served a notice AFTER a past week still stands in that week's customers and owed (their payments cannot, a payment is only counted from its notice's date), so a past week's Rec % can read lower than it did when the week ended. **The dashboard reads its own past weeks the same way** (`legalTotals_` over every notice in scope, the figure and the arrow of that week), and the two screens must say one thing; reading "as it stood on the Sunday" would change the dashboard's past weeks too, and nobody asked for that. It is the owner's to say (CHAT.md section 8).

**Found while building, not part of the ask: a table repaint drops what `wireForms()` attached.** `paint()` rebuilds `#view` whole (HEAD and the table), and `wireForms()` runs only from `drawView_()`, so after a table search or sort on a screen the elements wired there are new and unwired. **Verified in a real browser on the code as it stood before this change:** on the Legal tab, after one keystroke in the table's search box, the *Recovered today* card no longer opens its list and **+ New demand notice** no longer opens the form (both work before the search). The same holds for every element a screen puts in `HEAD` and `wireForms()` wires, on every screen that has a table search or a sort. **Not fixed here:** re-running `wireForms()` after every repaint would change every screen at once and needs its own careful reading of that long function (what it attaches, what it starts, what it does once per keystroke), so it is offered as its own matter (CHAT.md section 8); the weekly card is built so as not to depend on it (that it survives a table search is point 3 of `tools/browser-checks/portal-legal-week.mjs`); the two that do not survive were probed by hand, on the code as it was and on this change, with the same result.
